cards.subject: sociology
cards.unit: The Challenges of Unity in Diversity
cards.front: The term ‘diversity’ emphasises ____ rather than inequalities.
cards.back: The term ‘diversity’ emphasises differences rather than inequalities.
cards.quote: The term ‘diversity’ emphasises differences rather than inequalities.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.unit: The Challenges of Unity in Diversity
cards.front: What does ‘cultural diversity’ mean, as NCERT uses it for India?
cards.back: When we say that India is a nation of great cultural diversity, we mean that there are many different types of social groups and communities living here. These are communities defined by cultural markers such as language, religion, sect, race or caste.
cards.quote: When we say that India is a nation of great cultural diversity, we mean that there are many different types of social groups and communities living here. These are communities defined by cultural markers such as language, religion, sect, race or caste.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.note: Many distinct groups, marked by language, religion, sect, race or caste, live together in one country.

cards.subject: sociology
cards.unit: The Challenges of Unity in Diversity
cards.front: Sometimes cultural differences are accompanied by economic and social ____, and this further complicates things.
cards.back: Sometimes cultural differences are accompanied by economic and social inequalities, and this further complicates things.
cards.quote: Sometimes cultural differences are accompanied by economic and social inequalities, and this further complicates things.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.unit: The Challenges of Unity in Diversity
cards.front: Which scarce resources does NCERT say make cultural diversity harder to manage?
cards.back: The situation is made worse when scarce resources – like river waters, jobs or government funds – have to be shared.
cards.quote: The situation is made worse when scarce resources – like river waters, jobs or government funds – have to be shared.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.unit: The Challenges of Unity in Diversity
cards.front: What is community identity?
cards.back: Community identity is based on birth and ‘belonging’ rather than on some form of acquired qualifications or ‘accomplishment’. It is what we ‘are’ rather than what we have ‘become’.
cards.quote: Community identity is based on birth and ‘belonging’ rather than on some form of acquired qualifications or ‘accomplishment’. It is what we ‘are’ rather than what we have ‘become’.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.unit: The Challenges of Unity in Diversity
cards.front: What are ‘ascriptive’ identities?
cards.back: These kinds of identities are called ‘ascriptive’ – that is, they are determined by the birth and do not involve any choice on the part of the individuals concerned.
cards.quote: These kinds of identities are called ‘ascriptive’ – that is, they are determined by the birth and do not involve any choice on the part of the individuals concerned.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.unit: The Challenges of Unity in Diversity
cards.front: Our community provides us the language (our mother tongue) and the cultural values through which we comprehend the world. It also anchors our ____.
cards.back: Our community provides us the language (our mother tongue) and the cultural values through which we comprehend the world. It also anchors our self-identity.
cards.quote: Our community provides us the language (our mother tongue) and the cultural values through which we comprehend the world. It also anchors our self-identity.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.unit: The Challenges of Unity in Diversity
cards.front: Name the circles of community ties NCERT lists.
cards.back:
family
kinship
caste
ethnicity
language
region
religion
cards.quote: Expanding and overlapping circles of community ties (family, kinship, caste, ethnicity, language, region or religion) give meaning to our world and give us a sense of identity, of who we are.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.unit: The Challenges of Unity in Diversity
cards.front: That is why people often react emotionally or even violently whenever there is a perceived ____ to their community identity.
cards.back: That is why people often react emotionally or even violently whenever there is a perceived threat to their community identity.
cards.quote: That is why people often react emotionally or even violently whenever there is a perceived threat to their community identity.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.unit: The Challenges of Unity in Diversity
cards.front: A second feature of ascriptive identities and community feeling is that they are ____.
cards.back: A second feature of ascriptive identities and community feeling is that they are universal.
cards.quote: A second feature of ascriptive identities and community feeling is that they are universal.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.unit: The Challenges of Unity in Diversity
cards.front: What is a nation, at the simplest level?
cards.back: At the simplest level, a nation is a sort of large-scale community – it is a community of communities. Members of a nation share the desire to be part of the same political collectivity.
cards.quote: At the simplest level, a nation is a sort of large-scale community – it is a community of communities. Members of a nation share the desire to be part of the same political collectivity.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.unit: The Challenges of Unity in Diversity
cards.front: What does the desire for political unity among members of a nation usually express itself as the aspiration to form?
cards.back: Members of a nation share the desire to be part of the same political collectivity. This desire for political unity usually expresses itself as the aspiration to form a state.
cards.quote: Members of a nation share the desire to be part of the same political collectivity. This desire for political unity usually expresses itself as the aspiration to form a state.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.unit: The Challenges of Unity in Diversity
cards.front: What does the term ‘state’ refer to, in its most general sense?
cards.back: In its most general sense, the term state refers to an abstract entity consisting of a set of political-legal institutions claiming control over a particular geographical territory and the people living in it.
cards.quote: In its most general sense, the term state refers to an abstract entity consisting of a set of political-legal institutions claiming control over a particular geographical territory and the people living in it.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.unit: The Challenges of Unity in Diversity
cards.front: Define the state (Max Weber).
cards.back: In Max Weber’s well-known definition, a state is a “body that successfully claims a monopoly of legitimate force in a particular territory” (Weber 1970:78).
cards.quote: In Max Weber’s well-known definition, a state is a “body that successfully claims a monopoly of legitimate force in a particular territory” (Weber 1970:78).

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.unit: The Challenges of Unity in Diversity
cards.front: What is an ethnic group (NCERT)?
cards.back: an ethnic group (based on common descent in addition to other commonalities of language or culture)
cards.quote: an ethnic group (based on common descent in addition to other commonalities of language or culture)

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.unit: The Challenges of Unity in Diversity
cards.front: The criterion that comes closest to distinguishing a nation is the ____.
cards.back: The criterion that comes closest to distinguishing a nation is the state.
cards.quote: The criterion that comes closest to distinguishing a nation is the state.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.unit: The Challenges of Unity in Diversity
cards.front: Why are ‘nation’ and ‘state’ joined with a hyphen to form the term nation-state?
cards.back: Unlike the other kinds of communities mentioned before, nations are communities that have a state of their own. That is why the two are joined with a hyphen to form the term nation-state.
cards.quote: Unlike the other kinds of communities mentioned before, nations are communities that have a state of their own. That is why the two are joined with a hyphen to form the term nation-state.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.unit: The Challenges of Unity in Diversity
cards.front: What do ‘dual citizenship’ laws allow?
cards.back: These laws allow citizens of a particular state to also – simultaneously – be citizens of another state.
cards.quote: These laws allow citizens of a particular state to also – simultaneously – be citizens of another state.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.unit: The Challenges of Unity in Diversity
cards.front: How can a nation be defined today, according to NCERT?
cards.back: In short, today it is hard to define a nation in any way other than to say that it is a community that has succeeded in acquiring a state of its own.
cards.quote: In short, today it is hard to define a nation in any way other than to say that it is a community that has succeeded in acquiring a state of its own.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.unit: The Challenges of Unity in Diversity
cards.front: What are policies of assimilation (UNDP box)?
cards.back: Policies of assimilation – often involving outright suppression of the identities of ethnic, religious or linguistic groups – try to erode the cultural differences between groups.
cards.quote: Policies of assimilation – often involving outright suppression of the identities of ethnic, religious or linguistic groups – try to erode the cultural differences between groups.

source.book: Indian Society
source.section: Box: Threatened by community identities, states try to eliminate cultural diversity

cards.subject: sociology
cards.unit: The Challenges of Unity in Diversity
cards.front: What are policies of integration (UNDP box)?
cards.back: Policies of integration seek to assert a single national identity by attempting to eliminate ethnonational and cultural differences from the public and political arena, while allowing them in the private domain.
cards.quote: Policies of integration seek to assert a single national identity by attempting to eliminate ethnonational and cultural differences from the public and political arena, while allowing them in the private domain.

source.book: Indian Society
source.section: Box: Threatened by community identities, states try to eliminate cultural diversity

cards.subject: sociology
cards.unit: The Challenges of Unity in Diversity
cards.front: What do policies that promote assimilation aim at?
cards.back: Policies that promote assimilation are aimed at persuading, encouraging or forcing all citizens to adopt a uniform set of cultural values and norms.
cards.quote: Policies that promote assimilation are aimed at persuading, encouraging or forcing all citizens to adopt a uniform set of cultural values and norms.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.unit: The Challenges of Unity in Diversity
cards.front: Suppressing cultural diversity can be very costly in terms of what, for minority or subordinated communities?
cards.back: Suppressing cultural diversity can be very costly in terms of the alienation of the minority or subordinated communities whose culture is treated as ‘non-national’.
cards.quote: However, suppressing cultural diversity can be very costly in terms of the alienation of the minority or subordinated communities whose culture is treated as ‘non-national’.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.unit: The Challenges of Unity in Diversity
cards.front: What was India’s population according to Census of India 2011?
cards.back: It has a population of about 1.21 billion people, according to Census of India 2011, currently the second largest – and soon to become the largest – national population in the world.
cards.quote: It has a population of about 1.21 billion people, according to Census of India 2011, currently the second largest – and soon to become the largest – national population in the world.

source.book: Indian Society
source.section: Cultural Diversity and India as a Nation-state

cards.subject: sociology
cards.unit: The Challenges of Unity in Diversity
cards.front: How many languages and dialects are spoken in India, and how many are in the 8th Schedule?
cards.back: These billion-plus people speak about 1,632 different languages and dialects. As many as twenty two of these languages have been officially recognised and placed under the 8th Schedule of the Constitution, thus guaranteeing their legal status.
cards.quote: These billion-plus people speak about 1,632 different languages and dialects. As many as twenty two of these languages have been officially recognised and placed under the 8th Schedule of the Constitution, thus guaranteeing their legal status.

source.book: Indian Society
source.section: Cultural Diversity and India as a Nation-state

cards.subject: sociology
cards.unit: The Challenges of Unity in Diversity
cards.front: What share of India’s population are Hindus, and how are they described?
cards.back: In terms of religion, about 80% of the population are Hindus, who in turn are regionally specific, plural in beliefs and practices, and divided by castes and languages.
cards.quote: In terms of religion, about 80% of the population are Hindus, who in turn are regionally specific, plural in beliefs and practices, and divided by castes and languages.

source.book: Indian Society
source.section: Cultural Diversity and India as a Nation-state

cards.subject: sociology
cards.unit: The Challenges of Unity in Diversity
cards.front: What share of India’s population are Muslims, and where does India rank among Muslim countries?
cards.back: About 14.2% of the population are Muslims, which makes India the world’s second largest Muslim country after Indonesia and Pakistan.
cards.quote: About 14.2% of the population are Muslims, which makes India the world’s second largest Muslim country after Indonesia and Pakistan.

source.book: Indian Society
source.section: Cultural Diversity and India as a Nation-state

cards.subject: sociology
cards.unit: The Challenges of Unity in Diversity
cards.front: Name India’s other major religious communities and their shares (Census 2011).
cards.back:
Christians (2.3%)
Sikhs (1.7%)
Buddhists (0.7%)
Jains (0.4%)
cards.quote: The other major religious communities are Christians (2.3%), Sikhs (1.7%), Buddhists (0.7%) and Jains (0.4%).

source.book: Indian Society
source.section: Cultural Diversity and India as a Nation-state

cards.subject: sociology
cards.unit: The Challenges of Unity in Diversity
cards.front: From its very beginning the independent Indian state has ruled out an ____ model.
cards.back: From its very beginning the independent Indian state has ruled out an assimilationist model.
cards.quote: From its very beginning the independent Indian state has ruled out an assimilationist model.

source.book: Indian Society
source.section: Cultural Diversity and India as a Nation-state

cards.subject: sociology
cards.unit: The Challenges of Unity in Diversity
cards.front: What is a ‘state nation’, the alternative to the nation-state?
cards.back: An alternative to the nation-state, then, is the “state nation”, where various “nations” – be they ethnic, religious, linguistic or indigenous identities – can co-exist peacefully and cooperatively in a single state polity.
cards.quote: An alternative to the nation-state, then, is the “state nation”, where various “nations” – be they ethnic, religious, linguistic or indigenous identities – can co-exist peacefully and cooperatively in a single state polity.

source.book: Indian Society
source.section: Box: National unity with cultural diversity

cards.subject: sociology
cards.unit: The Challenges of Unity in Diversity
cards.front: National cohesion does not require the imposition of a ____ and the denunciation of diversity.
cards.back: National cohesion does not require the imposition of a single identity and the denunciation of diversity.
cards.quote: National cohesion does not require the imposition of a single identity and the denunciation of diversity.

source.book: Indian Society
source.section: Box: National unity with cultural diversity

cards.subject: sociology
cards.unit: The Challenges of Unity in Diversity
cards.front: In general, India’s problems have been more in the sphere of ____ and practice rather than laws or principles.
cards.back: In general, India’s problems have been more in the sphere of implementation and practice rather than laws or principles.
cards.quote: In general, India’s problems have been more in the sphere of implementation and practice rather than laws or principles.

source.book: Indian Society
source.section: Box: National unity with cultural diversity

cards.subject: sociology
cards.unit: The Challenges of Unity in Diversity
cards.front: But on the whole, India can be considered a good example of a ‘____’ though it is not entirely free from the problems common to nation-states.
cards.back: But on the whole, India can be considered a good example of a ‘state-nation’ though it is not entirely free from the problems common to nation-states.
cards.quote: But on the whole, India can be considered a good example of a ‘state-nation’ though it is not entirely free from the problems common to nation-states.

source.book: Indian Society
source.section: Box: National unity with cultural diversity

cards.subject: sociology
cards.unit: The Challenges of Unity in Diversity
cards.front: What is regionalism in India rooted in, and what encourages and fuels it?
cards.back: Regionalism in India is rooted in India’s diversity of languages, cultures, tribes, and religions. It is also encouraged by the geographical concentration of these identity markers in particular regions, and fuelled by a sense of regional deprivation.
cards.quote: Regionalism in India is rooted in India’s diversity of languages, cultures, tribes, and religions. It is also encouraged by the geographical concentration of these identity markers in particular regions, and fuelled by a sense of regional deprivation.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.unit: The Challenges of Unity in Diversity
cards.front: Indian ____ has been a means of accommodating these regional sentiments (Bhattacharyya 2005).
cards.back: Indian federalism has been a means of accommodating these regional sentiments (Bhattacharyya 2005).
cards.quote: Indian federalism has been a means of accommodating these regional sentiments (Bhattacharyya 2005).

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.unit: The Challenges of Unity in Diversity
cards.front: Which were the three major presidencies of the British-Indian arrangement?
cards.back: Madras, Bombay, and Calcutta were the three major presidencies
cards.quote: Madras, Bombay, and Calcutta were the three major presidencies

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.unit: The Challenges of Unity in Diversity
cards.front: Soon after the Constitution was adopted, the colonial-era units were reorganised into what kind of States?
cards.back: Soon after the adoption of the Constitution, all these units of the colonial era had to be reorganised into ethno-linguistic States within the Indian union in response to strong popular agitations.
cards.quote: Soon after the adoption of the Constitution, all these units of the colonial era had to be reorganised into ethno-linguistic States within the Indian union in response to strong popular agitations.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.unit: The Challenges of Unity in Diversity
cards.front: When was the Report of the States Reorganisation Commission (SRC) implemented?
cards.back: The Report of the States Reorganisation Commission (SRC) which was implemented on November 1, 1956, has helped transform the political and institutional life of the nation.
cards.quote: The Report of the States Reorganisation Commission (SRC) which was implemented on November 1, 1956, has helped transform the political and institutional life of the nation.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.unit: The Challenges of Unity in Diversity
cards.front: What did Gandhi and other leaders promise about the new nation’s provinces when freedom came?
cards.back: At the same time, Gandhi and other leaders promised their followers that when freedom came, the new nation would be based on a new set of provinces based on the principle of language.
cards.quote: At the same time, Gandhi and other leaders promised their followers that when freedom came, the new nation would be based on a new set of provinces based on the principle of language.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.unit: The Challenges of Unity in Diversity
cards.front: Who died on a fast unto death in October 1953, leading to Andhra Pradesh and the SRC?
cards.back: In October 1953, Potti Sriramulu, a former Gandhian, died seven weeks after beginning a fast unto death. Potti Sriramulu’s martyrdom provoked violent protests and led to the creation of the state of Andhra Pradesh. It also led to the formation of the SRC, which in 1956 put the formal, final seal of approval on the principle of linguistic states.
cards.quote: In October 1953, Potti Sriramulu, a former Gandhian, died seven weeks after beginning a fast unto death. Potti Sriramulu’s martyrdom provoked violent protests and led to the creation of the state of Andhra Pradesh. It also led to the formation of the SRC, which in 1956 put the formal, final seal of approval on the principle of linguistic states.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.unit: The Challenges of Unity in Diversity
cards.front: In India, what – not religion – has provided the most powerful instrument for forming ethno-national identity?
cards.back: Language coupled with regional and tribal identity – and not religion – has therefore provided the most powerful instrument for the formation of ethno-national identity in India.
cards.quote: Language coupled with regional and tribal identity – and not religion – has therefore provided the most powerful instrument for the formation of ethno-national identity in India.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.unit: The Challenges of Unity in Diversity
cards.front: Which three states were created in 2000, where language did not play a prominent role?
cards.back: For instance, in the creation of three new states in 2000, namely Chhatisgarh, Uttaranchal and Jharkhand, language did not play a prominent role.
cards.quote: For instance, in the creation of three new states in 2000, namely Chhatisgarh, Uttaranchal and Jharkhand, language did not play a prominent role.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.unit: The Challenges of Unity in Diversity
cards.front: What combination of factors gave rise to the new States of 2000?
cards.back:
ethnicity based on tribal identity
language
regional deprivation
ecology
cards.quote: Rather, a combination of ethnicity based on tribal identity, language, regional deprivation and ecology provided the basis for intense regionalism resulting in statehood.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.unit: The Challenges of Unity in Diversity
cards.front: How many States and Union territories are there in the Indian nation-state (as given in the chapter)?
cards.back: Currently there are 28 States (federal units) and 8 Union territories (centrally administered) within the Indian nation-state.
cards.quote: Currently there are 28 States (federal units) and 8 Union territories (centrally administered) within the Indian nation-state.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.unit: The Challenges of Unity in Diversity
cards.front: Which list in the Constitution names areas of governance where both the State and the Centre are allowed to operate?
cards.back: There are lists of ‘subjects’ or areas of governance which are the exclusive responsibility of either State or Centre, along with a ‘Concurrent List’ of areas where both are allowed to operate.
cards.quote: There are lists of ‘subjects’ or areas of governance which are the exclusive responsibility of either State or Centre, along with a ‘Concurrent List’ of areas where both are allowed to operate.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.unit: The Challenges of Unity in Diversity
cards.front: Who determines the composition of the Rajya Sabha?
cards.back: The State legislatures determine the composition of the upper house of Parliament, the Rajya Sabha.
cards.quote: The State legislatures determine the composition of the upper house of Parliament, the Rajya Sabha.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.unit: The Challenges of Unity in Diversity
cards.front: How often is the Finance Commission set up, and what does it decide?
cards.back: An example is the Finance Commission which is set up every five years to decide on sharing of tax revenues between Centre and States.
cards.quote: An example is the Finance Commission which is set up every five years to decide on sharing of tax revenues between Centre and States.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.unit: The Challenges of Unity in Diversity
cards.front: Into which two related groups are the religion-related issues of cultural diversity broadly divided?
cards.back: Perhaps the most contentious of all aspects of cultural diversity are issues relating to religious communities and religion-based identities. These issues may be broadly divided into two related groups – the secularism–communalism set and the minority–majority set.
cards.quote: Perhaps the most contentious of all aspects of cultural diversity are issues relating to religious communities and religion-based identities. These issues may be broadly divided into two related groups – the secularism–communalism set and the minority–majority set.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.unit: The Challenges of Unity in Diversity
cards.front: The term ‘people’ has not been seen in ____ terms, as referring to any specific group defined by religion, ethnicity, race or caste.
cards.back: The term ‘people’ has not been seen in exclusive terms, as referring to any specific group defined by religion, ethnicity, race or caste.
cards.quote: The term ‘people’ has not been seen in exclusive terms, as referring to any specific group defined by religion, ethnicity, race or caste.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.unit: The Challenges of Unity in Diversity
cards.front: Which leaders commented on the ugly aspects of exclusive nationalism?
cards.back: Ideas of humanism influenced Indian nationalists and the ugly aspects of exclusive nationalism were extensively commented upon by leading figures like Mahatma Gandhi and Rabindranath Tagore.
cards.quote: Ideas of humanism influenced Indian nationalists and the ugly aspects of exclusive nationalism were extensively commented upon by leading figures like Mahatma Gandhi and Rabindranath Tagore.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.unit: The Challenges of Unity in Diversity
cards.front: To be effective, the ideas of inclusive nationalism had to be built into the ____.
cards.back: To be effective, the ideas of inclusive nationalism had to be built into the Constitution.
cards.quote: To be effective, the ideas of inclusive nationalism had to be built into the Constitution.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.unit: The Challenges of Unity in Diversity
cards.front: What does ‘minority’ mean in sociology?
cards.back: The notion of minority groups is widely used in sociology and is more than a merely numerical distinction – it usually involves some sense of relative disadvantage.
cards.quote: The notion of minority groups is widely used in sociology and is more than a merely numerical distinction – it usually involves some sense of relative disadvantage.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.unit: The Challenges of Unity in Diversity
cards.front: What does ‘minority’ generally imply when used without qualification?
cards.back: When minority is used without qualification, it generally implies a relatively small but also disadvantaged group.
cards.quote: When minority is used without qualification, it generally implies a relatively small but also disadvantaged group.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.unit: The Challenges of Unity in Diversity
cards.front: What does the sociological sense of minority imply about its members?
cards.back: The sociological sense of minority also implies that the members of the minority form a collectivity – that is, they have a strong sense of group solidarity, a feeling of togetherness and belonging.
cards.quote: The sociological sense of minority also implies that the members of the minority form a collectivity – that is, they have a strong sense of group solidarity, a feeling of togetherness and belonging.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.unit: The Challenges of Unity in Diversity
cards.front: Which groups are minorities in a statistical but not a sociological sense?
cards.back: Thus, groups that may be minorities in a statistical sense, such as people who are left-handed or people born on 29th February, are not minorities in the sociological sense because they do not form a collectivity.
cards.quote: Thus, groups that may be minorities in a statistical sense, such as people who are left-handed or people born on 29th February, are not minorities in the sociological sense because they do not form a collectivity.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.unit: The Challenges of Unity in Diversity
cards.front: Which religious minorities may be well-off economically yet culturally disadvantaged?
cards.back: Thus, for example, religious minorities like the Parsis or Sikhs may be relatively well-off economically. But they may still be disadvantaged in a cultural sense because of their small numbers relative to the overwhelming majority of Hindus.
cards.quote: Thus, for example, religious minorities like the Parsis or Sikhs may be relatively well-off economically. But they may still be disadvantaged in a cultural sense because of their small numbers relative to the overwhelming majority of Hindus.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.unit: The Challenges of Unity in Diversity
cards.front: Religious or cultural minorities need special protection because of the ____ of the majority.
cards.back: Religious or cultural minorities need special protection because of the demographic dominance of the majority.
cards.quote: Religious or cultural minorities need special protection because of the demographic dominance of the majority.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.unit: The Challenges of Unity in Diversity
cards.front: How many Hindus are there in India (2011 Census), and what share of the population?
cards.back: As is well known, Hindus constitute an overwhelming majority in India: they number about 966 millions and account for 80% of the total population according to the 2011 Census.
cards.quote: As is well known, Hindus constitute an overwhelming majority in India: they number about 966 millions and account for 80% of the total population according to the 2011 Census.

source.book: Indian Society
source.section: Box: Relative size and distribution of religious minorities

cards.subject: sociology
cards.unit: The Challenges of Unity in Diversity
cards.front: How much larger is the Hindu population than all other minority religions combined, and than the Muslims?
cards.back: The Hindu population is four times larger than the combined population of all other minority religions, and about six times larger than the largest minority group, the Muslims.
cards.quote: The Hindu population is four times larger than the combined population of all other minority religions, and about six times larger than the largest minority group, the Muslims.

source.book: Indian Society
source.section: Box: Relative size and distribution of religious minorities

cards.subject: sociology
cards.unit: The Challenges of Unity in Diversity
cards.front: What are the numbers and share of Muslims, India’s largest religious minority (2011)?
cards.back: The Muslims are by far the largest religious minority in India – they numbered 172 millions and were 14.2% of the population in 2011.
cards.quote: The Muslims are by far the largest religious minority in India – they numbered 172 millions and were 14.2% of the population in 2011.

source.book: Indian Society
source.section: Box: Relative size and distribution of religious minorities

cards.subject: sociology
cards.unit: The Challenges of Unity in Diversity
cards.front: Where do Muslims constitute a majority, and where do they have sizeable pockets?
cards.back: They are scattered all over the country, constitute a majority in Jammu and Kashmir and have sizeable pockets in West Bengal, Uttar Pradesh, Kerala, Andhra Pradesh, Karnataka and Rajasthan.
cards.quote: They are scattered all over the country, constitute a majority in Jammu and Kashmir and have sizeable pockets in West Bengal, Uttar Pradesh, Kerala, Andhra Pradesh, Karnataka and Rajasthan.

source.book: Indian Society
source.section: Box: Relative size and distribution of religious minorities

cards.subject: sociology
cards.unit: The Challenges of Unity in Diversity
cards.front: What are the share and number of Christians in India?
cards.back: Christians constitute around 2.3% of the population (27.8 million) and are scattered all over, with sizeable pockets in the north eastern and southern states.
cards.quote: Christians constitute around 2.3% of the population (27.8 million) and are scattered all over, with sizeable pockets in the north eastern and southern states.

source.book: Indian Society
source.section: Box: Relative size and distribution of religious minorities

cards.subject: sociology
cards.unit: The Challenges of Unity in Diversity
cards.front: Which are the three Christian-majority states, and their shares?
cards.back: The three Christian-majority states are all in the North East – Nagaland (88%), Mizoram (87%) and Meghalaya (74%).
cards.quote: The three Christian-majority states are all in the North East – Nagaland (88%), Mizoram (87%) and Meghalaya (74%).

source.book: Indian Society
source.section: Box: Relative size and distribution of religious minorities

cards.subject: sociology
cards.unit: The Challenges of Unity in Diversity
cards.front: What are the share and number of Sikhs, and where are they in a majority?
cards.back: The Sikhs constitute 1.7% of the population (21 million) and although they are found scattered across the country, they are concentrated in Punjab where they are in a majority (58%).
cards.quote: The Sikhs constitute 1.7% of the population (21 million) and although they are found scattered across the country, they are concentrated in Punjab where they are in a majority (58%).

source.book: Indian Society
source.section: Box: Relative size and distribution of religious minorities

cards.subject: sociology
cards.unit: The Challenges of Unity in Diversity
cards.front: Indeed ‘____’ became a short hand to capture the plural and diverse nature of Indian society.
cards.back: Indeed ‘unity in diversity’ became a short hand to capture the plural and diverse nature of Indian society.
cards.quote: Indeed ‘unity in diversity’ became a short hand to capture the plural and diverse nature of Indian society.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.unit: The Challenges of Unity in Diversity
cards.front: Who is described as the chief architect of the Constitution who made the case for minority protection in the Constituent Assembly?
cards.back: Dr. B.R. Ambedkar, the chief architect of the Constitution, made this point clear in the Constituent Assembly
cards.quote: Dr. B.R. Ambedkar, the chief architect of the Constitution, made this point clear in the Constituent Assembly

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.unit: The Challenges of Unity in Diversity
cards.front: In the Constituent Assembly, how did Dr. Ambedkar describe minorities (Box on protection of minorities)?
cards.back: One is that minorities are an explosive force which, if it erupts, can blow up the whole fabric of the state.
cards.quote: One is that minorities are an explosive force which, if it erupts, can blow up the whole fabric of the state.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.unit: The Challenges of Unity in Diversity
cards.front: What was one of the key issues that led to the formation of Bangladesh?
cards.back: One of key issues that led to the formation of Bangladesh was the unwillingness of the Pakistani state to recognise the cultural and linguistic rights of the people of Bangladesh.
cards.quote: One of key issues that led to the formation of Bangladesh was the unwillingness of the Pakistani state to recognise the cultural and linguistic rights of the people of Bangladesh.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.unit: The Challenges of Unity in Diversity
cards.front: Which imposition formed a backdrop to the ethnic conflict in Sri Lanka?
cards.back: One of the many contentious issues that formed the backdrop of the ethnic conflict in Sri Lanka was the imposition of Sinhalese as a national language.
cards.quote: One of the many contentious issues that formed the backdrop of the ethnic conflict in Sri Lanka was the imposition of Sinhalese as a national language.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.unit: The Challenges of Unity in Diversity
cards.front: What does any forcible imposition of a language or religion on any group of people in India weaken?
cards.back: Any forcible imposition of a language or religion on any group of people in India weakens national unity which is based upon a recognition of differences.
cards.quote: Likewise any forcible imposition of a language or religion on any group of people in India weakens national unity which is based upon a recognition of differences.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.unit: The Challenges of Unity in Diversity
cards.front: What does Article 29(1) of the Constitution guarantee?
cards.back: Any section of the citizens residing in the territory of India or any part there of having a distinct language, script or culture of its own shall have the right to conserve the same.
cards.quote: Any section of the citizens residing in the territory of India or any part there of having a distinct language, script or culture of its own shall have the right to conserve the same.

source.book: Indian Society
source.section: Box: The Indian Constitution on minorities and cultural diversity

cards.subject: sociology
cards.unit: The Challenges of Unity in Diversity
cards.front: What does Article 29(2) of the Constitution say about admission to educational institutions?
cards.back: No citizen shall be denied admission into any educational institution maintained by the State or received out of State funds on grounds only of religion, race, caste, language or any of them.
cards.quote: No citizen shall be denied admission into any educational institution maintained by the State or received out of State funds on grounds only of religion, race, caste, language or any of them.

source.book: Indian Society
source.section: Box: The Indian Constitution on minorities and cultural diversity

cards.subject: sociology
cards.unit: The Challenges of Unity in Diversity
cards.front: What does Article 30(1) of the Constitution give all minorities?
cards.back: All minorities, whether based on religion or language, shall have the right to establish and administer educational institutions of their choice.
cards.quote: All minorities, whether based on religion or language, shall have the right to establish and administer educational institutions of their choice.

source.book: Indian Society
source.section: Box: The Indian Constitution on minorities and cultural diversity

cards.subject: sociology
cards.unit: The Challenges of Unity in Diversity
cards.front: What does Article 30(2) forbid the State from doing when granting aid?
cards.back: The State shall not, in granting aid to educational institutions, discriminate against any educational institution on the ground that it is under the management of a minority, whether based on religion or language.
cards.quote: The State shall not, in granting aid to educational institutions, discriminate against any educational institution on the ground that it is under the management of a minority, whether based on religion or language.

source.book: Indian Society
source.section: Box: The Indian Constitution on minorities and cultural diversity

cards.subject: sociology
cards.unit: The Challenges of Unity in Diversity
cards.front: What does ‘communalism’ refer to in everyday language?
cards.back: In everyday language, the word ‘communalism’ refers to aggressive chauvinism based on religious identity.
cards.quote: In everyday language, the word ‘communalism’ refers to aggressive chauvinism based on religious identity.

source.book: Indian Society
source.section: Communalism, Secularism and the Nation-state: Communalism

cards.subject: sociology
cards.unit: The Challenges of Unity in Diversity
cards.front: What is chauvinism?
cards.back: Chauvinism itself is an attitude that sees one’s own group as the only legitimate or worthy group, with other groups being seen – by definition – as inferior, illegitimate and opposed.
cards.quote: Chauvinism itself is an attitude that sees one’s own group as the only legitimate or worthy group, with other groups being seen – by definition – as inferior, illegitimate and opposed.

source.book: Indian Society
source.section: Communalism, Secularism and the Nation-state: Communalism

cards.subject: sociology
cards.unit: The Challenges of Unity in Diversity
cards.front: State the simplified meaning of communalism (NCERT).
cards.back: Thus, to simplify further, communalism is an aggressive political ideology linked to religion.
cards.quote: Thus, to simplify further, communalism is an aggressive political ideology linked to religion.

source.book: Indian Society
source.section: Communalism, Secularism and the Nation-state: Communalism

cards.subject: sociology
cards.unit: The Challenges of Unity in Diversity
cards.front: The English meaning is ____, whereas the South Asian meaning is strongly charged.
cards.back: The English meaning is neutral, whereas the South Asian meaning is strongly charged.
cards.quote: The English meaning is neutral, whereas the South Asian meaning is strongly charged.

source.book: Indian Society
source.section: Communalism, Secularism and the Nation-state: Communalism

cards.subject: sociology
cards.unit: The Challenges of Unity in Diversity
cards.front: According to NCERT, communalism is about what, not about religion?
cards.back: It is important to emphasise that communalism is about politics, not about religion.
cards.quote: It is important to emphasise that communalism is about politics, not about religion.

source.book: Indian Society
source.section: Communalism, Secularism and the Nation-state: Communalism

cards.subject: sociology
cards.unit: The Challenges of Unity in Diversity
cards.front: India has had a history of communal riots from pre-Independence times, often as a result of the ____ policy adopted by the colonial rulers.
cards.back: India has had a history of communal riots from pre-Independence times, often as a result of the divide-and-rule policy adopted by the colonial rulers.
cards.quote: India has had a history of communal riots from pre-Independence times, often as a result of the divide-and-rule policy adopted by the colonial rulers.

source.book: Indian Society
source.section: Communalism, Secularism and the Nation-state: Communalism

cards.subject: sociology
cards.unit: The Challenges of Unity in Diversity
cards.front: In which movements’ devotional songs and poetry is India’s syncretic heritage clearly evident?
cards.back: But we should not forget that we also have a long tradition of religious pluralism, ranging from peaceful co-existence to actual inter-mixing or syncretism. This syncretic heritage is clearly evident in the devotional songs and poetry of the Bhakti and Sufi movements (Box 6.9).
cards.quote: But we should not forget that we also have a long tradition of religious pluralism, ranging from peaceful co-existence to actual inter-mixing or syncretism. This syncretic heritage is clearly evident in the devotional songs and poetry of the Bhakti and Sufi movements (Box 6.9).

source.book: Indian Society
source.section: Communalism, Secularism and the Nation-state: Communalism

cards.subject: sociology
cards.unit: The Challenges of Unity in Diversity
cards.front: Whose poems synthesising Hindu and Muslim devotion are cherished symbols of pluralism?
cards.back: The poems of Kabir, synthesising Hindu and Muslim devotion are cherished symbols of pluralism
cards.quote: The poems of Kabir, synthesising Hindu and Muslim devotion are cherished symbols of pluralism

source.book: Indian Society
source.section: Communalism, Secularism and the Nation-state: Communalism

cards.subject: sociology
cards.unit: The Challenges of Unity in Diversity
cards.front: What is the main sense of secularism in the western context?
cards.back: Secularism is among the most complex terms in social and political theory. In the western context the main sense of these terms has to do with the separation of church and state.
cards.quote: Secularism is among the most complex terms in social and political theory. In the western context the main sense of these terms has to do with the separation of church and state.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.unit: The Challenges of Unity in Diversity
cards.front: Define ‘secularisation’ (NCERT).
cards.back: This separation was related to the process of “secularisation”, or the progressive retreat of religion from public life, as it was converted from a mandatory obligation to a voluntary personal practice.
cards.quote: This separation was related to the process of “secularisation”, or the progressive retreat of religion from public life, as it was converted from a mandatory obligation to a voluntary personal practice.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.unit: The Challenges of Unity in Diversity
cards.front: What is the most common use of ‘secular’ in everyday language in India?
cards.back: The most common use of secular in everyday language is as the opposite of communal. So, a secular person or state is one that does not favour any particular religion over others.
cards.quote: The most common use of secular in everyday language is as the opposite of communal. So, a secular person or state is one that does not favour any particular religion over others.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.unit: The Challenges of Unity in Diversity
cards.front: In terms of the state-religion relationship, this sense of secularism implies ____ for all religions, rather than separation or distancing.
cards.back: In terms of the state-religion relationship, this sense of secularism implies equal respect for all religions, rather than separation or distancing.
cards.quote: In terms of the state-religion relationship, this sense of secularism implies equal respect for all religions, rather than separation or distancing.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.unit: The Challenges of Unity in Diversity
cards.front: What example does NCERT give of the secular Indian state’s equal respect for all religions?
cards.back: For example, the secular Indian state declares public holidays to mark the festivals of all religions.
cards.quote: For example, the secular Indian state declares public holidays to mark the festivals of all religions.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.unit: The Challenges of Unity in Diversity
cards.front: But providing such protection immediately invites the accusation of favouritism or ‘____’ of minorities.
cards.back: But providing such protection immediately invites the accusation of favouritism or ‘appeasement’ of minorities.
cards.quote: But providing such protection immediately invites the accusation of favouritism or ‘appeasement’ of minorities.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.unit: The Challenges of Unity in Diversity
cards.front: Secularism and minority protection: what do opponents and supporters argue?
cards.back: Opponents argue that secularism of this sort is only an excuse to favour the minorities in return for their votes or other kinds of support. Supporters argue that without such special protection, secularism can turn into an excuse for imposing the majority community’s values and norms on the minorities.
cards.quote: Opponents argue that secularism of this sort is only an excuse to favour the minorities in return for their votes or other kinds of support. Supporters argue that without such special protection, secularism can turn into an excuse for imposing the majority community’s values and norms on the minorities.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.unit: The Challenges of Unity in Diversity
cards.front: Which arms does NCERT name as part of the state structure?
cards.back:
legislature
bureaucracy
judiciary
armed forces
police
other arms of the state
cards.quote: To the extent that the state structure – the legislature, bureaucracy, judiciary, armed forces, police and other arms of the state – becomes insulated from the people, it also has the potential of turning authoritarian.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.unit: The Challenges of Unity in Diversity
cards.front: What is an authoritarian state?
cards.back: An authoritarian state is the opposite of a democratic state. It is a state in which the people have no voice and those in power are not accountable to anyone.
cards.quote: An authoritarian state is the opposite of a democratic state. It is a state in which the people have no voice and those in power are not accountable to anyone.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.unit: The Challenges of Unity in Diversity
cards.front: Which civil liberties do authoritarian states often limit or abolish?
cards.back:
freedom of speech
freedom of the press
freedom of political activity
right to protection from wrongful use of authority
right to the due processes of the law
cards.quote: Authoritarian states often limit or abolish civil liberties like freedom of speech, freedom of the press, freedom of political activity, right to protection from wrongful use of authority, right to the due processes of the law, and so on.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.unit: The Challenges of Unity in Diversity
cards.front: Why may state institutions fail to respond to people’s needs, apart from authoritarianism?
cards.back:
corruption
inefficiency
lack of resources
cards.quote: Apart from authoritarianism, there is also the possibility that state institutions become unable or unwilling to respond to the needs of the people because of corruption, inefficiency, or lack of resources.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.unit: The Challenges of Unity in Diversity
cards.front: In what three ways can non-state actors and institutions act towards the state, according to NCERT?
cards.back: Non-state actors and institutions become important in this context, for they can keep a watch on the state, protest against its injustices or supplement its efforts.
cards.quote: Non-state actors and institutions become important in this context, for they can keep a watch on the state, protest against its injustices or supplement its efforts.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.unit: The Challenges of Unity in Diversity
cards.front: What is civil society?
cards.back: Civil society is the name given to the broad arena which lies beyond the private domain of the family, but outside the domain of both state and market. Civil society is the non-state and non-market part of the public domain in which individuals get together voluntarily to create institutions and organisations.
cards.quote: Civil society is the name given to the broad arena which lies beyond the private domain of the family, but outside the domain of both state and market. Civil society is the non-state and non-market part of the public domain in which individuals get together voluntarily to create institutions and organisations.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.unit: The Challenges of Unity in Diversity
cards.front: What does civil society include, according to NCERT?
cards.back:
political parties
media institutions
trade unions
non-governmental organisations (NGOs)
religious organisations
other kinds of collective entities
cards.quote: It includes political parties, media institutions, trade unions, non-governmental organisations (NGOs), religious organisations, and other kinds of collective entities.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.unit: The Challenges of Unity in Diversity
cards.front: What are the two main criteria for inclusion in civil society?
cards.back: The main criteria for inclusion in civil society are that the organisation should not be state-controlled, and it should not be a purely commercial profit-making entity.
cards.quote: The main criteria for inclusion in civil society are that the organisation should not be state-controlled, and it should not be a purely commercial profit-making entity.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.unit: The Challenges of Unity in Diversity
cards.front: What role have civil liberties organisations played?
cards.back: Civil liberties organisations have been particularly important in keeping a watch on the state and forcing it to obey the law.
cards.quote: Civil liberties organisations have been particularly important in keeping a watch on the state and forcing it to obey the law.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.unit: The Challenges of Unity in Diversity
cards.front: Where did the campaign for the Right to Information begin?
cards.back: Among the most significant recent initiatives is the campaign for the Right to Information. Beginning with an agitation in rural Rajasthan for the release of information on government funds spent on village development, this effort grew into a nation-wide campaign.
cards.quote: Among the most significant recent initiatives is the campaign for the Right to Information. Beginning with an agitation in rural Rajasthan for the release of information on government funds spent on village development, this effort grew into a nation-wide campaign.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.unit: The Challenges of Unity in Diversity
cards.front: What is the Right to Information Act 2005?
cards.back: The Right to Information Act 2005 (Act No. 22/2005) is a law enacted by the Parliament of India giving Indians access to Government records.
cards.quote: The Right to Information Act 2005 (Act No. 22/2005) is a law enacted by the Parliament of India giving Indians access to Government records.

source.book: Indian Society
source.section: Box: Forcing the State to Respond to the People: The Right to Information Act

cards.subject: sociology
cards.unit: The Challenges of Unity in Diversity
cards.front: Within how many days is a public authority expected to reply under the RTI Act?
cards.back: Under the terms of the Act, any person may request information from a “public authority” (a body of Government or instrumentality of State) which is expected to reply expeditiously or within thirty days.
cards.quote: Under the terms of the Act, any person may request information from a “public authority” (a body of Government or instrumentality of State) which is expected to reply expeditiously or within thirty days.

source.book: Indian Society
source.section: Box: Forcing the State to Respond to the People: The Right to Information Act

cards.subject: sociology
cards.unit: The Challenges of Unity in Diversity
cards.front: On which dates was the RTI law passed by Parliament and brought into force?
cards.back: This law was passed by Parliament on 15 June 2005 and came into force on 13 October 2005.
cards.quote: This law was passed by Parliament on 15 June 2005 and came into force on 13 October 2005.

source.book: Indian Society
source.section: Box: Forcing the State to Respond to the People: The Right to Information Act

cards.subject: sociology
cards.unit: The Challenges of Unity in Diversity
cards.front: Which earlier law restricted information disclosure, now overridden by the RTI Act?
cards.back: Information disclosure in India was hitherto restricted by the Official Secrets Act 1923 and various other special laws, which the new RTI Act now overrides.
cards.quote: Information disclosure in India was hitherto restricted by the Official Secrets Act 1923 and various other special laws, which the new RTI Act now overrides.

source.book: Indian Society
source.section: Box: Forcing the State to Respond to the People: The Right to Information Act

cards.subject: sociology
cards.unit: The Challenges of Unity in Diversity
cards.front: What does the RTI Act give citizens a right to do?
cards.back:
request any information (as defined)
take copies of documents
inspect documents, works and records
take certified samples of materials of work.
obtain information in the form of printouts, diskettes, floppies, tapes, video cassettes or in any other electronic mode.
cards.quote: The Act specifies that citizens have a right to: request any information (as defined) take copies of documents inspect documents, works and records take certified samples of materials of work. obtain information in the form of printouts, diskettes, floppies, tapes, video cassettes or in any other electronic mode.

source.book: Indian Society
source.section: Box: Forcing the State to Respond to the People: The Right to Information Act

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: What questions about work are sociologists interested in?
cards.back: Sociologists are interested in the questions of who produces what, who works where, who sells to whom and how.
cards.quote: Sociologists are interested in the questions of who produces what, who works where, who sells to whom and how.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Which thinkers linked industry with urbanisation and the loss of face-to-face relationships?
cards.back: Thinkers like Karl Marx, Max Weber and Emile Durkheim associated a number of social features with industry, such as urbanisation, the loss of face-to-face relationships that were found in rural areas where people worked on their own farms or for a landlord they knew, and their substitution by anonymous professional relationships in modern factories and workplaces.
cards.quote: Thinkers like Karl Marx, Max Weber and Emile Durkheim associated a number of social features with industry, such as urbanisation, the loss of face-to-face relationships that were found in rural areas where people worked on their own farms or for a landlord they knew, and their substitution by anonymous professional relationships in modern factories and workplaces.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: People often do not see the end result of their work because they are producing only ____ of a product.
cards.back: People often do not see the end result of their work because they are producing only one small part of a product.
cards.quote: People often do not see the end result of their work because they are producing only one small part of a product.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: What did Marx call the situation in which people do not enjoy work and do it only to survive?
cards.back: Marx called this situation alienation
cards.quote: Marx called this situation alienation

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.note: Alienation: people do not enjoy work and see it only as something to do to survive.

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Industrialisation leads to ____, at least in some spheres.
cards.back: Industrialisation leads to greater equality, at least in some spheres.
cards.quote: Industrialisation leads to greater equality, at least in some spheres.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: And even as social inequalities are reducing, ____ is growing in the world.
cards.back: And even as social inequalities are reducing, economic or income inequality is growing in the world.
cards.quote: And even as social inequalities are reducing, economic or income inequality is growing in the world.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Give NCERT's example of social inequality and income inequality overlapping.
cards.back: Often social inequality and income inequality overlap, for example, in the domination of upper caste men in well-paying professions like medicine, law or journalism.
cards.quote: Often social inequality and income inequality overlap, for example, in the domination of upper caste men in well-paying professions like medicine, law or journalism.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Comparative analysis of different countries suggests that there is ____ of industrial capitalism.
cards.back: Comparative analysis of different countries suggests that there is no standard model of industrial capitalism.
cards.quote: Comparative analysis of different countries suggests that there is no standard model of industrial capitalism.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: In developed countries, which sector employs the majority, and what share is in agriculture?
cards.back: In developed countries, the majority of people are in the services sector, followed by industry and less than 10% are in agriculture (ILO figures).
cards.quote: In developed countries, the majority of people are in the services sector, followed by industry and less than 10% are in agriculture (ILO figures).

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Share of Indian workers in the primary, secondary and tertiary sectors, 2018–19?
cards.back: In India, in 2018–19, nearly 43% were employed in the primary sector (agriculture and mining), 17% in the secondary sector (manufacturing, construction and utilities), and 32% in the tertiary sector (trade, transport, financial services, etc.)
cards.quote: In India, in 2018–19, nearly 43% were employed in the primary sector (agriculture and mining), 17% in the secondary sector (manufacturing, construction and utilities), and 32% in the tertiary sector (trade, transport, financial services, etc.)

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: The three sectors of employment in India, with what each includes.
cards.back:
primary sector (agriculture and mining)
secondary sector (manufacturing, construction and utilities)
tertiary sector (trade, transport, financial services, etc.)
cards.quote: In India, in 2018–19, nearly 43% were employed in the primary sector (agriculture and mining), 17% in the secondary sector (manufacturing, construction and utilities), and 32% in the tertiary sector (trade, transport, financial services, etc.)

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: What has happened to agriculture's share in economic growth, and what do services contribute?
cards.back: However, if we look at the contribution of these sectors to economic growth, the share of agriculture has declined sharply, and services contribute approximately more than half.
cards.quote: However, if we look at the contribution of these sectors to economic growth, the share of agriculture has declined sharply, and services contribute approximately more than half.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Why is it a very serious situation that agriculture employs the most Indians but its share of economic growth has fallen sharply?
cards.back: This is a very serious situation because it means that the sector where the maximum people are employed is not able to generate much income for them.
cards.quote: This is a very serious situation because it means that the sector where the maximum people are employed is not able to generate much income for them.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: India's workers by employment status: self-employed, regular salaried, casual labour?
cards.back: In India, over 52% of the workers are self-employed, only about 24% are in regular salaried employment, while approximately 24% are in casual labour.
cards.quote: In India, over 52% of the workers are self-employed, only about 24% are in regular salaried employment, while approximately 24% are in casual labour.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: What is the major difference in regular salaried employment between developing and developed countries?
cards.back: Another major difference between developing and developed countries is the number of people in regular salaried employment. In developed countries, the majority are formally employed.
cards.quote: Another major difference between developing and developed countries is the number of people in regular salaried employment. In developed countries, the majority are formally employed.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Economists and others often make a distinction between the organised or ____ and unorganised or ____ sector.
cards.back: Economists and others often make a distinction between the organised or formal and unorganised or informal sector.
cards.quote: Economists and others often make a distinction between the organised or formal and unorganised or informal sector.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Define the organised sector (one definition, NCERT).
cards.back: According to one definition, the organised sector consists of all units employing ten or more people throughout the year.
cards.quote: According to one definition, the organised sector consists of all units employing ten or more people throughout the year.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: What must organised-sector units be, to ensure employees get proper salaries or wages, pension and other benefits?
cards.back: According to one definition, the organised sector consists of all units employing ten or more people throughout the year. These have to be registered with the government to ensure that their employees get proper salaries or wages, pension and other benefits.
cards.quote: According to one definition, the organised sector consists of all units employing ten or more people throughout the year. These have to be registered with the government to ensure that their employees get proper salaries or wages, pension and other benefits.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: In India, over ____ of the work, whether it is in agriculture, industry or services is in the unorganised or informal sector.
cards.back: In India, over 90% of the work, whether it is in agriculture, industry or services is in the unorganised or informal sector.
cards.quote: In India, over 90% of the work, whether it is in agriculture, industry or services is in the unorganised or informal sector.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: First social implication of the small size of the organised sector (NCERT)?
cards.back: First, it means that very few people have the experience of employment in large firms where they get to meet people from other regions and backgrounds.
cards.quote: First, it means that very few people have the experience of employment in large firms where they get to meet people from other regions and backgrounds.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Second social implication of the small organised sector, and who employs two-thirds of those with secure jobs?
cards.back: Second, very few Indians have access to secure jobs with benefits. Of those who do, two-thirds work for the government.
cards.quote: Second, very few Indians have access to secure jobs with benefits. Of those who do, two-thirds work for the government.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Third social implication of the small organised sector (NCERT)?
cards.back: Third, since very few people are members of unions, a feature of the organised sector, the unorganised or informal sector workers do not have the experience of collectively fighting for proper wages and safe working conditions.
cards.quote: Third, since very few people are members of unions, a feature of the organised sector, the unorganised or informal sector workers do not have the experience of collectively fighting for proper wages and safe working conditions.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: In the small-scale workplaces where most Indians work, what determines many aspects of work?
cards.back: Here personal relationships determine many aspects of work.
cards.quote: Here personal relationships determine many aspects of work.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: ____ in India has played a major role in overcoming boundaries of caste, religion and region.
cards.back: Government employment in India has played a major role in overcoming boundaries of caste, religion and region.
cards.quote: Government employment in India has played a major role in overcoming boundaries of caste, religion and region.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Which public sector plant did one sociologist credit with the absence of communal riots in its town?
cards.back: the public sector Bhilai Steel Plant employs people from all over India who work together
cards.quote: One sociologist has argued that the reason why there have never been communal riots in a place like Bhilai is because the public sector Bhilai Steel Plant employs people from all over India who work together.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: What happens in practice to laws monitoring conditions in the unorganised sector?
cards.back: The government has laws to monitor conditions in the unorganised sector, but in practice they are left to the whims and fancies of the employer or contractor.
cards.quote: The government has laws to monitor conditions in the unorganised sector, but in practice they are left to the whims and fancies of the employer or contractor.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Since the ____, the government has followed a policy of liberalisation.
cards.back: Since the 1990s, the government has followed a policy of liberalisation.
cards.quote: Since the 1990s, the government has followed a policy of liberalisation.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India
source.section: Globalisation, Liberalisation and Changes in Indian Industry

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Which sectors, earlier reserved for the government, are now open to private and foreign firms?
cards.back: Private companies, especially foreign firms, are encouraged to invest in sectors earlier reserved for the government, including telecom, civil aviation, power, etc.
cards.quote: Private companies, especially foreign firms, are encouraged to invest in sectors earlier reserved for the government, including telecom, civil aviation, power, etc.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India
source.section: Globalisation, Liberalisation and Changes in Indian Industry

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: ____ are no longer required to open industries.
cards.back: Licenses are no longer required to open industries.
cards.quote: Licenses are no longer required to open industries.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India
source.section: Globalisation, Liberalisation and Changes in Indian Industry

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Parle drinks was bought by Coca Cola: which result of liberalisation does NCERT illustrate?
cards.back: As a result of liberalisation, many Indian companies— small and large, have been bought over by multinationals. At the same time some Indian companies are becoming multinational companies. An instance of the first is when, Parle drinks was bought by Coca Cola.
cards.quote: As a result of liberalisation, many Indian companies— small and large, have been bought over by multinationals. At the same time some Indian companies are becoming multinational companies. An instance of the first is when, Parle drinks was bought by Coca Cola.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India
source.section: Globalisation, Liberalisation and Changes in Indian Industry

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: What is disinvestment?
cards.back: The government is trying to sell its share in several public sector companies, a process which is known as disinvestment.
cards.quote: The government is trying to sell its share in several public sector companies, a process which is known as disinvestment.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India
source.section: Globalisation, Liberalisation and Changes in Indian Industry

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: More and more companies are reducing the number of permanent employees and ____ their work to smaller companies or even to homes.
cards.back: More and more companies are reducing the number of permanent employees and outsourcing their work to smaller companies or even to homes.
cards.quote: More and more companies are reducing the number of permanent employees and outsourcing their work to smaller companies or even to homes.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India
source.section: Globalisation, Liberalisation and Changes in Indian Industry

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: What do developing countries like India provide in the outsourcing done by multinational companies?
cards.back: For multinational companies, this outsourcing is done across the globe, with developing countries like India providing cheap labour.
cards.quote: For multinational companies, this outsourcing is done across the globe, with developing countries like India providing cheap labour.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India
source.section: Globalisation, Liberalisation and Changes in Indian Industry

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Why do small companies keep wages low, and what is difficult in smaller firms?
cards.back: Because small companies have to compete for orders from the big companies, they keep wages low, and working conditions are often poor. It is more difficult for trade unions to organise in smaller firms.
cards.quote: Because small companies have to compete for orders from the big companies, they keep wages low, and working conditions are often poor. It is more difficult for trade unions to organise in smaller firms.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India
source.section: Globalisation, Liberalisation and Changes in Indian Industry

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: To summarise, India is still largely an ____ country.
cards.back: To summarise, India is still largely an agricultural country.
cards.quote: To summarise, India is still largely an agricultural country.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India
source.section: Globalisation, Liberalisation and Changes in Indian Industry

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Why is even the small number in regular salaried employment becoming more insecure?
cards.back: But we also see that very few people in India have access to secure jobs, with even the small number in regular salaried employment becoming more insecure due to the rise in contract labour.
cards.quote: But we also see that very few people in India have access to secure jobs, with even the small number in regular salaried employment becoming more insecure due to the rise in contract labour.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India
source.section: Globalisation, Liberalisation and Changes in Indian Industry

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Some economists debate this, but liberalisation and privatisation worldwide appear to be associated with ____.
cards.back: Some economists debate this, but liberalisation and privatisation worldwide appear to be associated with rising income inequality.
cards.quote: Some economists debate this, but liberalisation and privatisation worldwide appear to be associated with rising income inequality.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India
source.section: Globalisation, Liberalisation and Changes in Indian Industry

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: At the same time as secure employment in large industry is declining, the government is embarking on a policy of ____ for industry.
cards.back: At the same time as secure employment in large industry is declining, the government is embarking on a policy of land acquisition for industry.
cards.quote: At the same time as secure employment in large industry is declining, the government is embarking on a policy of land acquisition for industry.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India
source.section: Globalisation, Liberalisation and Changes in Indian Industry

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: What share of those displaced by land acquisition for industry do adivasis constitute?
cards.back: Many farmers, especially adivasis, who constitute approximately 40% of those displaced, are protesting at the low rates of compensation and the fact that they will be forced to become casual labour living and working on the footpaths of India's big cities.
cards.quote: Many farmers, especially adivasis, who constitute approximately 40% of those displaced, are protesting at the low rates of compensation and the fact that they will be forced to become casual labour living and working on the footpaths of India's big cities.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India
source.section: Globalisation, Liberalisation and Changes in Indian Industry
