cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Through what do only a small percentage of people get jobs?
cards.back: Only a small percentage of people get jobs through advertisements or through the employment exchange.
cards.quote: Only a small percentage of people get jobs through advertisements or through the employment exchange.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: On what do self-employed people, from plumbers to architects, rely to find work?
cards.back: People who are self-employed, like plumbers, electricians and carpenters at one end and teachers who give private tuitions, architects and freelance photographers at the other end, all rely on personal contacts.
cards.quote: People who are self-employed, like plumbers, electricians and carpenters at one end and teachers who give private tuitions, architects and freelance photographers at the other end, all rely on personal contacts.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: In the Kanpur textile mills, these jobbers were known as ____, and were themselves workers.
cards.back: In the Kanpur textile mills, these jobbers were known as mistris, and were themselves workers.
cards.quote: In the Kanpur textile mills, these jobbers were known as mistris, and were themselves workers.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Why did the mistris boss over the workers, though from the same regions and communities?
cards.back: They came from the same regions and communities as the workers, but because they had the owner's backing they bossed over the workers.
cards.quote: They came from the same regions and communities as the workers, but because they had the owner's backing they bossed over the workers.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Who plays a role in recruiting workers now that the jobber's importance has come down?
cards.back: Nowadays, the importance of the jobber has come down, and both management and unions play a role in recruiting their own people.
cards.quote: Nowadays, the importance of the jobber has come down, and both management and unions play a role in recruiting their own people.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Many factories employ ____ workers who substitute for regular permanent workers who are on leave.
cards.back: Many factories employ badli workers who substitute for regular permanent workers who are on leave.
cards.quote: Many factories employ badli workers who substitute for regular permanent workers who are on leave.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: What is it called when badli workers serve for years without the same status and security?
cards.back: Many of these badli workers have actually worked for many years for the same company but are not given the same status and security. This is what is called contract work in the organised sector.
cards.quote: Many of these badli workers have actually worked for many years for the same company but are not given the same status and security. This is what is called contract work in the organised sector.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Name the two important components of employment opportunities.
cards.back:
job in an organisation as a casual wage labourer or regular salaried
Self-employment
cards.quote: Employment opportunities have two important components: (i) job in an organisation as a casual wage labourer or regular salaried (ii) Self-employment

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Name the schemes NCERT lists to generate employment and self-employment.
cards.back:
‘MUDRA’
‘Aatmanirbhar Bharat’
‘Make in India’
cards.quote: Recently the Government of India floated many schemes, such as ‘MUDRA’, ‘Aatmanirbhar Bharat’ and ‘Make in India’ in order to generate employment and self-employment to support all sections including the marginalised section of the society, like SC, ST and other backward classes.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: For what kind of work is the contractor system most visible in hiring?
cards.back: However, the contractor system is most visible in the hiring of casual labour for work at construction sites, brickyards, and so on.
cards.quote: However, the contractor system is most visible in the hiring of casual labour for work at construction sites, brickyards, and so on.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: How does the contractor treat the loan he gives casual labourers?
cards.back: The contractor goes to villages and asks if people want work. He will loan them some money. This loan includes the cost of transport to the work site. The loaned money is treated as an advance wage and the worker works without wages until the loan is repaid.
cards.quote: The contractor goes to villages and asks if people want work. He will loan them some money. This loan includes the cost of transport to the work site. The loaned money is treated as an advance wage and the worker works without wages until the loan is repaid.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: In what sense are casual industrial workers more free than debt-bound agricultural labourers?
cards.back: In the past, agricultural labourers were tied to their landlord by debt. Now, however, by moving to casual industrial work, while they are still in debt, they are not bound by other social obligations to the contractor. In that sense, they are more free in an industrial society.
cards.quote: In the past, agricultural labourers were tied to their landlord by debt. Now, however, by moving to casual industrial work, while they are still in debt, they are not bound by other social obligations to the contractor. In that sense, they are more free in an industrial society.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: The basic task of a manager is to ____ and get more work out of them.
cards.back: The basic task of a manager is to control workers and get more work out of them.
cards.quote: The basic task of a manager is to control workers and get more work out of them.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: The two main ways of making workers produce more.
cards.back:
extend the working hours
increase the amount that is produced within a given time period
cards.quote: There are two main ways of making workers produce more. One is to extend the working hours. The other is to increase the amount that is produced within a given time period.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Machinery helps to increase production, but it also creates the danger that eventually machines will ____.
cards.back: Machinery helps to increase production, but it also creates the danger that eventually machines will replace workers.
cards.quote: Machinery helps to increase production, but it also creates the danger that eventually machines will replace workers.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Which two thinkers saw mechanisation as a danger to employment?
cards.back: Both Marx and Mahatma Gandhi
cards.quote: Both Marx and Mahatma Gandhi saw mechanisation as a danger to employment.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Who said: “What I object to is the craze for machinery, not machinery as such”?
cards.back: Gandhi on Machinery, in Hind Swaraj 1924
cards.quote: Gandhi on Machinery, in Hind Swaraj 1924: “What I object to is the craze for machinery, not machinery as such.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: How did workers in textile mills often describe themselves?
cards.back: Workers in textile mills, which is one of the oldest industries in India, often described themselves as extensions of the machine.
cards.quote: Workers in textile mills, which is one of the oldest industries in India, often described themselves as extensions of the machine.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: The more mechanised an industry gets, the ____ are employed, but they too have to work at the pace of the machine.
cards.back: The more mechanised an industry gets, the fewer people are employed, but they too have to work at the pace of the machine.
cards.quote: The more mechanised an industry gets, the fewer people are employed, but they too have to work at the pace of the machine.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: How do parts suppliers around the Maruti factory send the parts?
cards.back: The parts suppliers are located around the factory and send the parts every two hours or just-in-time.
cards.quote: The parts suppliers are located around the factory and send the parts every two hours or just-in-time.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Why are workers very tense under outsourcing and just-in-time?
cards.back: Outsourcing and just-in-time keeps costs low for the company, but the workers are very tense, because if the supplies fail to arrive, their production targets get delayed, and when they do arrive they have to run to keep up.
cards.quote: Outsourcing and just-in-time keeps costs low for the company, but the workers are very tense, because if the supplies fail to arrive, their production targets get delayed, and when they do arrive they have to run to keep up.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Why has the joint family seemingly re-emerged in places with IT firms and call centres?
cards.back: The joint family, which was supposed to have disappeared with industrialisation, seems to have re-emerged, as grandparents are roped in to help with children.
cards.quote: The joint family, which was supposed to have disappeared with industrialisation, seems to have re-emerged, as grandparents are roped in to help with children.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: What common management practice legitimises extended working hours in the IT sector?
cards.back: ‘flexi-time’
cards.quote: Extended working hours are legitimised by the common management practice of ‘flexi-time’, which in theory gives an employee freedom to choose his or her working hours (within limits) but, which in practice, means that they have to work as long as necessary to finish the task at hand.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: We often hear the phrase ‘____’ to describe the growth of IT sector in India.
cards.back: We often hear the phrase ‘knowledge economy’ to describe the growth of IT sector in India.
cards.quote: We often hear the phrase ‘knowledge economy’ to describe the growth of IT sector in India.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Which sociologist argues that the use of machinery actually deskills workers?
cards.back: Harry Braverman
cards.quote: The famous sociologist, Harry Braverman, argues that the use of machinery actually deskills workers.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: What does the Mines Act 1952 specify, and where has it now been included?
cards.back: The Mines Act 1952, which has now been included in the Occupational Safety, Health and Working Condition Code, 2020, specifies the maximum number of hours a person can be made to work in a week, the need to pay overtime for any extra hours worked and safety rules.
cards.quote: The Mines Act 1952, which has now been included in the Occupational Safety, Health and Working Condition Code, 2020, specifies the maximum number of hours a person can be made to work in a week, the need to pay overtime for any extra hours worked and safety rules.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Where are the Mines Act rules not followed, and what is widespread?
cards.back: These rules may be followed in big companies, but not in smaller mines and quarries. Moreover, sub-contracting is widespread.
cards.quote: These rules may be followed in big companies, but not in smaller mines and quarries. Moreover, sub-contracting is widespread.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Why do many mining contractors avoid responsibility for accidents and benefits?
cards.back: Many contractors do not maintain proper registers of workers, thus avoiding any responsibility for accidents and benefits.
cards.quote: Many contractors do not maintain proper registers of workers, thus avoiding any responsibility for accidents and benefits.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Name the dangers faced by workers in underground mines (NCERT).
cards.back:
flooding
fire
the collapse of roofs and sides
the emission of gases
ventilation failures
cards.quote: Workers in underground mines face very dangerous conditions, due to flooding, fire, the collapse of roofs and sides, the emission of gases and ventilation failures.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Many workers develop breathing problems and diseases like ____ and ____.
cards.back: Many workers develop breathing problems and diseases like tuberculosis and silicosis.
cards.quote: Many workers develop breathing problems and diseases like tuberculosis and silicosis.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: The rate of mining accidents in India is ____ compared to other countries.
cards.back: The rate of mining accidents in India is very high compared to other countries.
cards.quote: The rate of mining accidents in India is very high compared to other countries.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Whom do the fish processing plants along the coastline mostly employ?
cards.back: The fish processing plants along the coastline employ mostly single young women from Tamil Nadu, Karnataka and Kerala.
cards.quote: The fish processing plants along the coastline employ mostly single young women from Tamil Nadu, Karnataka and Kerala.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Where is the nature of work in a globalised economy taking people, and what does it mean for many young women?
cards.back: From a nation of interfering joint families, the nature of work in a globalised economy is taking people in the direction of loneliness and vulnerability. Yet for many young women, it also represents some independence and economic autonomy.
cards.quote: From a nation of interfering joint families, the nature of work in a globalised economy is taking people in the direction of loneliness and vulnerability. Yet for many young women, it also represents some independence and economic autonomy.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Name the products of home-based work listed by NCERT.
cards.back:
lace
zari or brocade
carpets
bidis
agarbattis
cards.quote: This includes the manufacture of lace, zari or brocade, carpets, bidis, agarbattis and many such products.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Who mainly does home-based work such as making lace, zari, carpets, bidis and agarbattis?
cards.back: Home-based work is an important part of the economy. This includes the manufacture of lace, zari or brocade, carpets, bidis, agarbattis and many such products. This work is mainly done by women and children.
cards.quote: Home-based work is an important part of the economy. This includes the manufacture of lace, zari or brocade, carpets, bidis, agarbattis and many such products. This work is mainly done by women and children.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Home workers are paid on a ____ basis, depending on the number of pieces they make.
cards.back: Home workers are paid on a piece-rate basis, depending on the number of pieces they make.
cards.quote: Home workers are paid on a piece-rate basis, depending on the number of pieces they make.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Who provides raw materials to home-based workers and picks up the finished product?
cards.back: An agent
cards.quote: An agent provides raw materials and also picks up the finished product.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: After the government auctions tendu leaves to bidi factory owners, how do the leaves reach home-based workers?
cards.back: The government then auctions the leaves to bidi factory owners who give it to the contractors. The contractor in turn supplies tobacco and leaves to home-based workers.
cards.quote: The government then auctions the leaves to bidi factory owners who give it to the contractors. The contractor in turn supplies tobacco and leaves to home-based workers.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: What is a strike?
cards.back: In a strike, workers do not go to work.
cards.quote: In a strike, workers do not go to work.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: What is a lockout?
cards.back: In a lockout, the management shuts the gate and prevents workers from coming.
cards.quote: In a lockout, the management shuts the gate and prevents workers from coming.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Strike vs lockout: the difference.
cards.back: In a strike, workers do not go to work. In a lockout, the management shuts the gate and prevents workers from coming.
cards.quote: In a strike, workers do not go to work. In a lockout, the management shuts the gate and prevents workers from coming.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Why is calling a strike a difficult decision?
cards.back: To call a strike is a difficult decision as managers may try to use substitute labour. Workers also find it hard to sustain themselves without wages.
cards.quote: To call a strike is a difficult decision as managers may try to use substitute labour. Workers also find it hard to sustain themselves without wages.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Who led the Bombay Textile strike of 1982, and how many workers did it affect?
cards.back: Let us look at one famous strike, the Bombay Textile strike of 1982, which was led by the trade union leader, Dr. Datta Samant, and affected nearly a quarter of a million workers and their families.
cards.quote: Let us look at one famous strike, the Bombay Textile strike of 1982, which was led by the trade union leader, Dr. Datta Samant, and affected nearly a quarter of a million workers and their families.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: How long did the Bombay Textile strike last, and what did the workers want?
cards.back: The strike lasted nearly two years. The workers wanted better wages and also wanted the right to form their own union.
cards.quote: The strike lasted nearly two years. The workers wanted better wages and also wanted the right to form their own union.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: After the Bombay Textile strike, where did workers who lost their jobs go?
cards.back: Nearly one lakh workers lost their jobs and went back to their villages, or took up casual labour, others moved to smaller towns, like Bhiwandi, Malegaon and Icchalkaranji, to work in the powerloom sector.
cards.quote: Nearly one lakh workers lost their jobs and went back to their villages, or took up casual labour, others moved to smaller towns, like Bhiwandi, Malegaon and Icchalkaranji, to work in the powerloom sector.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: What share of India’s people lived in rural areas, according to the 2011 Census?
cards.back: The majority of India’s people live in rural areas (69 per cent, according to the 2011 Census).
cards.quote: The majority of India’s people live in rural areas (69 per cent, according to the 2011 Census).

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: For the many Indians who live by agriculture or related occupations, what is the most important productive resource?
cards.back: They make their living from agriculture or related occupations. This means that agricultural land is the most important productive resource for a great many Indians.
cards.quote: They make their living from agriculture or related occupations. This means that agricultural land is the most important productive resource for a great many Indians.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Pongal, Bihu, Baisakhi and Ugadi are New Year festivals that celebrate what?
cards.back: For example, most of the New Year festivals in different regions of India — such as Pongal in Tamil Nadu, Bihu in Assam, Baisakhi in Punjab and Ugadi in Karnataka to name just a few — actually celebrate the main harvest season and herald the beginning of a new agricultural season.
cards.quote: For example, most of the New Year festivals in different regions of India — such as Pongal in Tamil Nadu, Bihu in Assam, Baisakhi in Punjab and Ugadi in Karnataka to name just a few — actually celebrate the main harvest season and herald the beginning of a new agricultural season.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Since when have the numbers of rural artisans been steadily lessening?
cards.back: Their numbers have been steadily lessening since the colonial period.
cards.quote: Their numbers have been steadily lessening since the colonial period.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: What did the diversity of occupations in rural India reflect in the caste system?
cards.back: The diversity of occupations in rural India was reflected in the caste system, which in most regions included specialist and “service” castes such as Dry Cleaners, Potters and Goldsmiths.
cards.quote: The diversity of occupations in rural India was reflected in the caste system, which in most regions included specialist and “service” castes such as Dry Cleaners, Potters and Goldsmiths.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Many people living in rural areas are employed in, or have livelihoods based on rural ____ activities.
cards.back: Many people living in rural areas are employed in, or have livelihoods based on rural nonfarm activities.
cards.quote: Many people living in rural areas are employed in, or have livelihoods based on rural nonfarm activities.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: In some areas, what share of rural families do not own any land at all?
cards.back: In other areas as much as 40 to 50 per cent of families do not own any land at all.
cards.quote: In other areas as much as 40 to 50 per cent of families do not own any land at all.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India
source.section: 4.1 Agrarian Structure: Caste and Class in Rural India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: In most regions of India, women are usually excluded from ownership of land, because of the prevailing ____ kinship system and mode of inheritance.
cards.back: In most regions of India, women are usually excluded from ownership of land, because of the prevailing patrilineal kinship system and mode of inheritance.
cards.quote: In most regions of India, women are usually excluded from ownership of land, because of the prevailing patrilineal kinship system and mode of inheritance.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India
source.section: 4.1 Agrarian Structure: Caste and Class in Rural India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: What is meant by the term agrarian structure?
cards.back: The term agrarian structure is often used to refer to the structure or distribution of landholding.
cards.quote: The term agrarian structure is often used to refer to the structure or distribution of landholding.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India
source.section: 4.1 Agrarian Structure: Caste and Class in Rural India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Most agricultural labourers are daily-wage workers. And do not have work for many days of the year. This is known as ____.
cards.back: Most agricultural labourers are daily-wage workers. And do not have work for many days of the year. This is known as underemployment.
cards.quote: Most agricultural labourers are daily-wage workers. And do not have work for many days of the year. This is known as underemployment.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India
source.section: 4.1 Agrarian Structure: Caste and Class in Rural India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Who are tenants?
cards.back: tenants (cultivators who lease their land from landowners)
cards.quote: Similarly, tenants (cultivators who lease their land from landowners) have lower incomes than owner-cultivators.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India
source.section: 4.1 Agrarian Structure: Caste and Class in Rural India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: How much of the income from the crop do tenants often pay as rent?
cards.back: Because they have to pay a substantial rent to the landowner – often as much as 50 to 75 per cent of the income from the crop.
cards.quote: Because they have to pay a substantial rent to the landowner – often as much as 50 to 75 per cent of the income from the crop.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India
source.section: 4.1 Agrarian Structure: Caste and Class in Rural India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Why do the Brahmins fall outside the agrarian structure although part of rural society?
cards.back: For instance, in most areas the highest caste, the Brahmins, are not major landowners, and so they fall outside the agrarian structure although they are a part of rural society.
cards.quote: For instance, in most areas the highest caste, the Brahmins, are not major landowners, and so they fall outside the agrarian structure although they are a part of rural society.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India
source.section: 4.1 Agrarian Structure: Caste and Class in Rural India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Define dominant caste (M.N. Srinivas).
cards.back: Such groups were termed by the sociologist M.N. Srinivas as dominant castes. In each region, the dominant caste is the most powerful group, economically and politically, and dominates local society.
cards.quote: Such groups were termed by the sociologist M.N. Srinivas as dominant castes. In each region, the dominant caste is the most powerful group, economically and politically, and dominates local society.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India
source.section: 4.1 Agrarian Structure: Caste and Class in Rural India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Name NCERT’s examples of dominant landowning groups, by region.
cards.back:
the Jats and Rajputs of U.P.
the Vokkaligas and Lingayats in Karnataka
Kammas and Reddis in Andhra Pradesh
Jat Sikhs in Punjab
cards.quote: Examples of dominant landowning groups are the Jats and Rajputs of U.P., the Vokkaligas and Lingayats in Karnataka, Kammas and Reddis in Andhra Pradesh, and Jat Sikhs in Punjab.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India
source.section: 4.1 Agrarian Structure: Caste and Class in Rural India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: What were the former ‘Untouchable’ or dalit castes not allowed to do in many regions?
cards.back: In many regions of India, the former ‘Untouchable’ or dalit castes were not allowed to own land and they provided most of the agricultural labour for the dominant landowning groups.
cards.quote: In many regions of India, the former ‘Untouchable’ or dalit castes were not allowed to own land and they provided most of the agricultural labour for the dominant landowning groups.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India
source.section: 4.1 Agrarian Structure: Caste and Class in Rural India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Where did the most unequal agrarian structures develop (Box 4.1)?
cards.back: In areas of assured irrigation, those with plentiful rainfall or artificial irrigation works (such as rice-growing regions in river deltas, for instance the Kaveri basin in Tamil Nadu) more labour was needed for intensive cultivation. Here the most unequal agrarian structures developed.
cards.quote: In areas of assured irrigation, those with plentiful rainfall or artificial irrigation works (such as rice-growing regions in river deltas, for instance the Kaveri basin in Tamil Nadu) more labour was needed for intensive cultivation. Here the most unequal agrarian structures developed.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India
source.section: 4.1 Agrarian Structure: Caste and Class in Rural India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Until recently, practices such as ____ or free labour were prevalent in many parts of northern India.
cards.back: Until recently, practices such as begar or free labour were prevalent in many parts of northern India.
cards.quote: Until recently, practices such as begar or free labour were prevalent in many parts of northern India.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India
source.section: 4.1 Agrarian Structure: Caste and Class in Rural India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: What did begar require of members of low ranked caste groups?
cards.back: Members of low ranked caste groups had to provide labour for a fixed number of days per year to the village zamindar or landlord.
cards.quote: Members of low ranked caste groups had to provide labour for a fixed number of days per year to the village zamindar or landlord.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India
source.section: 4.1 Agrarian Structure: Caste and Class in Rural India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Who were zamindars?
cards.back: zamindars (landlords who were also politically powerful in their areas, and usually belonged to Kshatriya or other high castes)
cards.quote: Instead, ruling groups such as the local kings or zamindars (landlords who were also politically powerful in their areas, and usually belonged to Kshatriya or other high castes) controlled the land.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: What did the British do with the zamindars and land revenue?
cards.back: Under the British, the zamindars were given more control over land than they had before. Since the colonisers also imposed heavy land revenue (taxes) on agriculture, the zamindars extracted as much produce or money as they could out of the cultivators.
cards.quote: Under the British, the zamindars were given more control over land than they had before. Since the colonisers also imposed heavy land revenue (taxes) on agriculture, the zamindars extracted as much produce or money as they could out of the cultivators.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: What was one result of the zamindari system for agricultural production under British rule?
cards.back: One result of this zamindari system was that agricultural production stagnated or declined during much of the period of British rule.
cards.quote: One result of this zamindari system was that agricultural production stagnated or declined during much of the period of British rule.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: What was the raiyatwari system of land settlement?
cards.back: In other areas that were under direct British rule had what was called the raiyatwari system of land settlement (raiyat means cultivator in Telugu). In this system, the ‘actual cultivators’ (who were themselves often landlords and not cultivators) rather than the zamindars were responsible for paying the tax.
cards.quote: In other areas that were under direct British rule had what was called the raiyatwari system of land settlement (raiyat means cultivator in Telugu). In this system, the ‘actual cultivators’ (who were themselves often landlords and not cultivators) rather than the zamindars were responsible for paying the tax.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Why did raiyatwari areas become relatively more productive and prosperous?
cards.back: Because the colonial government dealt directly with the farmers or landlords, rather than through the overlords, the burden of taxation was less and cultivators had more incentive to invest in agriculture. As a result, these areas became relatively more productive and prosperous.
cards.quote: Because the colonial government dealt directly with the farmers or landlords, rather than through the overlords, the burden of taxation was less and cultivators had more incentive to invest in agriculture. As a result, these areas became relatively more productive and prosperous.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: What marked the dismal agricultural situation in India at Independence?
cards.back:
low productivity
dependence on imported food grains
the intense poverty of a large section of the rural population
cards.quote: This was marked by low productivity, dependence on imported food grains, and the intense poverty of a large section of the rural population.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: When were a series of land reform laws passed in India?
cards.back: From the 1950s to the 1970s, a series of land reform laws were passed – at the national level as well as in the states – that were intended to bring about these changes.
cards.quote: From the 1950s to the 1970s, a series of land reform laws were passed – at the national level as well as in the states – that were intended to bring about these changes.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: The first important legislation was the ____, which removed the layer of intermediaries who stood between the cultivators and the state.
cards.back: The first important legislation was the abolition of the zamindari system, which removed the layer of intermediaries who stood between the cultivators and the state.
cards.quote: The first important legislation was the abolition of the zamindari system, which removed the layer of intermediaries who stood between the cultivators and the state.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: What did the tenancy abolition and regulation acts attempt to do?
cards.back: They attempted either to outlaw tenancy altogether or to regulate rents to give some security to the tenants.
cards.quote: Among the other major land reform laws that were introduced were the tenancy abolition and regulation acts. They attempted either to outlaw tenancy altogether or to regulate rents to give some security to the tenants.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.note: Three major land reform categories: abolition of zamindari, tenancy acts, and Land Ceiling Acts.

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Where did tenancy laws radically restructure the agrarian structure and give tenants land rights?
cards.back: In most of the states, these laws were never implemented very effectively. In West Bengal and Kerala, there was a radical restructuring of the agrarian structure that gave land rights to the tenants.
cards.quote: In most of the states, these laws were never implemented very effectively. In West Bengal and Kerala, there was a radical restructuring of the agrarian structure that gave land rights to the tenants.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: What were the Land Ceiling Acts?
cards.back: The third major category of land reform laws were the Land Ceiling Acts. These laws imposed an upper limit on the amount of land that can be owned by a particular family.
cards.quote: The third major category of land reform laws were the Land Ceiling Acts. These laws imposed an upper limit on the amount of land that can be owned by a particular family.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: What is the state supposed to do with surplus land under the Land Ceiling Acts?
cards.back: According to these acts, the state is supposed to identify and take possession of surplus land (above the ceiling limit) held by each household, and redistribute it to landless families and households in other specified categories, such as SCs and STs.
cards.quote: According to these acts, the state is supposed to identify and take possession of surplus land (above the ceiling limit) held by each household, and redistribute it to landless families and households in other specified categories, such as SCs and STs.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: How did some rich farmers avoid the Land Ceiling Act? What were these called?
cards.back: In some places, some rich farmers actually divorced their wives (but continued to live with them) in order to avoid the provisions of the Land Ceiling Act, which allowed a separate share for unmarried women but not for wives. These were also called ‘benami transfers’.
cards.quote: In some places, some rich farmers actually divorced their wives (but continued to live with them) in order to avoid the provisions of the Land Ceiling Act, which allowed a separate share for unmarried women but not for wives. These were also called ‘benami transfers’.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Though it has changed substantially since colonial times, how does NCERT describe India’s agrarian structure today?
cards.back: On the whole, however, it can be said that the agrarian structure, although it has changed substantially from colonial times to the present, remains highly unequal.
cards.quote: On the whole, however, it can be said that the agrarian structure, although it has changed substantially from colonial times to the present, remains highly unequal.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Land reforms are necessary not only to boost agricultural growth but also to eradicate poverty in rural areas and bring about ____.
cards.back: Land reforms are necessary not only to boost agricultural growth but also to eradicate poverty in rural areas and bring about social justice.
cards.quote: Land reforms are necessary not only to boost agricultural growth but also to eradicate poverty in rural areas and bring about social justice.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: What was the Green Revolution?
cards.back: The Green Revolution, as you know, was a government programme of agricultural modernisation. It was largely funded by international agencies that was based on providing high-yielding variety(HYV) or hybrid seeds along with pesticides, fertilisers, and other inputs, to farmers.
cards.quote: The Green Revolution, as you know, was a government programme of agricultural modernisation. It was largely funded by international agencies that was based on providing high-yielding variety(HYV) or hybrid seeds along with pesticides, fertilisers, and other inputs, to farmers.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India
source.section: 4.3 The Green Revolution and its Social Consequences

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Where were Green Revolution programmes introduced, and which crops did they target?
cards.back: Green Revolution programmes were introduced only in areas that had assured irrigation, because sufficient water was necessary for the new seeds and methods of cultivation. It was also targeted mainly at the wheat and rice-growing areas.
cards.quote: Green Revolution programmes were introduced only in areas that had assured irrigation, because sufficient water was necessary for the new seeds and methods of cultivation. It was also targeted mainly at the wheat and rice-growing areas.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India
source.section: 4.3 The Green Revolution and its Social Consequences

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Name the regions that received the first wave of the Green Revolution package.
cards.back:
the Punjab
western U.P.
coastal Andhra Pradesh
parts of Tamil Nadu
cards.quote: As a result, only certain regions such as the Punjab, western U.P., coastal Andhra Pradesh, and parts of Tamil Nadu, received the first wave of the Green Revolution package.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India
source.section: 4.3 The Green Revolution and its Social Consequences

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: What did the new technology of the Green Revolution achieve for foodgrain production?
cards.back: Agricultural productivity increased sharply because of the new technology. India was able to become self-sufficient in foodgrain production for the first time in decades.
cards.quote: Agricultural productivity increased sharply because of the new technology. India was able to become self-sufficient in foodgrain production for the first time in decades.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India
source.section: 4.3 The Green Revolution and its Social Consequences

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: In most of the Green Revolution areas, it was primarily the ____ who were able to benefit from the new technology.
cards.back: In most of the Green Revolution areas, it was primarily the medium and large farmers who were able to benefit from the new technology.
cards.quote: In most of the Green Revolution areas, it was primarily the medium and large farmers who were able to benefit from the new technology.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India
source.section: 4.3 The Green Revolution and its Social Consequences

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: What is subsistence agriculture, and who are termed peasants?
cards.back: When agriculturists produce primarily for themselves and are unable to produce for the market, it is known as ‘subsistence agriculture’ and they are usually termed ‘peasants’.
cards.quote: When agriculturists produce primarily for themselves and are unable to produce for the market, it is known as ‘subsistence agriculture’ and they are usually termed ‘peasants’.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India
source.section: 4.3 The Green Revolution and its Social Consequences

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Who are agriculturists or farmers (as NCERT uses the term)?
cards.back: Agriculturists or farmers are those who are able to produce surplus, over and above the needs of the family, and so are linked to the market.
cards.quote: Agriculturists or farmers are those who are able to produce surplus, over and above the needs of the family, and so are linked to the market.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India
source.section: 4.3 The Green Revolution and its Social Consequences

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Peasants vs farmers: the difference on producing for the market.
cards.back: When agriculturists produce primarily for themselves and are unable to produce for the market, it is known as ‘subsistence agriculture’ and they are usually termed ‘peasants’. Agriculturists or farmers are those who are able to produce surplus, over and above the needs of the family, and so are linked to the market.
cards.quote: When agriculturists produce primarily for themselves and are unable to produce for the market, it is known as ‘subsistence agriculture’ and they are usually termed ‘peasants’. Agriculturists or farmers are those who are able to produce surplus, over and above the needs of the family, and so are linked to the market.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India
source.section: 4.3 The Green Revolution and its Social Consequences

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: In the first phase of the Green Revolution (1960s and 1970s), what did new technology seem to increase in rural society?
cards.back: Thus, in the first phase of the Green Revolution, in the 1960s and 1970s, the introduction of new technology seemed to be increasing inequalities in rural society.
cards.quote: Thus, in the first phase of the Green Revolution, in the 1960s and 1970s, the introduction of new technology seemed to be increasing inequalities in rural society.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India
source.section: 4.3 The Green Revolution and its Social Consequences

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: What happened to tenant-cultivators in the first phase of the Green Revolution?
cards.back: However, in many cases it led to the displacement of tenant-cultivators. For landowners began to take back land from their tenants and cultivate it directly because cultivation was becoming more profitable. This made the rich farmers better off, and worsened the condition of the landless and marginal holders.
cards.quote: However, in many cases it led to the displacement of tenant-cultivators. For landowners began to take back land from their tenants and cultivate it directly because cultivation was becoming more profitable. This made the rich farmers better off, and worsened the condition of the landless and marginal holders.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India
source.section: 4.3 The Green Revolution and its Social Consequences

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: What did machinery such as tillers, tractors, threshers and harvesters displace?
cards.back: In addition, the introduction of machinery such as tillers, tractors, threshers, and harvesters (in areas such as Punjab and parts of Madhya Pradesh) led to the displacement of the service caste groups who used to carry out these agriculture-related activities. This process of displacement also increased the pace of rural-urban migration.
cards.quote: In addition, the introduction of machinery such as tillers, tractors, threshers, and harvesters (in areas such as Punjab and parts of Madhya Pradesh) led to the displacement of the service caste groups who used to carry out these agriculture-related activities. This process of displacement also increased the pace of rural-urban migration.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India
source.section: 4.3 The Green Revolution and its Social Consequences

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: The ultimate outcome of the Green Revolution was a process of ____, in which the rich grew richer and many of the poor stagnated or grew poorer.
cards.back: The ultimate outcome of the Green Revolution was a process of ‘differentiation’, in which the rich grew richer and many of the poor stagnated or grew poorer.
cards.quote: The ultimate outcome of the Green Revolution was a process of ‘differentiation’, in which the rich grew richer and many of the poor stagnated or grew poorer.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India
source.section: 4.3 The Green Revolution and its Social Consequences

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: How did rising prices and the shift from grain to cash payment affect most rural workers?
cards.back: Moreover, rising prices and a shift in the mode of payment of agricultural workers from payment in kind (grain) to cash, actually worsened the economic condition of most rural workers.
cards.quote: Moreover, rising prices and a shift in the mode of payment of agricultural workers from payment in kind (grain) to cash, actually worsened the economic condition of most rural workers.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India
source.section: 4.3 The Green Revolution and its Social Consequences

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: When did the second phase of the Green Revolution begin, and where?
cards.back: The second phase of the Green Revolution which began in 1980s, farmers living in the dry and semi-arid regions of India began following Green Revolution cultivation practices.
cards.quote: The second phase of the Green Revolution which began in 1980s, farmers living in the dry and semi-arid regions of India began following Green Revolution cultivation practices.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India
source.section: 4.3 The Green Revolution and its Social Consequences

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: What have farmers in most Green Revolution areas switched to from a multi-crop system?
cards.back: In most of the Green Revolution areas, farmers have switched from a multi-crop system, which allowed them to spread risks, to a mono-crop regime, which means that there is nothing to fall back on in case of crop failure.
cards.quote: In most of the Green Revolution areas, farmers have switched from a multi-crop system, which allowed them to spread risks, to a mono-crop regime, which means that there is nothing to fall back on in case of crop failure.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India
source.section: 4.3 The Green Revolution and its Social Consequences

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Where was the Green Revolution promoted more than in the eastern parts of the country?
cards.back: For instance, the Green Revolution was promoted more in the western and southern parts of the country, and in Punjab, Haryana, and western U.P., than in the eastern parts of the country (Das, 1999).
cards.quote: For instance, the Green Revolution was promoted more in the western and southern parts of the country, and in Punjab, Haryana, and western U.P., than in the eastern parts of the country (Das, 1999).

source.book: Social Change and Development in India
source.section: 4.3 The Green Revolution and its Social Consequences

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: What is an entrenched ‘feudal’ agrarian structure?
cards.back: an entrenched ‘feudal’ agrarian structure, in which the landed castes and landlords maintain power over the lower castes, landless workers and small cultivators
cards.quote: There are regions that continue to have an entrenched ‘feudal’ agrarian structure, in which the landed castes and landlords maintain power over the lower castes, landless workers and small cultivators.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India
source.section: 4.3 The Green Revolution and its Social Consequences

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: What kind of knowledge do Indian farmers have about the land they till and the crops they sow?
cards.back: Indian farmers have been cultivating the land for centuries, much before the advent of the Green Revolution. They have very deep and extensive traditional knowledge about the land they till and the crops they sow.
cards.quote: Indian farmers have been cultivating the land for centuries, much before the advent of the Green Revolution. They have very deep and extensive traditional knowledge about the land they till and the crops they sow.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India
source.section: 4.3 The Green Revolution and its Social Consequences

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: What do some scientists and farmers’ movements now suggest, given the negative impact of modern cultivation?
cards.back: In view of the negative environmental and social impact of modern methods of cultivation that have been observed, a number of scientists as well as farmers’ movements now suggest a return to traditional, more organic seeds and methods of cultivation.
cards.quote: In view of the negative environmental and social impact of modern methods of cultivation that have been observed, a number of scientists as well as farmers’ movements now suggest a return to traditional, more organic seeds and methods of cultivation.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India
source.section: 4.3 The Green Revolution and its Social Consequences

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Name the transformations in rural social relations after Independence.
cards.back:
an increase in the use of agricultural labour as cultivation became more intensive
a shift from payment in kind (grain) to payment in cash
a loosening of traditional bonds or hereditary relationships between farmers or landowners and agricultural workers (known as bonded labour)
the rise of a class of ‘free’ wage labourers
cards.quote: These included: an increase in the use of agricultural labour as cultivation became more intensive; a shift from payment in kind (grain) to payment in cash; a loosening of traditional bonds or hereditary relationships between farmers or landowners and agricultural workers (known as bonded labour) and the rise of a class of ‘free’ wage labourers.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India
source.section: 4.4 Transformations in Rural Society after Independence

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Which shift did Jan Breman use to describe the change in landlord-worker relations?
cards.back: The change in the nature of the relationship between landlords (who usually belonged to the dominant castes) and agricultural workers (usually low caste), was described by the sociologist Jan Breman as a shift from ‘patronage to exploitation’ (Breman, 1974).
cards.quote: The change in the nature of the relationship between landlords (who usually belonged to the dominant castes) and agricultural workers (usually low caste), was described by the sociologist Jan Breman as a shift from ‘patronage to exploitation’ (Breman, 1974).

source.book: Social Change and Development in India
source.section: 4.4 Transformations in Rural Society after Independence

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Why is the change in labour relations seen as a transition to capitalist agriculture?
cards.back: The transformation in labour relations is regarded by some scholars as indicative of a transition to capitalist agriculture. Because the capitalist mode of production is based on the separation of the workers from the means of production (in this case, land), and the use of ‘free’ wage labour.
cards.quote: The transformation in labour relations is regarded by some scholars as indicative of a transition to capitalist agriculture. Because the capitalist mode of production is based on the separation of the workers from the means of production (in this case, land), and the use of ‘free’ wage labour.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India
source.section: 4.4 Transformations in Rural Society after Independence

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Name the rural infrastructure the state invested in after Independence.
cards.back:
irrigation facilities
roads
electricity
agricultural inputs, including credit through banks and cooperatives
cards.quote: The state invested in the development of rural infrastructure, such as irrigation facilities, roads and electricity, and on the provision of agricultural inputs, including credit through banks and cooperatives.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India
source.section: 4.4 Transformations in Rural Society after Independence

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Which scheme launched in 2014 aims at uninterrupted power supply to rural India?
cards.back: For regular agricultural growth, uninterupted power supply to rural India is one of the necessities. The ‘Deen Dayal Upadhyaya Gram Jyoti Yojna’ launched in 2014 is a laudable effort of the government of India in this direction.
cards.quote: For regular agricultural growth, uninterupted power supply to rural India is one of the necessities. The ‘Deen Dayal Upadhyaya Gram Jyoti Yojna’ launched in 2014 is a laudable effort of the government of India in this direction.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India
source.section: 4.4 Transformations in Rural Society after Independence

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: How was rural social structure altered by agricultural development since the 1960s?
cards.back: One way in which rural social structure was altered by agricultural development since the 1960s was through the enrichment of the medium and large farmers who adopted the new technologies, discussed in the previous section.
cards.quote: One way in which rural social structure was altered by agricultural development since the 1960s was through the enrichment of the medium and large farmers who adopted the new technologies, discussed in the previous section.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India
source.section: 4.4 Transformations in Rural Society after Independence

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: What did the diversification of dominant-caste farmers’ investments give rise to?
cards.back: This process of diversification gave rise to new entrepreneurial groups that moved out of rural areas and into the growing towns of these developing regions, giving rise to new regional elites that became economically as well as politically dominant (Rutten 1995).
cards.quote: This process of diversification gave rise to new entrepreneurial groups that moved out of rural areas and into the growing towns of these developing regions, giving rise to new regional elites that became economically as well as politically dominant (Rutten 1995).

source.book: Social Change and Development in India
source.section: 4.4 Transformations in Rural Society after Independence

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: How did the spread of higher education in rural areas feed the urban middle classes?
cards.back: Along with this change in the class structure, the spread of higher education, especially private professional colleges, in rural and semi-urban areas, allowed the new rural elites to educate their children – many of whom then joined professional or white collar occupations or started businesses, feeding into the expansion of the urban middle classes.
cards.quote: Along with this change in the class structure, the spread of higher education, especially private professional colleges, in rural and semi-urban areas, allowed the new rural elites to educate their children – many of whom then joined professional or white collar occupations or started businesses, feeding into the expansion of the urban middle classes.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India
source.section: 4.4 Transformations in Rural Society after Independence

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: What has happened to the old landed or cultivating groups in areas of rapid agricultural development?
cards.back: Thus, in areas of rapid agricultural development there has been a consolidation of the old landed or cultivating groups, who have transformed themselves into a dynamic entrepreneurial, rural-urban dominant class.
cards.quote: Thus, in areas of rapid agricultural development there has been a consolidation of the old landed or cultivating groups, who have transformed themselves into a dynamic entrepreneurial, rural-urban dominant class.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India
source.section: 4.4 Transformations in Rural Society after Independence

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Why have eastern U.P. and Bihar seen relatively few changes in the agrarian structure?
cards.back: But in other regions such as eastern U.P. and Bihar, the lack of effective land reforms, political mobilisation, and redistributive measures has meant that there have been relatively few changes in the agrarian structure and hence in the life conditions of most people.
cards.quote: But in other regions such as eastern U.P. and Bihar, the lack of effective land reforms, political mobilisation, and redistributive measures has meant that there have been relatively few changes in the agrarian structure and hence in the life conditions of most people.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India
source.section: 4.4 Transformations in Rural Society after Independence

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: What brought about a substantial transformation of the rural countryside in Kerala?
cards.back: In contrast, states such as Kerala have undergone a different process of development, in which political mobilisation, redistributive measures, and linkages to an external economy (primarily the Gulf countries) have brought about a substantial transformation of the rural countryside.
cards.quote: In contrast, states such as Kerala have undergone a different process of development, in which political mobilisation, redistributive measures, and linkages to an external economy (primarily the Gulf countries) have brought about a substantial transformation of the rural countryside.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India
source.section: 4.4 Transformations in Rural Society after Independence

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: What kind of economy is the rural in Kerala, and on what do many families depend?
cards.back: Far from the rural being primarily agrarian, the rural in Kerala is a mixed economy that integrates some agriculture with a wide network of retail sales and services, and where a large number of families are dependent on remittances from abroad.
cards.quote: Far from the rural being primarily agrarian, the rural in Kerala is a mixed economy that integrates some agriculture with a wide network of retail sales and services, and where a large number of families are dependent on remittances from abroad.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India
source.section: 4.4 Transformations in Rural Society after Independence

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Another significant change in rural society that is linked to the commercialisation of agriculture has been the growth of ____.
cards.back: Another significant change in rural society that is linked to the commercialisation of agriculture has been the growth of migrant agricultural labour.
cards.quote: Another significant change in rural society that is linked to the commercialisation of agriculture has been the growth of migrant agricultural labour.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: How did the pattern of seasonal migration of agricultural workers emerge?
cards.back: As ‘traditional’ bonds of patronage between labourers or tenants and landlords broke down, and as the seasonal demand for agricultural labour increased in prosperous Green Revolution regions such as the Punjab, a pattern of seasonal migration emerged in which thousands of workers circulate between their home villages and more prosperous areas where there is more demand for labour and higher wages.
cards.quote: As ‘traditional’ bonds of patronage between labourers or tenants and landlords broke down, and as the seasonal demand for agricultural labour increased in prosperous Green Revolution regions such as the Punjab, a pattern of seasonal migration emerged in which thousands of workers circulate between their home villages and more prosperous areas where there is more demand for labour and higher wages.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: What term did Jan Breman use for the migrant workers who circulate between home villages and more prosperous farming areas?
cards.back: These migrant workers have been termed ‘footloose labour’ by Jan Breman, but this does not imply freedom.
cards.quote: These migrant workers have been termed ‘footloose labour’ by Jan Breman, but this does not imply freedom.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Why do wealthy farmers often prefer to employ migrant workers?
cards.back: It should be noted here that wealthy farmers often prefer to employ migrant workers for harvesting and other such intensive operations, rather than the local working class, because migrants are more easily exploited and can be paid lower wages.
cards.quote: It should be noted here that wealthy farmers often prefer to employ migrant workers for harvesting and other such intensive operations, rather than the local working class, because migrants are more easily exploited and can be paid lower wages.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: What is the ‘feminisation of agricultural labour force’?
cards.back: Women are also emerging as the main source of agricultural labour, leading to the ‘feminisation of agricultural labour force.’
cards.quote: Women are also emerging as the main source of agricultural labour, leading to the ‘feminisation of agricultural labour force.’

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Why has cultivation become primarily a female task in poor areas?
cards.back: For instance, in poor areas where male family members spend much of the year working outside of their villages, cultivation has become primarily a female task.
cards.quote: For instance, in poor areas where male family members spend much of the year working outside of their villages, cultivation has become primarily a female task.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Why is the insecurity of women agricultural workers greater?
cards.back: The insecurity of women is greater because they earn lower wages than men for similar work.
cards.quote: The insecurity of women is greater because they earn lower wages than men for similar work.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: What does India’s liberalisation policy entail with respect to the WTO?
cards.back: The policy entails participation in the World Trade Organization (WTO), which aims to bring about a more free international trading system and requires the opening up of Indian markets to imports.
cards.quote: The policy entails participation in the World Trade Organization (WTO), which aims to bring about a more free international trading system and requires the opening up of Indian markets to imports.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: To what have Indian farmers been exposed after decades of state support and protected markets?
cards.back: After decades of state support and protected markets, Indian farmers have been exposed to competition from the global market.
cards.quote: After decades of state support and protected markets, Indian farmers have been exposed to competition from the global market.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: What is the globalisation of agriculture?
cards.back: the incorporation of agriculture into the larger global market
cards.quote: These are indicators of the process of globalisation of agriculture, or the incorporation of agriculture into the larger global market

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: What do farmers in Punjab and Karnataka do with multinational companies such as PepsiCo?
cards.back: For instance, in some regions such as Punjab and Karnataka, farmers enter into contracts with multinational companies (such as PepsiCo) to grow certain crops (such as tomatoes and potatoes), which the companies then buy from them for processing or export.
cards.quote: For instance, in some regions such as Punjab and Karnataka, farmers enter into contracts with multinational companies (such as PepsiCo) to grow certain crops (such as tomatoes and potatoes), which the companies then buy from them for processing or export.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: What is contract farming?
cards.back: In such ‘contract farming’ systems, the company identifies the crop to be grown, provides the seeds and other inputs, as well as the know-how and often also the working capital. In return, the farmer is assured of a market because the company guarantees that it will purchase the produce at a predetermined fixed price.
cards.quote: In such ‘contract farming’ systems, the company identifies the crop to be grown, provides the seeds and other inputs, as well as the know-how and often also the working capital. In return, the farmer is assured of a market because the company guarantees that it will purchase the produce at a predetermined fixed price.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Name the specialised items for which contract farming is very common.
cards.back:
cut flowers
fruits such as grapes, figs and pomegranates
cotton and oilseeds
cards.quote: Contract farming is very common now in the production of specialised items such as cut flowers, fruits such as grapes, figs and pomegranates, cotton and oilseeds.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: How can contract farming lead to greater insecurity for farmers?
cards.back: While contract farming appears to provide financial security to farmers, it can also lead to greater insecurity as farmers become dependent on these companies for their livelihoods.
cards.quote: While contract farming appears to provide financial security to farmers, it can also lead to greater insecurity as farmers become dependent on these companies for their livelihoods.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: What does contract farming of export-oriented products such as flowers and gherkins mean for land?
cards.back: Contract farming of export-oriented products such as flowers and gherkins also means that agricultural land is diverted away from food grain production.
cards.quote: Contract farming of export-oriented products such as flowers and gherkins also means that agricultural land is diverted away from food grain production.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: What is the sociological significance of contract farming?
cards.back: Contract farming has sociological significance in that it disengages many people from the production process and makes their own indigenous knowledge of agriculture irrelevant.
cards.quote: Contract farming has sociological significance in that it disengages many people from the production process and makes their own indigenous knowledge of agriculture irrelevant.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Why is contract farming often not ecologically sustainable?
cards.back: In addition, contract farming caters primarily to the production of elite items, and because it usually requires high doses of fertilisers and pesticides, it is often not ecologically sustainable.
cards.quote: In addition, contract farming caters primarily to the production of elite items, and because it usually requires high doses of fertilisers and pesticides, it is often not ecologically sustainable.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: What is the more widespread aspect of the globalisation of agriculture?
cards.back: Another, and more widespread aspect of the globalisation of agriculture is the entry of multinationals into this sector as sellers of agricultural inputs such as seeds, pesticides and fertilisers.
cards.quote: Another, and more widespread aspect of the globalisation of agriculture is the entry of multinationals into this sector as sellers of agricultural inputs such as seeds, pesticides and fertilisers.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: What has the increased dependence on expensive fertilisers and pesticides led to?
cards.back: This has led to the increased dependence of farmers on expensive fertilisers and pesticides, which has reduced their profits, put many farmers into debt, and also created an ecological crisis in rural areas.
cards.quote: This has led to the increased dependence of farmers on expensive fertilisers and pesticides, which has reduced their profits, put many farmers into debt, and also created an ecological crisis in rural areas.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Since when have farmers’ suicides occurred, and to what are they linked (Box 4.3)?
cards.back: The spate of farmers’ suicides that has been occurring in different parts of the country since 1997–98 can be linked to the ‘agrarian distress’ caused by structural changes in agriculture and changes in economic and agricultural policies.
cards.quote: The spate of farmers’ suicides that has been occurring in different parts of the country since 1997–98 can be linked to the ‘agrarian distress’ caused by structural changes in agriculture and changes in economic and agricultural policies.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Name the causes of agrarian distress listed in Box 4.3.
cards.back:
the changed pattern of landholdings
changing cropping patterns, especially due to shift to cash crops
liberalisation policies that have exposed Indian agriculture to the forces of globalisation
heavy dependence on high-cost inputs
withdrawal of the State from agricultural extension activities to be replaced by multinational seed and fertiliser companies
decline in state support for agriculture
individualisation of agricultural operations
cards.quote: These include: the changed pattern of landholdings; changing cropping patterns, especially due to shift to cash crops; liberalisation policies that have exposed Indian agriculture to the forces of globalisation; heavy dependence on high-cost inputs; withdrawal of the State from agricultural extension activities to be replaced by multinational seed and fertiliser companies; decline in state support for agriculture; and individualisation of agricultural operations.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: How many farmer suicides were officially recorded between 2001 and 2006, and where?
cards.back: According to official statistics, there have been 8,900 suicides by farmers between 2001 and 2006 in Andhra Pradesh, Karnataka, Kerala and Maharashtra (Suri 2006:1523).
cards.quote: According to official statistics, there have been 8,900 suicides by farmers between 2001 and 2006 in Andhra Pradesh, Karnataka, Kerala and Maharashtra (Suri 2006:1523).

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Who were many of the farmers who committed suicide, and what were they attempting?
cards.back: Many farmers, who have committed suicide were marginal farmers, who were attempting to increase their productivity, primarily by practising Green Revolution methods.
cards.quote: Many farmers, who have committed suicide were marginal farmers, who were attempting to increase their productivity, primarily by practising Green Revolution methods.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: What risks did Green Revolution methods bring for marginal farmers?
cards.back: However, undertaking such production meant facing several risks: the cost of production has increased tremendously due to a decrease in agricultural subsidies, the markets are not stable, and many farmers borrow heavily in order to invest in expensive inputs and improve their production.
cards.quote: However, undertaking such production meant facing several risks: the cost of production has increased tremendously due to a decrease in agricultural subsidies, the markets are not stable, and many farmers borrow heavily in order to invest in expensive inputs and improve their production.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: With what is the suicide of farmers basically associated?
cards.back: Suicides of farmers is basically associated with debt, as well as, natural disasters, resulting in the failure of agricutural produce.
cards.quote: Suicides of farmers is basically associated with debt, as well as, natural disasters, resulting in the failure of agricutural produce.
