cards.front: NCERT’s everyday example of tradition being modified: how the modern middle class woman wears the sari.
cards.back: Traditionally the sari, a loose unstitched piece of cloth was differently worn in different regions. The standard way that the modern middle class woman wears it was a novel combination of the traditional sari with the western ‘petticoat’ and ‘blouse’.
cards.quote: Traditionally the sari, a loose unstitched piece of cloth was differently worn in different regions. The standard way that the modern middle class woman wears it was a novel combination of the traditional sari with the western ‘petticoat’ and ‘blouse’.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.unit: Process of Social Change in India
cards.front: Who coined the term sanskritisation?
cards.back: The term sanskritisation was coined by M.N. Srinivas.
cards.quote: The term sanskritisation was coined by M.N. Srinivas.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India
source.section: 2.3 Different Kinds of Social Change: Sanskritisation

cards.subject: sociology
cards.unit: Process of Social Change in India
cards.front: Define sanskritisation (M.N. Srinivas).
cards.back: the process by which a ‘low’ caste or tribe or other group takes over the customs, ritual, beliefs, ideology and style of life of a high and, in particular, a ‘twice-born (dwija) caste’
cards.quote: It may be briefly defined as the process by which a ‘low’ caste or tribe or other group takes over the customs, ritual, beliefs, ideology and style of life of a high and, in particular, a ‘twice-born (dwija) caste’.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India
source.section: 2.3 Different Kinds of Social Change: Sanskritisation

cards.subject: sociology
cards.unit: Process of Social Change in India
cards.front: Name the areas in which the influence of sanskritisation can be seen.
cards.back:
language
literature
ideology
music
dance
drama
style of life
ritual
cards.quote: Its influence can be seen in language, literature, ideology, music, dance, drama, style of life and ritual.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India
source.section: 2.3 Different Kinds of Social Change: Sanskritisation

cards.subject: sociology
cards.unit: Process of Social Change in India
cards.front: What is ‘sanskritisation’?
cards.back: ‘Sanskritisation’ refers to a process whereby members of a (usually middle or lower) caste attempt to raise their own social status by adopting the ritual, domestic and social practices of a caste (or castes) of higher status.
cards.quote: ‘Sanskritisation’ refers to a process whereby members of a (usually middle or lower) caste attempt to raise their own social status by adopting the ritual, domestic and social practices of a caste (or castes) of higher status.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.note: Sanskritisation: a lower or middle caste copies the practices of a higher caste to rise in status.

cards.subject: sociology
cards.unit: Process of Social Change in India
cards.front: Within which space does Sanskritisation primarily take place, though Srinivas saw it outside Hinduism too?
cards.back: It is primarily a process that takes place within the Hindu space though Srinivas argued that it was visible even in sects and religious groups outside Hinduism.
cards.quote: It is primarily a process that takes place within the Hindu space though Srinivas argued that it was visible even in sects and religious groups outside Hinduism.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India
source.section: 2.3 Different Kinds of Social Change: Sanskritisation

cards.subject: sociology
cards.unit: Process of Social Change in India
cards.front: In those areas where a ____ was dominant, the culture of the entire region underwent a certain amount of Sanskritisation.
cards.back: In those areas where a highly Sanskritised caste was dominant, the culture of the entire region underwent a certain amount of Sanskritisation.
cards.quote: In those areas where a highly Sanskritised caste was dominant, the culture of the entire region underwent a certain amount of Sanskritisation.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India
source.section: 2.3 Different Kinds of Social Change: Sanskritisation

cards.subject: sociology
cards.unit: Process of Social Change in India
cards.front: In regions where the non-Sanskritic castes were dominant, it was their influence that was stronger. This can be termed the process of ‘____’.
cards.back: In regions where the non-Sanskritic castes were dominant, it was their influence that was stronger. This can be termed the process of ‘de-Sanskritisation’.
cards.quote: In regions where the non-Sanskritic castes were dominant, it was their influence that was stronger. This can be termed the process of ‘de-Sanskritisation’.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India
source.section: 2.3 Different Kinds of Social Change: Sanskritisation

cards.subject: sociology
cards.unit: Process of Social Change in India
cards.front: In Punjab, which influence was dominant for many centuries until the third quarter of the 19th century?
cards.back: For many centuries until the third quarter of the 19th century, the Persian influence was the dominant one.
cards.quote: In Punjab culturally Sanskritic influence was never very strong. For many centuries until the third quarter of the 19th century, the Persian influence was the dominant one.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India
source.section: 2.3 Different Kinds of Social Change: Sanskritisation

cards.subject: sociology
cards.unit: Process of Social Change in India
cards.front: What is the usual effect of the Sanskritisation of a group, according to Srinivas?
cards.back: the Sanskritisation of a group has usually the effect of improving its position in the local caste hierarchy.
cards.quote: the Sanskritisation of a group has usually the effect of improving its position in the local caste hierarchy.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India
source.section: 2.3 Different Kinds of Social Change: Sanskritisation

cards.subject: sociology
cards.unit: Process of Social Change in India
cards.front: Sanskritisation normally presupposes which two things (Srinivas)?
cards.back:
an improvement in the economic or political position of the group concerned
a higher group self-consciousness resulting from its contact with a source of the ‘Great Tradition’ of Hinduism such as a pilgrim centre or a monastery or a proselytising sect
cards.quote: It normally presupposes either an improvement in the economic or political position of the group concerned or a higher group self-consciousness resulting from its contact with a source of the ‘Great Tradition’ of Hinduism such as a pilgrim centre or a monastery or a proselytising sect.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India
source.section: 2.3 Different Kinds of Social Change: Sanskritisation

cards.subject: sociology
cards.unit: Process of Social Change in India
cards.front: First criticism of sanskritisation: what has it been criticised for exaggerating?
cards.back: One, it has been criticised for exaggerating social mobility or the scope of ‘lower castes’ to move up the social ladder.
cards.quote: One, it has been criticised for exaggerating social mobility or the scope of ‘lower castes’ to move up the social ladder.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India
source.section: 2.3 Different Kinds of Social Change: Sanskritisation

cards.subject: sociology
cards.unit: Process of Social Change in India
cards.front: Second criticism of sanskritisation: what does its ideology accept?
cards.back: Two, it has been pointed out that the ideology of sanskritisation accepts the ways of the ‘upper caste’ as superior and that of the ‘lower caste’ as inferior.
cards.quote: Two, it has been pointed out that the ideology of sanskritisation accepts the ways of the ‘upper caste’ as superior and that of the ‘lower caste’ as inferior.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India
source.section: 2.3 Different Kinds of Social Change: Sanskritisation

cards.subject: sociology
cards.unit: Process of Social Change in India
cards.front: Third criticism of sanskritisation: what model does it seem to justify?
cards.back: Third, ‘sanskritisation’ seems to justify a model that rests on inequality and exclusion.
cards.quote: Third, ‘sanskritisation’ seems to justify a model that rests on inequality and exclusion.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India
source.section: 2.3 Different Kinds of Social Change: Sanskritisation

cards.subject: sociology
cards.unit: Process of Social Change in India
cards.front: Fourth criticism of sanskritisation: what practices does adopting upper caste rites and rituals lead to (the gender angle)?
cards.back: Fourth, since sanskritisation results in the adoption of upper caste rites and rituals it leads to practices of secluding girls and women, adopting dowry practices instead of bride-price and practising caste discrimination against other groups, etc.
cards.quote: Fourth, since sanskritisation results in the adoption of upper caste rites and rituals it leads to practices of secluding girls and women, adopting dowry practices instead of bride-price and practising caste discrimination against other groups, etc.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India
source.section: 2.3 Different Kinds of Social Change: Sanskritisation

cards.subject: sociology
cards.unit: Process of Social Change in India
cards.front: Fifth criticism of sanskritisation: what is eroded?
cards.back: Fifth, the effect of such a trend is that the key characteristics of dalit culture and society are eroded.
cards.quote: Fifth, the effect of such a trend is that the key characteristics of dalit culture and society are eroded.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India
source.section: 2.3 Different Kinds of Social Change: Sanskritisation

cards.subject: sociology
cards.unit: Process of Social Change in India
cards.front: For example the very worth of labour which ‘lower castes’ do is degraded and rendered ‘____’.
cards.back: For example the very worth of labour which ‘lower castes’ do is degraded and rendered ‘shameful’.
cards.quote: For example the very worth of labour which ‘lower castes’ do is degraded and rendered ‘shameful’.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India
source.section: 2.3 Different Kinds of Social Change: Sanskritisation

cards.subject: sociology
cards.unit: Process of Social Change in India
cards.front: With the growth of which movement did several Indian languages try to drop Sanskrit words and phrases in the twentieth century?
cards.back: With the growth of the anti-Brahminical movement and the development of regional self-consciousness in the twentieth century there was an attempt in several Indian languages to drop Sanskrit words and phrases.
cards.quote: With the growth of the anti-Brahminical movement and the development of regional self-consciousness in the twentieth century there was an attempt in several Indian languages to drop Sanskrit words and phrases.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India
source.section: 2.3 Different Kinds of Social Change: Sanskritisation

cards.subject: sociology
cards.unit: Process of Social Change in India
cards.front: A crucial result of the Backward Classes Movement was to emphasise the role of ____ in the upward mobility of caste groups and individuals.
cards.back: A crucial result of the Backward Classes Movement was to emphasise the role of secular factors in the upward mobility of caste groups and individuals.
cards.quote: A crucial result of the Backward Classes Movement was to emphasise the role of secular factors in the upward mobility of caste groups and individuals.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India
source.section: 2.3 Different Kinds of Social Change: Sanskritisation

cards.subject: sociology
cards.unit: Process of Social Change in India
cards.front: What have recent years seen among Dalits regarding their identity?
cards.back: Recent years have seen likewise assertions of Dalits who now pride their identity as Dalits.
cards.quote: Recent years have seen likewise assertions of Dalits who now pride their identity as Dalits.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India
source.section: 2.3 Different Kinds of Social Change: Sanskritisation

cards.subject: sociology
cards.unit: Process of Social Change in India
cards.front: Define westernisation (M.N. Srinivas).
cards.back: the changes brought about in Indian society and culture as a result of over 150 years of British rule, the term subsuming changes occurring at different levels…technology, institutions, ideology and values
cards.quote: M.N. Srinivas defines westernisation as “the changes brought about in Indian society and culture as a result of over 150 years of British rule, the term subsuming changes occurring at different levels…technology, institutions, ideology and values”.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India
source.section: 2.3 Different Kinds of Social Change: Westernisation

cards.subject: sociology
cards.unit: Process of Social Change in India
cards.front: NCERT’s example of the general spread of Western cultural traits in middle class homes.
cards.back: Across the country a very wide section of middle class homes have a television set, a fridge, some kind of sofa set, a dining table and chair in the living room.
cards.quote: Across the country a very wide section of middle class homes have a television set, a fridge, some kind of sofa set, a dining table and chair in the living room.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India
source.section: 2.3 Different Kinds of Social Change: Westernisation

cards.subject: sociology
cards.unit: Process of Social Change in India
cards.front: Westernisation does involve the imitation of ____ of culture.
cards.back: Westernisation does involve the imitation of external forms of culture.
cards.quote: Westernisation does involve the imitation of external forms of culture.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India
source.section: 2.3 Different Kinds of Social Change: Westernisation

cards.subject: sociology
cards.unit: Process of Social Change in India
cards.front: Does westernisation necessarily mean that people adopt modern values?
cards.back: It does not necessarily mean that people adopt modern values of democracy and equality.
cards.quote: It does not necessarily mean that people adopt modern values of democracy and equality.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India
source.section: 2.3 Different Kinds of Social Change: Westernisation

cards.subject: sociology
cards.unit: Process of Social Change in India
cards.front: NCERT’s example of a practice that combines a discriminatory attitude towards women with very modern technology.
cards.back: The practice of female foeticide combines discriminatory attitude towards women and the use of very modern technology.
cards.quote: The practice of female foeticide combines discriminatory attitude towards women and the use of very modern technology.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India
source.section: 2.3 Different Kinds of Social Change: Westernisation

cards.subject: sociology
cards.unit: Process of Social Change in India
cards.front: Which artists and writers does NCERT name as grappling with the colonial encounter?
cards.back: Artists like Ravi Varma, Abanindranath Tagore, Chandu Menon and Bankimchandra Chattopadhya were all grappling with the colonial encounter.
cards.quote: Apart from ways of life and thinking, the west influenced Indian art and literature. Artists like Ravi Varma, Abanindranath Tagore, Chandu Menon and Bankimchandra Chattopadhya were all grappling with the colonial encounter.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India
source.section: 2.3 Different Kinds of Social Change: Westernisation

cards.subject: sociology
cards.unit: Process of Social Change in India
cards.front: NCERT’s example (Raja Ravi Varma’s portrait) of a matrilineal Kerala family resembling the western nuclear family.
cards.back: It discusses the portrait of a family in a matrilineal community of Kerala but one that significantly resembles the very typical patrilineal nuclear family of the modern west consisting of the father, mother and children.
cards.quote: It discusses the portrait of a family in a matrilineal community of Kerala but one that significantly resembles the very typical patrilineal nuclear family of the modern west consisting of the father, mother and children.

source.section: 2.3 Different Kinds of Social Change: Westernisation

cards.subject: sociology
cards.unit: Process of Social Change in India
cards.front: In the contemporary context often conflicts between ____ are seen as cultural conflicts resulting from westernisation.
cards.back: In the contemporary context often conflicts between generations are seen as cultural conflicts resulting from westernisation.
cards.quote: In the contemporary context often conflicts between generations are seen as cultural conflicts resulting from westernisation.

cards.subject: sociology
cards.unit: Process of Social Change in India
cards.front: Srinivas: which process did ‘lower castes’ seek and which did ‘upper castes’ seek?
cards.back: Srinivas suggested that while ‘lower castes’ sought to be Sanskritised, ‘upper castes’ sought to be Westernised.
cards.quote: Srinivas suggested that while ‘lower castes’ sought to be Sanskritised, ‘upper castes’ sought to be Westernised.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India
source.section: 2.3 Different Kinds of Social Change: Westernisation

cards.unit: Process of Social Change in India
cards.front: NCERT’s example that ‘lower castes’ also sought westernisation: the Thiyyas of Kerala.
cards.back: For instance, studies of Thiyyas (by no means considered ‘upper caste’) in Kerala show conscious efforts to westernise. Elite Thiyyas appropriated British culture as a move towards a more cosmopolitan life that critiqued caste.
cards.quote: For instance, studies of Thiyyas (by no means considered ‘upper caste’) in Kerala show conscious efforts to westernise. Elite Thiyyas appropriated British culture as a move towards a more cosmopolitan life that critiqued caste.

cards.unit: Process of Social Change in India

cards.back: Likewise, Western education often implied opening up to new opportunities for different groups of people in the North-East.
cards.quote: Likewise, Western education often implied opening up to new opportunities for different groups of people in the North-East.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India
source.section: 2.3 Different Kinds of Social Change: Westernisation

cards.subject: sociology
cards.unit: Process of Social Change in India
cards.front: In the early years, what did modernisation refer to?
cards.back: In the early years, modernisation referred to improvement in technology and production processes.
cards.quote: In the early years, modernisation referred to improvement in technology and production processes.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.unit: Process of Social Change in India
cards.front: In its wider usage, modernisation referred to the path of development that much of which regions has taken?
cards.back: It referred to the path of development that much of west Europe or North America has taken. And suggested that other societies both have to and ought to follow the same path of development.
cards.quote: It referred to the path of development that much of west Europe or North America has taken. And suggested that other societies both have to and ought to follow the same path of development.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.unit: Process of Social Change in India
cards.front: In India the beginnings of capitalism, as we saw in Chapter 1, took place within the ____.
cards.back: In India the beginnings of capitalism, as we saw in Chapter 1, took place within the colonial context.
cards.quote: In India the beginnings of capitalism, as we saw in Chapter 1, took place within the colonial context.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.unit: Process of Social Change in India
cards.front: Name the features of ‘modernity’ (Rudolph and Rudolph, 1967).
cards.back:
local ties and parochial perspectives give way to universal commitments and cosmopolitan attitudes
the truths of utility, calculation, and science take precedence over those of the emotions, the sacred, and the non-rational
the individual rather than the group be the primary unit of society and politics
the associations in which men live and work be based on choice not birth
mastery rather than fatalism orient their attitude toward the material and human environment
identity be chosen and achieved, not ascribed and affirmed
work be separated from family, residence, and community in bureaucratic organisation
cards.quote: ‘[M]odernity’ assumes that local ties and parochial perspectives give way to universal commitments and cosmopolitan attitudes; that the truths of utility, calculation, and science take precedence over those of the emotions, the sacred, and the non-rational; that the individual rather than the group be the primary unit of society and politics; that the associations in which men live and work be based on choice not birth; that mastery rather than fatalism orient their attitude toward the material and human environment; that identity be chosen and achieved, not ascribed and affirmed; that work be separated from family, residence, and community in bureaucratic organisation….

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.unit: Process of Social Change in India
cards.front: In Rudolph and Rudolph’s account of modernity, what rather than fatalism orients attitude to the material and human environment?
cards.back: that mastery rather than fatalism orient their attitude toward the material and human environment
cards.quote: that mastery rather than fatalism orient their attitude toward the material and human environment

cards.back: In other words it means that people are influenced not just by local but universal contexts.

cards.subject: sociology
cards.unit: Process of Social Change in India
cards.front: What job you wish to do is decided not by the job your parent does, but by what you wish to do. Work gets based on ____, not birth.

cards.unit: Process of Social Change in India
cards.front: All theorists of modernisation assume that modern societies become what?

cards.unit: Process of Social Change in India

cards.back: Recent years have, however, seen an unprecedented growth of religious consciousness and conflict world over.
cards.quote: Recent years have, however, seen an unprecedented growth of religious consciousness and conflict world over.

cards.subject: sociology
cards.unit: Process of Social Change in India
cards.front: You will recall how western and modern forms of communication, organisation and ideas led to the emergence of new kinds of ____.

cards.unit: Process of Social Change in India

cards.back: Furthermore, a considerable part of ritual in India has direct reference to the pursuit of secular ends.

cards.unit: Process of Social Change in India

cards.unit: Process of Social Change in India
cards.front: What is meant by the ‘secularisation of caste’?

cards.quote: Today it often functions as political pressure groups. Contemporary India has seen such formation of caste associations and caste based political parties. They seek to press upon the state their demands. Such a changed role of caste has been described as secularisation of caste.

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Define demography.
cards.back: Demography is the systematic study of population.
cards.quote: Demography is the systematic study of population.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: From which two Greek words does ‘demography’ come, and what do they mean?
cards.back: The term is of Greek origin and is composed of the two words, demos (people) and graphein (describe), implying the description of people.
cards.quote: The term is of Greek origin and is composed of the two words, demos (people) and graphein (describe), implying the description of people.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: What does demography study?
cards.back:
changes in population size
patterns of births, deaths, and migration
the structure and composition of the population, such as the relative proportions of women, men and different age groups
cards.quote: Demography studies the trends and processes associated with population including – changes in population size; patterns of births, deaths, and migration; and the structure and composition of the population, such as the relative proportions of women, men and different age groups.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Formal demography vs social demography: the difference in nature or focus.
cards.back: There are different varieties of demography, including formal demography which is a largely quantitative field, and social demography which focuses on the social, economic or political aspects of populations.
cards.quote: There are different varieties of demography, including formal demography which is a largely quantitative field, and social demography which focuses on the social, economic or political aspects of populations.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: On what processes are all demographic studies based?
cards.back: All demographic studies are based on processes of counting or enumeration – such as the census or the survey – which involve the systematic collection of data on the people residing within a specified territory.
cards.quote: All demographic studies are based on processes of counting or enumeration – such as the census or the survey – which involve the systematic collection of data on the people residing within a specified territory.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Which two processes in Europe in the late eighteenth century tied demography to the rise of sociology?
cards.back: Two different processes happened to take place at roughly the same time in Europe during the latter half of the eighteenth century – the formation of nation-states as the principal form of political organisation, and the beginnings of the modern science of statistics.
cards.quote: Two different processes happened to take place at roughly the same time in Europe during the latter half of the eighteenth century – the formation of nation-states as the principal form of political organisation, and the beginnings of the modern science of statistics.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: The American census of ____ was probably the first modern census
cards.back: The American census of 1790 was probably the first modern census
cards.quote: The American census of 1790 was probably the first modern census

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: When did censuses begin in India, and since when have regular decennial censuses been held?
cards.back: In India, censuses began to be conducted by the British Indian government between 1867–72, and regular ten yearly (or decennial) censuses have been conducted since 1881.
cards.quote: In India, censuses began to be conducted by the British Indian government between 1867–72, and regular ten yearly (or decennial) censuses have been conducted since 1881.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: How many decennial censuses has independent India conducted since 1951, and which was the latest?
cards.back: Independent India continued the practice, and seven decennial censuses have been conducted since 1951, the most recent being in 2011.
cards.quote: Independent India continued the practice, and seven decennial censuses have been conducted since 1951, the most recent being in 2011.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Why is the Indian census the largest such exercise in the world, although China has a slightly larger population?
cards.back: The Indian census is the largest such exercise in the world (since China, which has a slightly larger population, does not conduct regular censuses).
cards.quote: The Indian census is the largest such exercise in the world (since China, which has a slightly larger population, does not conduct regular censuses).

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: What did Durkheim argue about the rate of suicide?
cards.back: Durkheim argued that the rate of suicide (i.e., number of suicides per 100,000 population) had to be explained by social causes even though each particular instance of suicide may have involved reasons specific to that individual or her/his circumstances.
cards.quote: Durkheim argued that the rate of suicide (i.e., number of suicides per 100,000 population) had to be explained by social causes even though each particular instance of suicide may have involved reasons specific to that individual or her/his circumstances.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: What is formal demography?
cards.back: Formal demography is primarily concerned with the measurement and analysis of the components of population change.
cards.quote: Formal demography is primarily concerned with the measurement and analysis of the components of population change.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: What is population studies or social demography?
cards.back: Population studies or social demography, on the other hand, enquires into the wider causes and consequences of population structures and change.
cards.quote: Population studies or social demography, on the other hand, enquires into the wider causes and consequences of population structures and change.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Which English political economist (1766–1834) is associated with a famous theory of population growth?
cards.back: Among the most famous theories of demography is the one associated with the English political economist Thomas Robert Malthus (1766–1834).
cards.quote: Among the most famous theories of demography is the one associated with the English political economist Thomas Robert Malthus (1766–1834).

source.book: Indian Society
source.section: The Malthusian Theory of Population Growth

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: In which work and year did Malthus outline his theory of population growth?
cards.back: Malthus’s theory of population growth – outlined in his Essay on Population (1798) – was a rather pessimistic one.
cards.quote: Malthus’s theory of population growth – outlined in his Essay on Population (1798) – was a rather pessimistic one.

source.book: Indian Society
source.section: The Malthusian Theory of Population Growth

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: What did Malthus argue about the growth of human populations and of the means of subsistence?
cards.back: He argued that human populations tend to grow at a much faster rate than the rate at which the means of human subsistence (specially food, but also clothing and other agriculture-based products) can grow.
cards.quote: He argued that human populations tend to grow at a much faster rate than the rate at which the means of human subsistence (specially food, but also clothing and other agriculture-based products) can grow.

source.book: Indian Society
source.section: The Malthusian Theory of Population Growth

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Malthus: growth of population vs growth of agricultural production.
cards.back: While population rises in geometric progression (i.e., like 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, etc.), agricultural production can only grow in arithmetic progression (i.e., like 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, etc.).
cards.quote: While population rises in geometric progression (i.e., like 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, etc.), agricultural production can only grow in arithmetic progression (i.e., like 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, etc.).

source.book: Indian Society
source.section: The Malthusian Theory of Population Growth

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: According to Malthus, what is the only way to increase prosperity?
cards.back: Because population growth always outstrips growth in production of subsistence resources, the only way to increase prosperity is by controlling the growth of population.
cards.quote: Because population growth always outstrips growth in production of subsistence resources, the only way to increase prosperity is by controlling the growth of population.

source.book: Indian Society
source.section: The Malthusian Theory of Population Growth

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Types of checks to population growth in Malthus’s theory, with their forms.
cards.back:
‘preventive checks’ such as postponing marriage or practicing sexual abstinence or celibacy
‘positive checks’ to population growth – in the form of famines and diseases
cards.quote: Unfortunately, humanity has only a limited ability to voluntarily reduce the growth of its population (through ‘preventive checks’ such as postponing marriage or practicing sexual abstinence or celibacy). Malthus believed therefore that ‘positive checks’ to population growth – in the form of famines and diseases – were inevitable because they were nature’s way of dealing with the imbalance between food supply and increasing population.

source.book: Indian Society
source.section: The Malthusian Theory of Population Growth

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Malthus believed therefore that ‘____’ to population growth – in the form of ____ – were inevitable
cards.back: Malthus believed therefore that ‘positive checks’ to population growth – in the form of famines and diseases – were inevitable
cards.quote: Malthus believed therefore that ‘positive checks’ to population growth – in the form of famines and diseases – were inevitable

source.book: Indian Society
source.section: The Malthusian Theory of Population Growth

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: What provided the most effective refutation of Malthus’s theory?
cards.back: However, the most effective refutation of his theory was provided by the historical experience of European countries.
cards.quote: However, the most effective refutation of his theory was provided by the historical experience of European countries.

source.book: Indian Society
source.section: The Malthusian Theory of Population Growth

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Why were Malthus’s predictions proved false?
cards.back: Malthus’s predictions were proved false because both food production and standards of living continued to rise despite the rapid growth of population.
cards.quote: Malthus’s predictions were proved false because both food production and standards of living continued to rise despite the rapid growth of population.

source.book: Indian Society
source.section: The Malthusian Theory of Population Growth

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: How did liberal and Marxist scholars criticise Malthus’s claim about poverty?
cards.back: Malthus was also criticised by liberal and Marxist scholars for asserting that poverty was caused by population growth. The critics argued that problems like poverty and starvation were caused by the unequal distribution of economic resources rather than by population growth.
cards.quote: Malthus was also criticised by liberal and Marxist scholars for asserting that poverty was caused by population growth. The critics argued that problems like poverty and starvation were caused by the unequal distribution of economic resources rather than by population growth.

source.book: Indian Society
source.section: The Malthusian Theory of Population Growth

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: What is the theory of demographic transition?
cards.back: Another significant theory in demography is the theory of demographic transition. This suggests that population growth is linked to overall levels of economic development and that every society follows a typical pattern of development-related population growth.
cards.quote: Another significant theory in demography is the theory of demographic transition. This suggests that population growth is linked to overall levels of economic development and that every society follows a typical pattern of development-related population growth.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Demographic transition, first stage: what is population growth like and why?
cards.back: The first stage is that of low population growth in a society that is underdeveloped and technologically backward. Growth rates are low because both the death rate and the birth rate are very high
cards.quote: The first stage is that of low population growth in a society that is underdeveloped and technologically backward. Growth rates are low because both the death rate and the birth rate are very high

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Why does the transitional stage bring a ‘population explosion’?
cards.back: This ‘population explosion’ happens because death rates are brought down relatively quickly through advanced methods of disease control, public health, and better nutrition.
cards.quote: This ‘population explosion’ happens because death rates are brought down relatively quickly through advanced methods of disease control, public health, and better nutrition.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Why is India’s demographic transition not yet complete?
cards.back: In India too, the demographic transition is not yet complete as the mortality rate has been reduced but the birth rate has not been brought down to the same extent.
cards.quote: In India too, the demographic transition is not yet complete as the mortality rate has been reduced but the birth rate has not been brought down to the same extent.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Define birth rate.
cards.back: For example, the birth rate is the total number of live births in a particular area (an entire country, a state, a district or other territorial unit) during a specified period (usually a year) divided by the total population of that area in thousands. In other words, the birth rate is the number of live births per 1000 population.
cards.quote: For example, the birth rate is the total number of live births in a particular area (an entire country, a state, a district or other territorial unit) during a specified period (usually a year) divided by the total population of that area in thousands. In other words, the birth rate is the number of live births per 1000 population.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Define death rate.
cards.back: The death rate is a similar statistic, expressed as the number of deaths in a given area during a given time per 1000 population.
cards.quote: The death rate is a similar statistic, expressed as the number of deaths in a given area during a given time per 1000 population.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: What is the rate of natural increase (the growth rate of population)?
cards.back: The rate of natural increase or the growth rate of population refers to the difference between the birth rate and the death rate.
cards.quote: The rate of natural increase or the growth rate of population refers to the difference between the birth rate and the death rate.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: What is the ‘replacement level’ of population?
cards.back: When this difference is zero (or, in practice, very small) then we say that the population has ‘stabilised’, or has reached the ‘replacement level’, which is the rate of growth required for new generations to replace the older ones that are dying out.
cards.quote: When this difference is zero (or, in practice, very small) then we say that the population has ‘stabilised’, or has reached the ‘replacement level’, which is the rate of growth required for new generations to replace the older ones that are dying out.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: When do societies have a negative growth rate, and which countries are examples?
cards.back: Sometimes, societies can experience a negative growth rate, that is, their fertility levels are below the replacement rate. This is true of many countries and regions in the world today, such as Japan, Russia, Italy and Eastern Europe.
cards.quote: Sometimes, societies can experience a negative growth rate, that is, their fertility levels are below the replacement rate. This is true of many countries and regions in the world today, such as Japan, Russia, Italy and Eastern Europe.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Define the fertility rate.
cards.back: The fertility rate refers to the number of live births per 1000 women in the child-bearing age group, usually taken to be 15 to 49 years.
cards.quote: The fertility rate refers to the number of live births per 1000 women in the child-bearing age group, usually taken to be 15 to 49 years.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Define the infant mortality rate.
cards.back: The infant mortality rate is the number of deaths of babies before the age of one year per 1000 live births.
cards.quote: The infant mortality rate is the number of deaths of babies before the age of one year per 1000 live births.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Define the maternal mortality rate.
cards.back: Likewise, the maternal mortality rate is the number of women who die in childbirth per 1,00,000 live births.
cards.quote: Likewise, the maternal mortality rate is the number of women who die in childbirth per 1,00,000 live births.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: What is life expectancy?
cards.back: One concept which is somewhat complicated is that of life expectancy. This refers to the estimated number of years that an average person is expected to survive. It is calculated on the basis of data on age-specific death rates in a given area over a period of time.
cards.quote: One concept which is somewhat complicated is that of life expectancy. This refers to the estimated number of years that an average person is expected to survive. It is calculated on the basis of data on age-specific death rates in a given area over a period of time.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Define the sex ratio.
cards.back: The sex ratio refers to the number of females per 1000 males in a given area at a specified time period.
cards.quote: The sex ratio refers to the number of females per 1000 males in a given area at a specified time period.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Two reasons why the sex ratio is somewhat in favour of females, despite more male births.
cards.back:
girl babies appear to have an advantage over boy babies in terms of resistance to disease in infancy
women have tended to outlive men in most societies, so that there are more older women than men
cards.quote: If despite this fact the sex ratio is somewhat in favour of females, this seems to be due to two reasons. First, girl babies appear to have an advantage over boy babies in terms of resistance to disease in infancy. At the other end of the life cycle, women have tended to outlive men in most societies, so that there are more older women than men.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: The combination of these two factors leads to a sex ratio of roughly ____ females per 1000 males in most contexts
cards.back: The combination of these two factors leads to a sex ratio of roughly 1050 females per 1000 males in most contexts
cards.quote: The combination of these two factors leads to a sex ratio of roughly 1050 females per 1000 males in most contexts

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: What social factor is linked to the declining sex ratio in China, South Korea and India?
cards.back: However, it has been found that the sex ratio has been declining in some countries like China, South Korea and specially India. This phenomenon has been linked to prevailing social norms that tend to value males much more than females, which leads to ‘son preference’ and the relative neglect of girl babies.
cards.quote: However, it has been found that the sex ratio has been declining in some countries like China, South Korea and specially India. This phenomenon has been linked to prevailing social norms that tend to value males much more than females, which leads to ‘son preference’ and the relative neglect of girl babies.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Define the age structure of the population.
cards.back: The age structure of the population refers to the proportion of persons in different age groups relative to the total population.
cards.quote: The age structure of the population refers to the proportion of persons in different age groups relative to the total population.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: What is the ‘ageing of the population’?
cards.back: This changes the age structure: relatively smaller proportions of the population are found in the younger age groups and larger proportions in the older age groups. This is also referred to as the ageing of the population.
cards.quote: This changes the age structure: relatively smaller proportions of the population are found in the younger age groups and larger proportions in the older age groups. This is also referred to as the ageing of the population.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Define the dependency ratio.
cards.back: The dependency ratio is a measure comparing the portion of a population which is composed of dependents (i.e., elderly people who are too old to work, and children who are too young to work) with the portion that is in the working age group, generally defined as 15 to 64 years.
cards.quote: The dependency ratio is a measure comparing the portion of a population which is composed of dependents (i.e., elderly people who are too old to work, and children who are too young to work) with the portion that is in the working age group, generally defined as 15 to 64 years.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Formula: the dependency ratio.
cards.back: The dependency ratio is equal to the population below 15 or above 64, divided by population in the 15-64 age group. This is usually expressed as a percentage.
cards.quote: The dependency ratio is equal to the population below 15 or above 64, divided by population in the 15-64 age group. This is usually expressed as a percentage.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Why is a rising dependency ratio a worry for countries with an ageing population?
cards.back: A rising dependency ratio is a cause for worry in countries that are facing an ageing population, since it becomes difficult for a relatively smaller proportion of working-age people to carry the burden of providing for a relatively larger proportion of dependents.
cards.quote: A rising dependency ratio is a cause for worry in countries that are facing an ageing population, since it becomes difficult for a relatively smaller proportion of working-age people to carry the burden of providing for a relatively larger proportion of dependents.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: What is the ‘demographic dividend’?
cards.back: On the other hand, a falling dependency ratio can be a source of economic growth and prosperity due to the larger proportion of workers relative to non-workers. This is sometimes refered to as the ‘demographic dividend’, or benefit flowing from the changing age structure.
cards.quote: On the other hand, a falling dependency ratio can be a source of economic growth and prosperity due to the larger proportion of workers relative to non-workers. This is sometimes refered to as the ‘demographic dividend’, or benefit flowing from the changing age structure.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Why is the benefit of the demographic dividend only temporary?
cards.back: However, this benefit is temporary because the larger pool of working age people will eventually turn into non-working old people.
cards.quote: However, this benefit is temporary because the larger pool of working age people will eventually turn into non-working old people.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: What was India’s population according to the Census of India 2011, and its world rank?
cards.back: India is the second most populous country in the world after China, with a total population of 121 crores (or 1.21 billion) according to the Census of India 2011.
cards.quote: India is the second most populous country in the world after China, with a total population of 121 crores (or 1.21 billion) according to the Census of India 2011.

source.book: Indian Society
source.section: 2.2 Size and Growth of India's Population

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Why did India have a negative growth rate between 1911 and 1921?
cards.back: In fact between 1911 and 1921 there was a negative rate of growth of – 0.03%. This was because of the influenza epidemic during 1918–19 which killed about 12.5 million persons or 5% of the total population of the country
cards.quote: In fact between 1911 and 1921 there was a negative rate of growth of – 0.03%. This was because of the influenza epidemic during 1918–19 which killed about 12.5 million persons or 5% of the total population of the country

source.book: Indian Society
source.section: 2.2 Size and Growth of India's Population

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: What did the growth rate of India’s population go up to during 1961–1981?
cards.back: The growth rate of population substantially increased after independence from British rule going up to 2.2% during 1961-1981.
cards.quote: The growth rate of population substantially increased after independence from British rule going up to 2.2% during 1961-1981.

source.book: Indian Society
source.section: 2.2 Size and Growth of India's Population

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: How did birth and death rates behave before and after 1931 in India?
cards.back: Before 1931, both death rates and birth rates were high, whereas, after this transitional moment the death rates fell sharply but the birth rate only fell slightly.
cards.quote: Before 1931, both death rates and birth rates were high, whereas, after this transitional moment the death rates fell sharply but the birth rate only fell slightly.

source.book: Indian Society
source.section: 2.2 Size and Growth of India's Population

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: What were the principal reasons for the decline in India’s death rate after 1921?
cards.back: The principal reasons for the decline in the death rate after 1921 were increased levels of control over famines and epidemic diseases.
cards.quote: The principal reasons for the decline in the death rate after 1921 were increased levels of control over famines and epidemic diseases.

source.book: Indian Society
source.section: 2.2 Size and Growth of India's Population

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Name the major epidemic diseases of the past in India.
cards.back:
fevers of various sorts
plague
smallpox
cholera
cards.quote: The major epidemic diseases in the past were fevers of various sorts, plague, smallpox and cholera.

source.book: Indian Society
source.section: 2.2 Size and Growth of India's Population

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: What is a pandemic?
cards.back: A pandemic is an epidemic that affects a very wide geographical area
cards.quote: A pandemic is an epidemic that affects a very wide geographical area

source.book: Indian Society
source.section: 2.2 Size and Growth of India's Population

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: What helped to control epidemics in India?
cards.back: Improvements in medical cures for these diseases, programmes for mass vaccination, and efforts to improve sanitation helped to control epidemics.
cards.quote: Improvements in medical cures for these diseases, programmes for mass vaccination, and efforts to improve sanitation helped to control epidemics.

source.book: Indian Society
source.section: 2.2 Size and Growth of India's Population

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: What did Amartya Sen and others show about the cause of famines?
cards.back: However, as scholars like Amartya Sen and others have shown, famines were not necessarily due to fall in foodgrains production; they were also caused by a ‘failure of entitlements’, or the inability of people to buy or otherwise obtain food.
cards.quote: However, as scholars like Amartya Sen and others have shown, famines were not necessarily due to fall in foodgrains production; they were also caused by a ‘failure of entitlements’, or the inability of people to buy or otherwise obtain food.

source.book: Indian Society
source.section: 2.2 Size and Growth of India's Population

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: What helped to drastically reduce deaths from famine in India?
cards.back:
Substantial improvements in the productivity of Indian agriculture (specially through the expansion of irrigation)
improved means of communication
more vigorous relief and preventive measures by the state
cards.quote: Substantial improvements in the productivity of Indian agriculture (specially through the expansion of irrigation); improved means of communication; and more vigorous relief and preventive measures by the state have all helped to drastically reduce deaths from famine.

source.book: Indian Society
source.section: 2.2 Size and Growth of India's Population

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Which Act is the latest state initiative to tackle hunger and starvation in rural areas?
cards.back: The Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act is the latest state initiative to tackle the problem of hunger and starvation in rural areas.
cards.quote: The Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act is the latest state initiative to tackle the problem of hunger and starvation in rural areas.

source.book: Indian Society
source.section: 2.2 Size and Growth of India's Population

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Why has India’s birth rate not fallen as sharply as its death rate?
cards.back: Unlike the death rate, the birth rate has not registered a sharp fall. This is because the birth rate is a sociocultural phenomenon that is relatively slow to change.
cards.quote: Unlike the death rate, the birth rate has not registered a sharp fall. This is because the birth rate is a sociocultural phenomenon that is relatively slow to change.

source.book: Indian Society
source.section: 2.2 Size and Growth of India's Population

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: What happens to family size once infant mortality declines and education and awareness increase?
cards.back: By and large, increased levels of prosperity exert a strong downward pull on the birth rate. Once infant mortality rates decline, and there is an overall increase in the levels of education and awareness, family size begins to fall.
cards.quote: By and large, increased levels of prosperity exert a strong downward pull on the birth rate. Once infant mortality rates decline, and there is an overall increase in the levels of education and awareness, family size begins to fall.

source.book: Indian Society
source.section: 2.2 Size and Growth of India's Population

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Which states had brought their total fertility rate (TFR) down to 1.7 each in 2016?
cards.back: Some states, like Andhra Pradesh, Himachal Pradesh, Punjab, Tamil Nadu and West Bengal have managed to bring down their total fertility rates (TFR) to 1.7 each (2016).
cards.quote: Some states, like Andhra Pradesh, Himachal Pradesh, Punjab, Tamil Nadu and West Bengal have managed to bring down their total fertility rates (TFR) to 1.7 each (2016).

source.book: Indian Society
source.section: 2.2 Size and Growth of India's Population

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Which states still had very high TFRs in 2016, and what were they?
cards.back: But there are some states, notably Bihar, Madhya Pradesh, Rajasthan and Uttar Pradesh, which still have very high TFRs. In 2016, the TFRs of these states were 3.3, 2.8, 2.7 and 3.1, respectively.
cards.quote: But there are some states, notably Bihar, Madhya Pradesh, Rajasthan and Uttar Pradesh, which still have very high TFRs. In 2016, the TFRs of these states were 3.3, 2.8, 2.7 and 3.1, respectively.

source.book: Indian Society
source.section: 2.2 Size and Growth of India's Population

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: What share of additions to India’s population up to 2041 will Bihar and Uttar Pradesh account for?
cards.back: Furthermore, as per economic survey 2018-19, these two states will also account for almost half (50%) of the additions to the Indian population up to the year 2041. Uttar Pradesh alone is expected to account for a little less than one-quarter (22%) of this increase.
cards.quote: Furthermore, as per economic survey 2018-19, these two states will also account for almost half (50%) of the additions to the Indian population up to the year 2041. Uttar Pradesh alone is expected to account for a little less than one-quarter (22%) of this increase.

source.book: Indian Society
source.section: 2.2 Size and Growth of India's Population

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: How does the age structure of India’s population compare with most other countries?
cards.back: India has a very young population -- that is, the majority of Indians tend to be young, and the average age is also less than that for most other countries.
cards.quote: India has a very young population -- that is, the majority of Indians tend to be young, and the average age is also less than that for most other countries.

source.book: Indian Society
source.section: 2.3 Age Structure of the Indian Population

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: How has the share of the under-15 age group changed from 1971 to 2011?
cards.back: Table 2 shows that the share of the under 15 age group in the total population has come down from its highest level of 42% in 1971 to 29% in 2011.
cards.quote: Table 2 shows that the share of the under 15 age group in the total population has come down from its highest level of 42% in 1971 to 29% in 2011.

source.book: Indian Society
source.section: 2.3 Age Structure of the Indian Population

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: How will the 0–14 and 60-plus age groups change between 2001 and 2026, according to the projection?
cards.back: the 0 -14 age group will reduce its share by about 11% (from 34% in 2001 to 23% in 2026) while the 60 plus age group will increase its share by about 5% (from 7% in 2001 to about 12% in 2026.)
cards.quote: the 0 -14 age group will reduce its share by about 11% (from 34% in 2001 to 23% in 2026) while the 60 plus age group will increase its share by about 5% (from 7% in 2001 to about 12% in 2026.)

source.book: Indian Society
source.section: 2.3 Age Structure of the Indian Population

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: What do the top and bottom of the population pyramid show as people live longer and fewer births occur?
cards.back: As more and more people begin to live to an older age, the top of the pyramid grows wider. As relatively fewer new births take place, the bottom of the pyramid grows narrower.
cards.quote: As more and more people begin to live to an older age, the top of the pyramid grows wider. As relatively fewer new births take place, the bottom of the pyramid grows narrower.

source.book: Indian Society
source.section: 2.3 Age Structure of the Indian Population

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: How do the age structures of Kerala and Uttar Pradesh differ?
cards.back: While a state like Kerala is beginning to acquire an age structure like that of the developed countries, Uttar Pradesh presents a very different picture with high proportions in the younger age groups and relatively low proportions among the aged.
cards.quote: While a state like Kerala is beginning to acquire an age structure like that of the developed countries, Uttar Pradesh presents a very different picture with high proportions in the younger age groups and relatively low proportions among the aged.

source.book: Indian Society
source.section: 2.3 Age Structure of the Indian Population

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: What is the source of India’s ‘demographic dividend’?
cards.back: This dividend arises from the fact that the current generation of working-age people is a relatively large one, and it has only a relatively small preceding generation of old people to support.
cards.quote: This dividend arises from the fact that the current generation of working-age people is a relatively large one, and it has only a relatively small preceding generation of old people to support.

source.book: Indian Society
source.section: 2.3 Age Structure of the Indian Population

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: What does the ‘demographic dividend’ result from, according to Box 2.3?
cards.back: The ‘demographic dividend’ results from an increase in the proportion of workers relative to non-workers in the population.
cards.quote: The ‘demographic dividend’ results from an increase in the proportion of workers relative to non-workers in the population.

source.book: Indian Society
source.section: Box 2.3: Does the changing age structure offer a 'demographic dividend' for India?

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: In 2020, what was the average age of an Indian compared with China and the US, Western Europe and Japan?
cards.back: In 2020, the average Indian was only 29 years old, compared with an average age of 37 in China and the United States, 45 in Western Europe, and 48 in Japan.
cards.quote: In 2020, the average Indian was only 29 years old, compared with an average age of 37 in China and the United States, 45 in Western Europe, and 48 in Japan.

source.book: Indian Society
source.section: Box 2.3: Does the changing age structure offer a 'demographic dividend' for India?

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: On what condition can the demographic dividend turn into actual growth?
cards.back: But this potential can be converted into actual growth only if the rise in the working age group is accompanied by increasing levels of education and employment.
cards.quote: But this potential can be converted into actual growth only if the rise in the working age group is accompanied by increasing levels of education and employment.

source.book: Indian Society
source.section: Box 2.3: Does the changing age structure offer a 'demographic dividend' for India?

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: How did India’s age-based dependency ratio change between 1970 and 2050 (projected)?
cards.back: The total dependency ratio fell from 79 in 1970 to 64 in 2005. But the process is likely to extend well into this century with the age-based dependency ratio projected to fall to 48 in 2025 because of continued fall in the proportion of children and then rise to 50 by 2050 because of an increase in the proportion of the aged.
cards.quote: The total dependency ratio fell from 79 in 1970 to 64 in 2005. But the process is likely to extend well into this century with the age-based dependency ratio projected to fall to 48 in 2025 because of continued fall in the proportion of children and then rise to 50 by 2050 because of an increase in the proportion of the aged.

source.book: Indian Society
source.section: Box 2.3: Does the changing age structure offer a 'demographic dividend' for India?

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: How has India’s sex ratio changed from the turn of the twentieth to the twenty-first century?
cards.back: From 972 females per 1000 males at the turn of the twentieth century, the sex ratio has declined to 933 at the turn of the twenty-first century.
cards.quote: From 972 females per 1000 males at the turn of the twentieth century, the sex ratio has declined to 933 at the turn of the twenty-first century.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: What was India’s all-time low sex ratio and in which census year?
cards.back: from 941 in 1961 the sex ratio had fallen to an all-time low of 927 in 1991 before posting a modest increase in 2001.
cards.quote: from 941 in 1961 the sex ratio had fallen to an all-time low of 927 in 1991 before posting a modest increase in 2001.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: What was India’s sex ratio according to the Census of India 2011?
cards.back: According to Census of India 2011 sex ratio has increased and now it is 943 females per 1000 males.
cards.quote: According to Census of India 2011 sex ratio has increased and now it is 943 females per 1000 males.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: What is the juvenile or child sex ratio?
cards.back: As is shown in Table 3, the sex ratio for the 0–6 years age group (known as the juvenile or child sex ratio) has generally been substantially higher than the overall sex ratio for all age groups, but it has been falling very sharply.
cards.quote: As is shown in Table 3, the sex ratio for the 0–6 years age group (known as the juvenile or child sex ratio) has generally been substantially higher than the overall sex ratio for all age groups, but it has been falling very sharply.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: What was unusual about the decade 1991–2001 for the overall and child sex ratios?
cards.back: In fact the decade 1991–2001 represents an anomaly in that the overall sex ratio has posted its highest ever increase of 6 points from the all time low of 927 to 933, but the child sex ratio has dropped from 945 to 927, a plunge of 18 points taking it below the overall sex ratio for the first time.
cards.quote: In fact the decade 1991–2001 represents an anomaly in that the overall sex ratio has posted its highest ever increase of 6 points from the all time low of 927 to 933, but the child sex ratio has dropped from 945 to 927, a plunge of 18 points taking it below the overall sex ratio for the first time.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: What was India’s child sex ratio in the 2011 Census?
cards.back: In 2011 Census (provisional) the child sex ratio again decreased by 13 points and now it is 919.
cards.quote: In 2011 Census (provisional) the child sex ratio again decreased by 13 points and now it is 919.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.note: Table 3 gives 927 in 2001 and 919 in 2011, a fall of 8 points.

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Which state has the lowest child sex ratio, and what is it?
cards.back: Haryana is the worst state with an incredibly low child sex ratio of 793 (the only state below 800)
cards.quote: Haryana is the worst state with an incredibly low child sex ratio of 793 (the only state below 800)

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Which state has the highest child sex ratio, and what is it?
cards.back: while the highest child sex ratio of 972 is found in Arunachal Pradesh.
cards.quote: while the highest child sex ratio of 972 is found in Arunachal Pradesh.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: How many States and Union Territories have a child sex ratio under 900 females per 1000 males?
cards.back: As many as nine States and Union Territories have a child sex ratio of under 900 females per 1000 males.
cards.quote: As many as nine States and Union Territories have a child sex ratio of under 900 females per 1000 males.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: The child sex ratio has declined much more steeply than the overall figure: where do social scientists seek the cause?
cards.back: social scientists believe that the cause has to be sought in the differential treatment of girl babies.
cards.quote: social scientists believe that the cause has to be sought in the differential treatment of girl babies.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Name the factors held responsible for the decline in the child sex ratio.
cards.back:
severe neglect of girl babies in infancy, leading to higher death rates
sex-specific abortions that prevent girl babies from being born
female infanticide (or the killing of girl babies due to religious or cultural beliefs)
cards.quote: Several factors may be held responsible for the decline in the child sex ratio, including severe neglect of girl babies in infancy, leading to higher death rates; sex-specific abortions that prevent girl babies from being born; and female infanticide (or the killing of girl babies due to religious or cultural beliefs).

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: How is the sonogram misused in India?
cards.back: The availability of the sonogram (an x-ray like diagnostic device based on ultra-sound technology), originally developed to identify genetic or other disorders in the foetus, are misused to identify and selectively abort female foetuses.
cards.quote: The availability of the sonogram (an x-ray like diagnostic device based on ultra-sound technology), originally developed to identify genetic or other disorders in the foetus, are misused to identify and selectively abort female foetuses.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: In which regions of India are the lowest child sex ratios found?
cards.back: It is striking that the lowest child sex ratios are found in the most prosperous regions of India.
cards.quote: It is striking that the lowest child sex ratios are found in the most prosperous regions of India.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Name the law banning sex determination before birth and the year it came into force.
cards.back: Known as the Pre-natal Diagnostic Techniques (Regulation and Prevention of Misuse) Act, this law has been in force since 1996, and has been further strengthened in 2003.
cards.quote: Known as the Pre-natal Diagnostic Techniques (Regulation and Prevention of Misuse) Act, this law has been in force since 1996, and has been further strengthened in 2003.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Which Government of India programme can help increase the child sex ratio?
cards.back: Recently, the Government of India has introduced the programme, ‘Beti-Bachao, Beti-Padhao’. It can prove to be an important policy to increase the child sex ratio in the country.
cards.quote: Recently, the Government of India has introduced the programme, ‘Beti-Bachao, Beti-Padhao’. It can prove to be an important policy to increase the child sex ratio in the country.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Why is literacy called an instrument of empowerment?
cards.back: Literacy as a prerequisite to education is an instrument of empowerment. The more literate the population the greater the consciousness of career options, as well as participation in the knowledge economy.
cards.quote: Literacy as a prerequisite to education is an instrument of empowerment. The more literate the population the greater the consciousness of career options, as well as participation in the knowledge economy.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Across which factors does literacy vary considerably in India?
cards.back: Literacy varies considerably across gender, across regions, and across social groups.
cards.quote: Literacy varies considerably across gender, across regions, and across social groups.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Why has female literacy been rising faster than male literacy?
cards.back: However, female literacy has been rising faster than male literacy, partly because it started from relatively low levels.
cards.quote: However, female literacy has been rising faster than male literacy, partly because it started from relatively low levels.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: How does literacy differ for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes?
cards.back: Literacy rates also vary by social group – historically disadvantaged communities like the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes have lower rates of literacy, and rates of female literacy within these groups are even lower.
cards.quote: Literacy rates also vary by social group – historically disadvantaged communities like the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes have lower rates of literacy, and rates of female literacy within these groups are even lower.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Which state is approaching universal literacy, and which lags far behind?
cards.back: Regional variations are still very wide, with states like Kerala approaching universal literacy, while states like Bihar are lagging far behind.
cards.quote: Regional variations are still very wide, with states like Kerala approaching universal literacy, while states like Bihar are lagging far behind.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Why are inequalities in the literacy rate specially important?
cards.back: The inequalities in the literacy rate are specially important because they tend to reproduce inequality across generations.
cards.quote: The inequalities in the literacy rate are specially important because they tend to reproduce inequality across generations.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: What share of India’s population lives in rural and urban areas, according to Census 2011?
cards.back: Now 68.8% population lives in rural areas while 31.2% people live in urban areas.
cards.quote: Now 68.8% population lives in rural areas while 31.2% people live in urban areas.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: How has the urban share of population grown since the beginning of the twentieth century?
cards.back: the urban population has been increasing its share steadily, from about 11% at the beginning of the twentieth century to about 28% at the beginning of the twenty-first century, an increase of about two-and-a-half times.
cards.quote: the urban population has been increasing its share steadily, from about 11% at the beginning of the twentieth century to about 28% at the beginning of the twenty-first century, an increase of about two-and-a-half times.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: What happens to the significance of the agrarian-rural way of life through modern development?
cards.back: processes of modern development ensure that the economic and social significance of the agrarian-rural way of life declines relative to the significance of the industrial-urban way of life.
cards.quote: processes of modern development ensure that the economic and social significance of the agrarian-rural way of life declines relative to the significance of the industrial-urban way of life.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Roughly what share of GDP does agriculture contribute today?
cards.back: Agriculture used to be by far the largest contributor to the country, but today it only contributes about one-sixth of the gross domestic product.
cards.quote: Agriculture used to be by far the largest contributor to the country, but today it only contributes about one-sixth of the gross domestic product.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: How are mass media bringing urban norms into rural areas?
cards.back: Mass media and communication channels are now bringing images of urban life styles and patterns of consumption into the rural areas. Consequently, urban norms and standards are becoming well known even in the remote villages, creating new desires and aspirations for consumption.
cards.quote: Mass media and communication channels are now bringing images of urban life styles and patterns of consumption into the rural areas. Consequently, urban norms and standards are becoming well known even in the remote villages, creating new desires and aspirations for consumption.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: What does rapid urbanisation show about the town or city from an urban point of view?
cards.back: Considered from an urban point of view, the rapid growth in urbanisation shows that the town or city has been acting as a magnet for the rural population.
cards.quote: Considered from an urban point of view, the rapid growth in urbanisation shows that the town or city has been acting as a magnet for the rural population.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: What has accelerated the flow of rural-to-urban migration, besides lack of work?
cards.back: This flow of rural-to-urban migration has also been accelerated by the continuous decline of common property resources like ponds, forests and grazing lands.
cards.quote: This flow of rural-to-urban migration has also been accelerated by the continuous decline of common property resources like ponds, forests and grazing lands.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Why may the city be preferred for social reasons?
cards.back: Sometimes the city may also be preferred for social reasons, specially the relative anonymity it offers.
cards.quote: Sometimes the city may also be preferred for social reasons, specially the relative anonymity it offers.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: How does the anonymity of the city help Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes?
cards.back: For the socially oppressed groups like the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes, this may offer some partial protection from the daily humiliation they may suffer in the village where everyone knows their caste identity.
cards.quote: For the socially oppressed groups like the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes, this may offer some partial protection from the daily humiliation they may suffer in the village where everyone knows their caste identity.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Which cities are growing the fastest in India’s urbanisation?
cards.back: While urbanisation has been occurring at a rapid pace, it is the biggest cities – the metropolises – that have been growing the fastest.
cards.quote: While urbanisation has been occurring at a rapid pace, it is the biggest cities – the metropolises – that have been growing the fastest.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: How much of the urban population lives in India’s 27 million-plus cities?
cards.back: There are now 5,161 towns and cities in India, where 286 million people live. What is striking, however, is that more than two-thirds of the urban population lives in 27 big cities with million-plus populations.
cards.quote: There are now 5,161 towns and cities in India, where 286 million people live. What is striking, however, is that more than two-thirds of the urban population lives in 27 big cities with million-plus populations.
