source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: In which year did India announce an official population policy, and why is it notable?
cards.back: It is hardly surprising therefore that India has had an official population policy for more than a half century. In fact, India was perhaps the first country to explicitly announce such a policy in 1952.
cards.quote: It is hardly surprising therefore that India has had an official population policy for more than a half century. In fact, India was perhaps the first country to explicitly announce such a policy in 1952.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: In what concrete form did India’s population policy take shape?
cards.back: The population policy took the concrete form of the National Family Planning Programme.
cards.quote: The population policy took the concrete form of the National Family Planning Programme.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: What was the broad objective of the National Family Planning Programme?
cards.back: The broad objectives of this programme have remained the same – to try to influence the rate and pattern of population growth in socially desirable directions.
cards.quote: The broad objectives of this programme have remained the same – to try to influence the rate and pattern of population growth in socially desirable directions.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: During which period did the Family Planning Programme suffer a setback?
cards.back: The Family Planning Programme suffered a setback during the years of the National Emergency (1975–76).
cards.quote: The Family Planning Programme suffered a setback during the years of the National Emergency (1975–76).

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: What coercive programme did the government introduce during the Emergency?
cards.back: During this time the government tried to intensify the effort to bring down the growth rate of population by introducing a coercive programme of mass sterilisation.
cards.quote: During this time the government tried to intensify the effort to bring down the growth rate of population by introducing a coercive programme of mass sterilisation.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: What does sterilisation refer to?
cards.back: Here sterilisation refers to medical procedures like vasectomy (for men) and tubectomy (for women) which prevent conception and childbirth.
cards.quote: Here sterilisation refers to medical procedures like vasectomy (for men) and tubectomy (for women) which prevent conception and childbirth.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: What was the National Family Planning Programme renamed after the Emergency?
cards.back: The National Family Planning Programme was renamed as the National Family Welfare Programme after the Emergency, and coercive methods were no longer used.
cards.quote: The National Family Planning Programme was renamed as the National Family Welfare Programme after the Emergency, and coercive methods were no longer used.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Which policies of 2000 and 2017 now carry India’s socio-demographic goals?
cards.back: A new set of guidelines were formulated as part of the National Population Policy of the year 2000. In 2017, Government of India came out with National Health Policy 2017 in which most of these socio–demographic goals were incorporated with new targets (Box 2.5).
cards.quote: A new set of guidelines were formulated as part of the National Population Policy of the year 2000. In 2017, Government of India came out with National Health Policy 2017 in which most of these socio–demographic goals were incorporated with new targets (Box 2.5).

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: What does the history of the National Family Welfare Programme teach about demographic change?
cards.back: The history of India’s National Family Welfare Programme teaches us that while the state can do a lot to try and create the conditions for demographic change, most demographic variables (specially those related to human fertility) are ultimately matters of economic, social and cultural change.
cards.quote: The history of India’s National Family Welfare Programme teaches us that while the state can do a lot to try and create the conditions for demographic change, most demographic variables (specially those related to human fertility) are ultimately matters of economic, social and cultural change.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: What is population momentum?
cards.back: Population momentum refers to a situation, where a large cohort of women of reproductive age will fuel population growth over the next generation, even if each woman has fewer children than previous generations did.
cards.quote: Population momentum refers to a situation, where a large cohort of women of reproductive age will fuel population growth over the next generation, even if each woman has fewer children than previous generations did.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: What is India’s population projected to be by 2050, and why does it keep rising despite falling fertility?
cards.back: Even though the fertility and population growth rates are declining, India’s population is projected to increase from 1.2 billion today to an estimated 1.6 billion by 2050 due to population momentum.
cards.quote: Even though the fertility and population growth rates are declining, India’s population is projected to increase from 1.2 billion today to an estimated 1.6 billion by 2050 due to population momentum.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: What TFR does National Health Policy 2017 aim for at national and sub-national level by 2025?
cards.back: Reduction of TFR to 2.1 at national and sub-national level by 2025.
cards.quote: Reduction of TFR to 2.1 at national and sub-national level by 2025.

source.book: Indian Society
source.section: Box 2.5: Important Goals of National Health Policy 2017

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: What does sociology use to link the individual and society, the micro and the macro, the local and the global?
cards.back: What Sociology does is use the sociological imagination to make sense of the connections between the individual and society, the micro and the macro, the local and the global.
cards.quote: What Sociology does is use the sociological imagination to make sense of the connections between the individual and society, the micro and the macro, the local and the global.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: From which date were all quantitative restrictions (QR) on imports withdrawn?
cards.back: Since April 1, 2001, all types of quantitative restrictions (QR) on imports were withdrawn.
cards.quote: Since April 1, 2001, all types of quantitative restrictions (QR) on imports were withdrawn.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: The sociologist or social anthropologist cannot study society as though it was an isolated entity. The ____ has changed this.
cards.back: The sociologist or social anthropologist cannot study society as though it was an isolated entity. The compression of space and time has changed this.
cards.quote: The sociologist or social anthropologist cannot study society as though it was an isolated entity. The compression of space and time has changed this.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Globalisation may mean new opportunities for some; for others it may mean what?
cards.back: Thus, while for some it may mean new opportunities, for others the loss of livelihood.
cards.quote: Thus, while for some it may mean new opportunities, for others the loss of livelihood.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Name the three views about the impact of globalisation.
cards.back:
Some believe that it is necessary to herald a better world.
Others fear that the impact of globalisation on different sections of people is vastly different.
There are yet others who argue that globalisation is not a new development at all.
cards.quote: Some believe that it is necessary to herald a better world. Others fear that the impact of globalisation on different sections of people is vastly different. They argue that while many in the more privileged section may benefit, the condition of a large section of the already excluded population worsens. There are yet others who argue that globalisation is not a new development at all.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Which famous route centuries ago connected India to China, Persia, Egypt and Rome?
cards.back: We have read in our history textbooks about the famous Silk route, which centuries ago connected India to the great civilisations, which existed in China, Persia, Egypt and Rome.
cards.quote: We have read in our history textbooks about the famous Silk route, which centuries ago connected India to the great civilisations, which existed in China, Persia, Egypt and Rome.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India
source.section: Are Global Interconnections New to World and to India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: What is the kupamanduka, the well-frog of old Sanskrit texts?
cards.back: The kupamanduka is a frog that lives its whole life within a well, knows nothing else, and is suspicious of everything outside it.
cards.quote: The kupamanduka is a frog that lives its whole life within a well, knows nothing else, and is suspicious of everything outside it.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India
source.section: Are Global Interconnections New to World and to India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Global interactions or even a ____ are thus not novel developments unique to the modern period or unique to modern India.
cards.back: Global interactions or even a global outlook are thus not novel developments unique to the modern period or unique to modern India.
cards.quote: Global interactions or even a global outlook are thus not novel developments unique to the modern period or unique to modern India.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India
source.section: Are Global Interconnections New to World and to India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: You will recall from Chapter 1 that modern capitalism had a ____ from its very inception.
cards.back: You will recall from Chapter 1 that modern capitalism had a global dimension from its very inception.
cards.quote: You will recall from Chapter 1 that modern capitalism had a global dimension from its very inception.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India
source.section: Are Global Interconnections New to World and to India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: What was perhaps the greatest movement of people, according to NCERT?
cards.back: You know, however, that perhaps the greatest movement of people was the migration of European people who settled down in the Americas and Australia.
cards.quote: You know, however, that perhaps the greatest movement of people was the migration of European people who settled down in the Americas and Australia.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India
source.section: Are Global Interconnections New to World and to India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Where were indentured labourers taken from India in ships to work?
cards.back: You will remember how indentured labourers were taken away in ships from India to work in distant parts of Asia, Africa and Americas.
cards.quote: You will remember how indentured labourers were taken away in ships from India to work in distant parts of Asia, Africa and Americas.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India
source.section: Are Global Interconnections New to World and to India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Independent India retained a global outlook. In many senses this was inherited from the ____.
cards.back: Independent India retained a global outlook. In many senses this was inherited from the Indian nationalist movement.
cards.quote: Independent India retained a global outlook. In many senses this was inherited from the Indian nationalist movement.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India
source.section: Are Global Interconnections New to World and to India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Define globalisation.
cards.back: Globalisation refers to the growing interdependence between different people, regions and countries in the world as social and economic relationships come to stretch world-wide.
cards.quote: Globalisation refers to the growing interdependence between different people, regions and countries in the world as social and economic relationships come to stretch world-wide.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: What has driven globalisation forward above all, intensifying the speed and scope of interaction between people worldwide?
cards.back: It has been driven forward above all by the development of information and communication technologies that have intensified the speed and scope of interaction between people all over the world.
cards.quote: It has been driven forward above all by the development of information and communication technologies that have intensified the speed and scope of interaction between people all over the world.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Although ____ are an integral part of globalisation, it would be wrong to suggest that they alone produce it.
cards.back: Although economic forces are an integral part of globalisation, it would be wrong to suggest that they alone produce it.
cards.quote: Although economic forces are an integral part of globalisation, it would be wrong to suggest that they alone produce it.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: What does the term liberalisation refer to?
cards.back: The term liberalisation refers to a range of policy decisions that the Indian state took since 1991 to open up the Indian economy to the world market.
cards.quote: The term liberalisation refers to a range of policy decisions that the Indian state took since 1991 to open up the Indian economy to the world market.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: In which year did the Indian state decide to bring changes in its economic policy (liberalisation)?
cards.back: In India we have seen how the state decided to bring some changes in its economic policy in 1991.
cards.quote: In India we have seen how the state decided to bring some changes in its economic policy in 1991.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: What did the laws put in place after independence protect the Indian market and indigenous business from?
cards.back: The state after independence had put in place a large number of laws that ensured that the Indian market and Indian indigenous business were protected from competition of the wider world.
cards.quote: The state after independence had put in place a large number of laws that ensured that the Indian market and Indian indigenous business were protected from competition of the wider world.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: The underlying assumption of such a policy was that an ____ would be at disadvantage in a free market situation.
cards.back: The underlying assumption of such a policy was that an erstwhile colonial country would be at disadvantage in a free market situation.
cards.quote: The underlying assumption of such a policy was that an erstwhile colonial country would be at disadvantage in a free market situation.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: ____ of the economy meant the steady removal of the rules that regulated Indian trade and finance regulations.
cards.back: Liberalisation of the economy meant the steady removal of the rules that regulated Indian trade and finance regulations.
cards.quote: Liberalisation of the economy meant the steady removal of the rules that regulated Indian trade and finance regulations.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Liberalisation steadily removed rules regulating Indian trade and finance. What are these measures also described as?
cards.back: Liberalisation of the economy meant the steady removal of the rules that regulated Indian trade and finance regulations. These measures are also described as economic reforms.
cards.quote: Liberalisation of the economy meant the steady removal of the rules that regulated Indian trade and finance regulations. These measures are also described as economic reforms.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Name the sectors of the economy in which reforms have taken place since July 1991.
cards.back:
agriculture
industry
trade
foreign investment and technology
public sector
financial institutions
cards.quote: Since July 1991, the Indian economy has witnessed a series of reforms in all major sectors of the economy (agriculture, industry, trade, foreign investment and technology, public sector, financial institutions, etc).

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: The basic assumption was that ____ into the global market would be beneficial to Indian economy.
cards.back: The basic assumption was that greater integration into the global market would be beneficial to Indian economy.
cards.quote: The basic assumption was that greater integration into the global market would be beneficial to Indian economy.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: The process of liberalisation also involved the taking of loans from international institutions such as the ____ (IMF).
cards.back: The process of liberalisation also involved the taking of loans from international institutions such as the International Monetary Fund (IMF).
cards.quote: The process of liberalisation also involved the taking of loans from international institutions such as the International Monetary Fund (IMF).

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: What do structural adjustments usually mean for state expenditure on health, education and social security?
cards.back: These adjustments usually mean cuts in state expenditure on the social sector such as health, education and social security.
cards.quote: These adjustments usually mean cuts in state expenditure on the social sector such as health, education and social security.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: What are transnational corporations (TNCs)?
cards.back: TNCs are companies that produce goods or market services in more than one country.
cards.quote: TNCs are companies that produce goods or market services in more than one country.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: What are transnational corporations oriented to, even if they have a clear national base?
cards.back: They are oriented to the global markets and global profits even if they have a clear national base.
cards.quote: They are oriented to the global markets and global profits even if they have a clear national base.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: In contrast to previous eras, the global economy is no longer primarily ____ in its basis.
cards.back: In contrast to previous eras, the global economy is no longer primarily agricultural or industrial in its basis.
cards.quote: In contrast to previous eras, the global economy is no longer primarily agricultural or industrial in its basis.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India
source.section: The weightless economy or knowledge economy

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: What is the weightless economy?
cards.back: The weightless economy is one in which products have their base in information, as in the case with computer software, media and entertainment products and internet-based services.
cards.quote: The weightless economy is one in which products have their base in information, as in the case with computer software, media and entertainment products and internet-based services.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India
source.section: The weightless economy or knowledge economy

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: What is a knowledge economy?
cards.back: A knowledge economy is one in which much of the workforce is involved not in the physical production or distribution of material goods, but in their design, development, technology, marketing, sale and servicing.
cards.quote: A knowledge economy is one in which much of the workforce is involved not in the physical production or distribution of material goods, but in their design, development, technology, marketing, sale and servicing.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India
source.section: The weightless economy or knowledge economy

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Mainly due to the information technology revolution, what has happened for the first time in the world economy?
cards.back: It should also be noted that for the first time, mainly due to the information technology revolution, there has been a globalisation of finance.
cards.quote: It should also be noted that for the first time, mainly due to the information technology revolution, there has been a globalisation of finance.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Which cities are the key centres for financial trading, and which is India's financial capital?
cards.back: Cities such as New York, Tokyo and London are the key centres for financial trading. Within India, Mumbai is known as the financial capital of the country.
cards.quote: Cities such as New York, Tokyo and London are the key centres for financial trading. Within India, Mumbai is known as the financial capital of the country.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: What kind of trading is there in capital and security markets in globally integrated financial markets?
cards.back: There is a 24-hour trading in capital and security markets.
cards.quote: There is a 24-hour trading in capital and security markets.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: What is the gap between those with and without telecom and internet links in India often termed?
cards.back: This is indicative of what is often termed as the digital divide in our country.
cards.quote: This is indicative of what is often termed as the digital divide in our country.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Despite this digital divide, these forms of technology do facilitate the ____ of time and space.
cards.back: Despite this digital divide, these forms of technology do facilitate the compression of time and space.
cards.quote: Despite this digital divide, these forms of technology do facilitate the compression of time and space.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Which programme did the Government of India initiate to create global interconnectedness more efficiently?
cards.back: To create global interconnectedness more efficiently, the Government of India has initiated an ambitious programme in the form of Digital India, in which every exchange will incorporate digitisation.
cards.quote: To create global interconnectedness more efficiently, the Government of India has initiated an ambitious programme in the form of Digital India, in which every exchange will incorporate digitisation.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Into what two things will the Digital India programme transform India?
cards.back: It will transform India into a digitally empowered society and a knowledge economy.
cards.quote: It will transform India into a digitally empowered society and a knowledge economy.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: How many Internet users were there worldwide by 2000?
cards.back: By 2000, the number of Internet users had risen to 325 million.
cards.quote: By 2000, the number of Internet users had risen to 325 million.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: What were India's Internet subscribers and users by 2000, according to NCERT?
cards.back: India had 3 million Internet subscribers and 15 million users by 2000, and this has now increased to 700 million.
cards.quote: India had 3 million Internet subscribers and 15 million users by 2000, and this has now increased to 700 million.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: The emergence of PCOs satisfies the strong Indian ____ of keeping in touch with family members.
cards.back: The emergence of PCOs satisfies the strong Indian sociocultural need of keeping in touch with family members.
cards.quote: The emergence of PCOs satisfies the strong Indian sociocultural need of keeping in touch with family members.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: By 2006, India had become the country with which rank in the usage of cell phones?
cards.back: By 2006, we have become the country with the fourth largest usage of cell phones.
cards.quote: By 2006, we have become the country with the fourth largest usage of cell phones.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: A ____ has emerged in which more and more routine manufacturing production and employment is done in the Third World cities.
cards.back: A new international division of labour has emerged in which more and more routine manufacturing production and employment is done in the Third World cities.
cards.quote: A new international division of labour has emerged in which more and more routine manufacturing production and employment is done in the Third World cities.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: NCERT draws on one company to show the new international division of labour. Which company?
cards.back:
Nike
Here we simply draw upon the example of Nike company to illustrate how this works.
cards.quote: Here we simply draw upon the example of Nike company to illustrate how this works.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Under globalisation, besides money, goods, people and images, what circulates rapidly around the world?
cards.back: Under globalisation, not only money and goods, but also people, cultural products, and images circulate rapidly around the world, enter new circuits of exchange, and create new markets.
cards.quote: Under globalisation, not only money and goods, but also people, cultural products, and images circulate rapidly around the world, enter new circuits of exchange, and create new markets.

source.book: Indian Society
source.section: Globalisation — Interlinking of Local, Regional, National and International Markets

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Where was Nike produced over time, in order?
cards.back:
In the 1960s they were made in Japan.
As costs increased production shifted to South Korea in mid-1970s.
Labour costs grew in South Korea, so in the 1980s production widened to Thailand and Indonesia.
Since the 1990s we in India produce Nike.
cards.quote: In the 1960s they were made in Japan. As costs increased production shifted to South Korea in mid-1970s. Labour costs grew in South Korea, so in the 1980s production widened to Thailand and Indonesia. Since the 1990s we in India produce Nike.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: In the Nike example, what does shifting production to wherever labour is cheaper make the labouring population?
cards.back: This entire process makes the labouring population very vulnerable and insecure.
cards.quote: This entire process makes the labouring population very vulnerable and insecure.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Fordism vs post-Fordism: the difference in how goods are produced.
cards.back: Instead of mass production of goods at a centralised location (Fordism), we have moved to a system of flexible production at dispersed locations (post-Fordism).
cards.quote: Instead of mass production of goods at a centralised location (Fordism), we have moved to a system of flexible production at dispersed locations (post-Fordism).

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: In the General Motors Pontiac Le Mans example, how much of the $20,000 showroom price goes to Americans?
cards.back: General Motors produces an ostensibly American car such as Pontiac Le Mans. Of the showroom price of $20,000, only $7,600 goes to Americans (workers and management in Detroit, lawyers and bankers in New York, lobbyists in Washington, and General Motors shareholders all over the country).
cards.quote: General Motors produces an ostensibly American car such as Pontiac Le Mans. Of the showroom price of $20,000, only $7,600 goes to Americans (workers and management in Detroit, lawyers and bankers in New York, lobbyists in Washington, and General Motors shareholders all over the country).

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: For the middle class youth from urban centres, globalisation and the IT revolution has opened up ____.
cards.back: For the middle class youth from urban centres, globalisation and the IT revolution has opened up new career opportunities.
cards.quote: For the middle class youth from urban centres, globalisation and the IT revolution has opened up new career opportunities.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: In many ways it was a major political change, namely, the ____ that hastened globalisation.
cards.back: In many ways it was a major political change, namely, the collapse of the erstwhile socialist world that hastened globalisation.
cards.quote: In many ways it was a major political change, namely, the collapse of the erstwhile socialist world that hastened globalisation.
blanks: collapse of the erstwhile socialist world

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: What are the economic policies underpinning globalisation, shaped after the collapse of the socialist world, often termed?
cards.back: These changes are often termed as neo-liberal economic measures.
cards.quote: These changes are often termed as neo-liberal economic measures.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Besides loss of jobs in some sectors, what has closing public sector industries led to?
cards.back: The privatisation or closing of public sector industries has led to loss of employment in some sectors, and to growth of unorganised sector employment at the expense of the organised sector.
cards.quote: The privatisation or closing of public sector industries has led to loss of employment in some sectors, and to growth of unorganised sector employment at the expense of the organised sector.

source.book: Indian Society
source.section: Debate on Liberalisation — Market Versus State

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Broadly these policies reflect a political vision of ____ which believes that a free reign to market forces will be both efficient and fair.
cards.back: Broadly these policies reflect a political vision of free enterprise which believes that a free reign to market forces will be both efficient and fair.
cards.quote: Broadly these policies reflect a political vision of free enterprise which believes that a free reign to market forces will be both efficient and fair.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: The political vision behind neo-liberal policies (free enterprise) is critical of which two things?
cards.back: It is, therefore, critical of both state regulation and state subsidies.
cards.quote: It is, therefore, critical of both state regulation and state subsidies.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: What is inclusive globalisation?
cards.back: We, thus have the concept of an inclusive globalisation, that is one, which includes all the sections of society.
cards.quote: We, thus have the concept of an inclusive globalisation, that is one, which includes all the sections of society.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Name the regional associations NCERT gives as examples of the greater role of regional associations.
cards.back:
The European Union (EU)
the Association of South East Asian Nations (ASEAN)
South Asian Association for Regional Corporation (SAARC)
cards.quote: The European Union (EU), the Association of South East Asian Nations (ASEAN), South Asian Association for Regional Corporation (SAARC) are just some of the examples that indicate the greater role of regional associations.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: What is an intergovernmental organisation?
cards.back: An intergovernmental organisation is a body that is established by participating governments and given responsibility for regulating, or overseeing a particular domain of activity that is transnational in scope.
cards.quote: An intergovernmental organisation is a body that is established by participating governments and given responsibility for regulating, or overseeing a particular domain of activity that is transnational in scope.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Which organisation increasingly has a major say in the rules that govern trade practices?
cards.back: The World Trade Organisation (WTO), for instance, increasingly has a major say in the rules that govern trade practices.
cards.quote: The World Trade Organisation (WTO), for instance, increasingly has a major say in the rules that govern trade practices.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: What are International Non-Governmental Organisations (INGOs)?
cards.back: As the name suggests, INGOs differ from intergovernmental organisations in that they are not affiliated with government institutions. Rather they are independent organisations, which make policy decisions and address international issues.
cards.quote: As the name suggests, INGOs differ from intergovernmental organisations in that they are not affiliated with government institutions. Rather they are independent organisations, which make policy decisions and address international issues.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Name the best known INGOs given by NCERT.
cards.back:
Greenpeace
The Red Cross
Amnesty International
Medecins Sans Frontieres (Doctors Without Borders)
cards.quote: Some of the best known INGOs are Greenpeace (see Chapter 8), The Red Cross, Amnesty International and Medecins Sans Frontieres (Doctors Without Borders).

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: A central contention is that all cultures will become similar, that is ____.
cards.back: A central contention is that all cultures will become similar, that is homogeneous.
cards.quote: A central contention is that all cultures will become similar, that is homogeneous.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: What is glocalisation?
cards.back: Glocalisation refers to the mixing of the global with the local.
cards.quote: Glocalisation refers to the mixing of the global with the local.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Who often adopts glocalisation as a strategy with local traditions to enhance marketability?
cards.back: It is a strategy often adopted by foreign firms while dealing with local traditions in order to enhance their marketability.
cards.quote: It is a strategy often adopted by foreign firms while dealing with local traditions in order to enhance their marketability.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Star, MTV, Channel V and Cartoon Network all use Indian languages. Which concept does this show?
cards.back:
Glocalisation
In India, we find that all the foreign television channels like Star, MTV, Channel V and Cartoon Network use Indian languages.
cards.quote: In India, we find that all the foreign television channels like Star, MTV, Channel V and Cartoon Network use Indian languages.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: McDonald's sells only vegetarian and chicken products in India. Which concept does this show?
cards.back:
Glocalisation
Even McDonald's sells only vegetarian and chicken products in India and not its beef products, which are popular abroad.
cards.quote: Even McDonald's sells only vegetarian and chicken products in India and not its beef products, which are popular abroad.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: What does McDonald's do during the Navaratri festival, and which concept does it show?
cards.back:
Glocalisation
McDonald's goes vegetarian during the Navaratri festival.
cards.quote: McDonald's goes vegetarian during the Navaratri festival.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Bhangra pop, Indi pop, fusion music and remixes show which concept in music?
cards.back:
Glocalisation
In the field of music, one can see the growth of popularity of ‘Bhangra pop’, ‘Indi pop’, fusion music and even remixes.
cards.quote: In the field of music, one can see the growth of popularity of ‘Bhangra pop’, ‘Indi pop’, fusion music and even remixes.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Culture cannot be seen as an ____ that can either collapse or remain the same when faced with social change.
cards.back: Culture cannot be seen as an unchanging fixed entity that can either collapse or remain the same when faced with social change.
cards.quote: Culture cannot be seen as an unchanging fixed entity that can either collapse or remain the same when faced with social change.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: What is more likely even today is that globalisation will lead to the creation of not just ____ but global ones too.
cards.back: What is more likely even today is that globalisation will lead to the creation of not just new local traditions but global ones too.
cards.quote: What is more likely even today is that globalisation will lead to the creation of not just new local traditions but global ones too.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Often when we speak of culture we refer to dresses, music, dances, food. However, culture as we know refers to a ____.
cards.back: Often when we speak of culture we refer to dresses, music, dances, food. However, culture as we know refers to a whole way of life.
cards.quote: Often when we speak of culture we refer to dresses, music, dances, food. However, culture as we know refers to a whole way of life.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Name the two uses of culture that any chapter on globalisation should mention.
cards.back:
culture of consumption
corporate culture
cards.quote: There are two uses of culture that any chapter on globalisation should mention. They are the culture of consumption and corporate culture.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Till the 1970s, what played a major role in the growth of cities?
cards.back: Till the 1970s the manufacturing industries used to play a major role in the growth of cities.
cards.quote: Till the 1970s the manufacturing industries used to play a major role in the growth of cities.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Presently, ____ (of art, food, fashion, music, tourism) shapes to a large extent the growth of cities.
cards.back: Presently, cultural consumption (of art, food, fashion, music, tourism) shapes to a large extent the growth of cities.
cards.quote: Presently, cultural consumption (of art, food, fashion, music, tourism) shapes to a large extent the growth of cities.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Which new spaces show the spurt in cultural consumption in every major city in India?
cards.back: This is evident in the spurt in the growth of shopping malls, multiplex cinema halls, amusement parks and ‘water world’ in every major city in India.
cards.quote: This is evident in the spurt in the growth of shopping malls, multiplex cinema halls, amusement parks and ‘water world’ in every major city in India.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Most significantly advertisements and the media in general promote a culture where ____ is important.
cards.back: Most significantly advertisements and the media in general promote a culture where spending is important.
cards.quote: Most significantly advertisements and the media in general promote a culture where spending is important.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: What is corporate culture?
cards.back: Corporate culture is a branch of management theory that seeks to increase productivity and competitiveness though the creation of a unique organisational culture involving all members of a firm.
cards.quote: Corporate culture is a branch of management theory that seeks to increase productivity and competitiveness though the creation of a unique organisational culture involving all members of a firm.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Which class of professionals has the spread of MNCs and the IT revolution created in India's metropolitan cities?
cards.back: The spread of multinational companies and the opportunities opened up by the information technology revolution has created in the metropolitan cities in India a class of upwardly mobile professionals working in software companies, multinational banks, chartered accountancy firms, stock markets, travel, fashion designing, entertainment, media and other allied fields.
cards.quote: The spread of multinational companies and the opportunities opened up by the information technology revolution has created in the metropolitan cities in India a class of upwardly mobile professionals working in software companies, multinational banks, chartered accountancy firms, stock markets, travel, fashion designing, entertainment, media and other allied fields.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Which items did multinational companies try to patent, highlighting the need to protect indigenous knowledge systems?
cards.back: Recent attempts by some multinational companies to patent the use of Tulsi, Haldi (turmeric), Rudraksha and Basmati rice have highlighted the need for protecting the base of its indigenous knowledge systems.
cards.quote: Recent attempts by some multinational companies to patent the use of Tulsi, Haldi (turmeric), Rudraksha and Basmati rice have highlighted the need for protecting the base of its indigenous knowledge systems.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India
source.section: Threat to many indigenous craft and literary traditions and knowledge systems

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Unlike other subjects, how is much of our knowledge about society acquired?
cards.back: Other subjects are learnt because they are taught (at school, at home, or elsewhere); but much of our knowledge about society is acquired without explicit teaching.
cards.quote: Other subjects are learnt because they are taught (at school, at home, or elsewhere); but much of our knowledge about society is acquired without explicit teaching.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: The disadvantage is that this prior knowledge can be a problem – in order to learn Sociology, we need to "____" what we already know about society.
cards.back: The disadvantage is that this prior knowledge can be a problem – in order to learn Sociology, we need to "unlearn" what we already know about society.
cards.quote: The disadvantage is that this prior knowledge can be a problem – in order to learn Sociology, we need to "unlearn" what we already know about society.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.note: To learn sociology you must first set aside what you think you know about society.

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Why must we “unlearn” what we already know about society in order to learn Sociology?
cards.back: This is necessary because our prior knowledge about society – our common sense – is acquired from a particular viewpoint.
cards.quote: This is necessary because our prior knowledge about society – our common sense – is acquired from a particular viewpoint.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Our common sense about society is acquired from a particular viewpoint. Whose viewpoint is it?
cards.back: This is the viewpoint of the social group and the social environment that we are socialised into.
cards.quote: This is the viewpoint of the social group and the social environment that we are socialised into.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Two senses in which common-sense knowledge is ‘partial’, per NCERT.
cards.back:
incomplete (the opposite of whole)
biased (the opposite of impartial)
cards.quote: The word partial is being used here in two different senses – incomplete (the opposite of whole), and biased (the opposite of impartial).

source.book: Indian Society

cards.note: Common sense is partial: it shows only part of reality, tilted to our own group.

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: What two limits does our “unlearnt” knowledge or common sense have as a view of social reality?
cards.back: So our “unlearnt” knowledge or common sense usually allows us to see only a part of social reality; moreover, it is liable to be tilted towards the viewpoints and interests of our own social group.
cards.quote: So our “unlearnt” knowledge or common sense usually allows us to see only a part of social reality; moreover, it is liable to be tilted towards the viewpoints and interests of our own social group.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Sociology can show you what you look like to others; it can teach you how to look at yourself ‘from the ____’, so to speak.
cards.back: Sociology can show you what you look like to others; it can teach you how to look at yourself ‘from the outside’, so to speak.
cards.quote: Sociology can show you what you look like to others; it can teach you how to look at yourself ‘from the outside’, so to speak.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: What is ‘self-reflexivity’ (reflexivity) in sociology?
cards.back: This is the ability to reflect upon yourself, to turn back your gaze (which is usually directed outward) back towards yourself.
cards.quote: This is called ‘self-reflexivity’, or sometimes just reflexivity. This is the ability to reflect upon yourself, to turn back your gaze (which is usually directed outward) back towards yourself.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.note: Reflexivity is looking critically at yourself from the outside.

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: But this self-inspection must be ____ – i.e., it should be quick to criticise and slow to ____ oneself.
cards.back: But this self-inspection must be critical – i.e., it should be quick to criticise and slow to praise oneself.
cards.quote: But this self-inspection must be critical – i.e., it should be quick to criticise and slow to praise oneself.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Which American sociologist wrote that sociology maps the links between ‘personal troubles’ and ‘social issues’?
cards.back: As C.Wright Mills, a well-known American sociologist has written, sociology can help you to map the links and connections between "personal troubles" and "social issues".
cards.quote: As C.Wright Mills, a well-known American sociologist has written, sociology can help you to map the links and connections between "personal troubles" and "social issues".

source.book: Indian Society

cards.note: Mills: sociology links private worries to wider social issues.

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: What does C. Wright Mills mean by ‘personal troubles’?
cards.back: By personal troubles Mills means the kinds of individual worries, problems or concerns that everyone has.
cards.quote: By personal troubles Mills means the kinds of individual worries, problems or concerns that everyone has.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: What is a ‘social issue’, as distinct from a personal trouble?
cards.back: A social issue, on the other hand, is about large groups and not about the individuals who make them up.
cards.quote: A social issue, on the other hand, is about large groups and not about the individuals who make them up.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: In this very broad sense, then, ‘the market’ is almost equivalent to ‘the ____’.
cards.back: In this very broad sense, then, ‘the market’ is almost equivalent to ‘the economy’.
cards.quote: In this very broad sense, then, ‘the market’ is almost equivalent to ‘the economy’.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Everyday meanings of the word ‘market’.
cards.back:
particular markets that we may know of, such as the market next to the railway station, the fruit market, or the wholesale market
the gathering of people — buyers and sellers — who constitute the market
an area or category of trade or business, such as the market for cars or the market for readymade clothes
the demand for a particular product or service, such as the market for computer professionals
cards.quote: In this common everyday usage, the word ‘market’ may refer to particular markets that we may know of, such as the market next to the railway station, the fruit market, or the wholesale market. Sometimes we refer not to the physical place, but to the gathering of people — buyers and sellers — who constitute the market. Thus, for example, a weekly vegetable market may be found in different places on different days of the week in neighbouring villages or urban neighbourhoods. In yet another sense, ‘market’ refers to an area or category of trade or business, such as the market for cars or the market for readymade clothes. A related sense refers to the demand for a particular product or service, such as the market for computer professionals.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: We are used to thinking of the market as an economic institution, but this chapter will show you that the market is also a ____.
cards.back: We are used to thinking of the market as an economic institution, but this chapter will show you that the market is also a social institution.
cards.quote: We are used to thinking of the market as an economic institution, but this chapter will show you that the market is also a social institution.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Who was the most famous early political economist, and which book did he write?
cards.back: The most famous of the early political economists was Adam Smith, who in his book, The Wealth of Nations, attempted to understand the market economy that was just emerging at that time.
cards.quote: The most famous of the early political economists was Adam Smith, who in his book, The Wealth of Nations, attempted to understand the market economy that was just emerging at that time.

source.book: Indian Society
source.section: Sociological Perspectives on Markets and the Economy

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: What was modern economics called at its beginnings in eighteenth century England?
cards.back: eighteenth century England and the beginnings of modern economics, which at that time was called ‘political economy’.
cards.quote: eighteenth century England and the beginnings of modern economics, which at that time was called ‘political economy’.

source.book: Indian Society
source.section: Sociological Perspectives on Markets and the Economy

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Smith argued that the market economy is made up of a series of ____, which automatically create a functioning and ordered system.
cards.back: Smith argued that the market economy is made up of a series of individual exchanges or transactions, which automatically create a functioning and ordered system.
cards.quote: Smith argued that the market economy is made up of a series of individual exchanges or transactions, which automatically create a functioning and ordered system.

source.book: Indian Society
source.section: Sociological Perspectives on Markets and the Economy

cards.note: This is the idea behind Smith's 'invisible hand': no one planned the system, yet it works.

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Sociologists view markets as social institutions that are constructed in ____.
cards.back: Sociologists view markets as social institutions that are constructed in culturally specific ways.
cards.quote: Sociologists view markets as social institutions that are constructed in culturally specific ways.

source.book: Indian Society
source.section: Sociological Perspectives on Markets and the Economy

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Sociologists often express this idea by saying that economies are socially ____.
cards.back: Sociologists often express this idea by saying that economies are socially ‘embedded’.
cards.quote: Sociologists often express this idea by saying that economies are socially ‘embedded’.

source.book: Indian Society
source.section: Sociological Perspectives on Markets and the Economy

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Which two examples illustrate that economies are socially embedded?
cards.back: This is illustrated by two examples, one of a weekly tribal haat, and the other of a ‘traditional business community’ and its trading networks in colonial India.
cards.quote: This is illustrated by two examples, one of a weekly tribal haat, and the other of a ‘traditional business community’ and its trading networks in colonial India.

source.book: Indian Society
source.section: Sociological Perspectives on Markets and the Economy

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: What do periodic markets, such as cattle markets, link together in rural India?
cards.back: In rural India there are also specialised markets that take place at less frequent intervals, for instance, cattle markets. These periodic markets link different regional and local economies together, and link them to the wider national economy and to towns and metropolitan centres.
cards.quote: In rural India there are also specialised markets that take place at less frequent intervals, for instance, cattle markets. These periodic markets link different regional and local economies together, and link them to the wider national economy and to towns and metropolitan centres.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: In far-flung hilly and forested areas, the weekly market is the major institution for what?
cards.back: In hilly and forested areas (especially those inhabited by adivasis), where settlements are far-flung, roads and communications poor, and the economy relatively undeveloped, the weekly market is the major institution for the exchange of goods as well as for social intercourse.
cards.quote: In hilly and forested areas (especially those inhabited by adivasis), where settlements are far-flung, roads and communications poor, and the economy relatively undeveloped, the weekly market is the major institution for the exchange of goods as well as for social intercourse.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: For many visitors to the weekly haat, what is the primary reason to come?
cards.back: But for many visitors, the primary reason to come to the market is social — to meet kin, to arrange marriages, exchange gossip, and so on.
cards.quote: But for many visitors, the primary reason to come to the market is social — to meet kin, to arrange marriages, exchange gossip, and so on.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Why were tribal areas ‘opened up’ under colonial rule?
cards.back: Tribal areas were ‘opened up’ by building roads and ‘pacifying’ the local people (many of whom resisted colonial rule through their so-called ‘tribal rebellions’), so that the rich forest and mineral resources of these areas could be exploited.
cards.quote: Tribal areas were ‘opened up’ by building roads and ‘pacifying’ the local people (many of whom resisted colonial rule through their so-called ‘tribal rebellions’), so that the rich forest and mineral resources of these areas could be exploited.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Once tribal economies were linked into wider markets, what did the entry of outside traders lead to?
cards.back: For example, the entry of traders and moneylenders from outside the local area led to the impoverishment of adivasis, many of whom lost their land to outsiders.
cards.quote: For example, the entry of traders and moneylenders from outside the local area led to the impoverishment of adivasis, many of whom lost their land to outsiders.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Which adivasi group mainly populates the Bastar district of the weekly-market study?
cards.back: This district is populated mainly by Gonds, an adivasi group.
cards.quote: This district is populated mainly by Gonds, an adivasi group.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: In the market, the buyers are mostly adivasis while the sellers are mainly ____.
cards.back: In the market, the buyers are mostly adivasis while the sellers are mainly caste Hindus.
cards.quote: In the market, the buyers are mostly adivasis while the sellers are mainly caste Hindus.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Which non-market exchange system does NCERT cite as existing in many villages and regions?
cards.back: And while various kinds of non-market exchange systems (such as the ‘jajmani system’) did exist in many villages and regions
cards.quote: And while various kinds of non-market exchange systems (such as the ‘jajmani system’) did exist in many villages and regions

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: How sharp is the line between the ‘traditional’ and the ‘modern’ economy, per recent research?
cards.back: It now seems that the sharp line that was often drawn between the ‘traditional’ and the ‘modern’ (or the pre-capitalist and capitalist) economy is actually rather fuzzy.
cards.quote: It now seems that the sharp line that was often drawn between the ‘traditional’ and the ‘modern’ (or the pre-capitalist and capitalist) economy is actually rather fuzzy.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: What is a hundi?
cards.back: For instance, an important instrument of exchange and credit was the hundi, or bill of exchange (like a credit note), which allowed merchants to engage in long-distance trade.
cards.quote: For instance, an important instrument of exchange and credit was the hundi, or bill of exchange (like a credit note), which allowed merchants to engage in long-distance trade.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Why could a merchant's hundi be honoured by a merchant in another place?
cards.back: Because trade took place primarily within the caste and kinship networks of these communities, a merchant in one part of the country could issue a hundi that would be honoured by a merchant in another place.
cards.quote: Because trade took place primarily within the caste and kinship networks of these communities, a merchant in one part of the country could issue a hundi that would be honoured by a merchant in another place.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: On what bases did the Nakarattars lend and deposit money with one another?
cards.back: The Nakarattars loaned and deposited money with one another in caste-defined social relationships based on business territory, residential location, descent, marriage, and common cult membership.
cards.quote: The Nakarattars loaned and deposited money with one another in caste-defined social relationships based on business territory, residential location, descent, marriage, and common cult membership.

source.book: Indian Society
source.section: Box 4.2: Caste-based trade among the Nakarattars of Tamil Nadu

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: What kind of banking system was the Nakarattar banking system?
cards.back: The Nakarattar banking system was a caste-based banking system.
cards.quote: In other words, the Nakarattar banking system was a caste-based banking system.

source.book: Indian Society
source.section: Box 4.2: Caste-based trade among the Nakarattars of Tamil Nadu

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: What does the place of ‘Vaisyas’ among the four varnas indicate?
cards.back: In fact, ‘Vaisyas’ constitute one of the four varnas — an indication of the importance of the merchant and of trade or business in Indian society since ancient times.
cards.quote: In fact, ‘Vaisyas’ constitute one of the four varnas — an indication of the importance of the merchant and of trade or business in Indian society since ancient times.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: What does NCERT say ‘Vaisya’ often is, rather than a fixed identity or social status?
cards.back: Like the other varnas, ‘Vaisya’ is often a status that is claimed or aspired to rather than a fixed identity or social status.
cards.quote: However, like the other varnas, ‘Vaisya’ is often a status that is claimed or aspired to rather than a fixed identity or social status.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Which North Indian ‘Vaisya’ community is NCERT's example of a trading community?
cards.back: Although there are ‘Vaisya’ communities (such as banias in North India), whose traditional occupation has been trade or commerce for a long time, there are some caste groups that have entered into trade.
cards.quote: Although there are ‘Vaisya’ communities (such as banias in North India), whose traditional occupation has been trade or commerce for a long time, there are some caste groups that have entered into trade.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Who are included among India's ‘traditional business communities’?
cards.back:
‘Vaisyas’
other groups with distinctive religious or other community identities, such as the Parsis, Sindhis, Bohras, or Jains
cards.quote: The ‘traditional business communities’ in India include not only ‘Vaisyas’, but also other groups with distinctive religious or other community identities, such as the Parsis, Sindhis, Bohras, or Jains.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Which marginalised ‘tribal’ group controlled the long-distance salt trade in the colonial period?
cards.back: Merchant communities did not always have a high status in society; for instance, during the colonial period the long-distance trade in salt was controlled by a marginalised ‘tribal’ group, the Banjaras.
cards.quote: Merchant communities did not always have a high status in society; for instance, during the colonial period the long-distance trade in salt was controlled by a marginalised ‘tribal’ group, the Banjaras.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Because businessmen trust their own community, what do business networks tend to create?
cards.back: Because businessmen are more likely to trust others of their own community or kin group, they tend to do business within such networks rather than with others outside – and this tends to create a caste monopoly within certain areas of business.
cards.quote: Because businessmen are more likely to trust others of their own community or kin group, they tend to do business within such networks rather than with others outside – and this tends to create a caste monopoly within certain areas of business.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Which well-known example shows the upheaval colonialism caused in the economy?
cards.back: A well-known example is the demise of the handloom industry due to the flooding of the market with cheap manufactured textiles from England.
cards.quote: A well-known example is the demise of the handloom industry due to the flooding of the market with cheap manufactured textiles from England.

source.book: Indian Society
source.section: Colonialism and the Emergence of New Markets

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Which business community became successful only during the colonial period, using opportunities in cities like Calcutta?
cards.back: The Marwaris became a successful business community only during the colonial period, when they took advantage of new opportunities in colonial cities such as Calcutta
cards.quote: The Marwaris became a successful business community only during the colonial period, when they took advantage of new opportunities in colonial cities such as Calcutta

source.book: Indian Society
source.section: Colonialism and the Emergence of New Markets

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: What did the success of the Marwaris, like that of the Nakarattars, rest on?
cards.back: Like the Nakarattars, the success of the Marwaris rested on their extensive social networks, which created the relations of trust necessary to operate their banking system.
cards.quote: Like the Nakarattars, the success of the Marwaris rested on their extensive social networks, which created the relations of trust necessary to operate their banking system.

source.book: Indian Society
source.section: Colonialism and the Emergence of New Markets

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: The Marwari transformation under colonialism, in order.
cards.back:
small migrant traders
merchant bankers
industrialists
cards.quote: This story of the emergence of a new business community under colonialism, and its transformation from small migrant traders to merchant bankers to industrialists, illustrates the importance of the social context to economic processes.

source.book: Indian Society
source.section: Colonialism and the Emergence of New Markets

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: How did Karl Marx understand capitalism?
cards.back: Marx understood capitalism as a system of commodity production, or production for the market, through the use of wage labour.
cards.quote: Marx understood capitalism as a system of commodity production, or production for the market, through the use of wage labour.

source.book: Indian Society
source.section: Understanding Capitalism as a Social System

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: What did Marx emphasise the economy is made up of, rather than things (goods circulating in the market)?
cards.back: He emphasised that the economy does not consist of things (goods circulating in the market), but is made up of relations between people who are connected to one another through the process of production.
cards.quote: He emphasised that the economy does not consist of things (goods circulating in the market), but is made up of relations between people who are connected to one another through the process of production.

source.book: Indian Society
source.section: Understanding Capitalism as a Social System

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Under the capitalist mode of production, what does labour itself become, and why?
cards.back: Under the capitalist mode of production, labour itself becomes a commodity, because workers must sell their labour power in the market to earn a wage.
cards.quote: Under the capitalist mode of production, labour itself becomes a commodity, because workers must sell their labour power in the market to earn a wage.

source.book: Indian Society
source.section: Understanding Capitalism as a Social System

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: The two basic classes under the capitalist mode of production.
cards.back:
capitalists, who own the means of production (such as the factories)
workers, who sell their labour to the capitalists
cards.quote: This gives rise to two basic classes — capitalists, who own the means of production (such as the factories), and workers, who sell their labour to the capitalists.

source.book: Indian Society
source.section: Understanding Capitalism as a Social System

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: What does the capitalist class extract by paying workers less than the value of what they produce?
cards.back: The capitalist class is able to profit from this system by paying the workers less than the value of what they actually produce, and so extracting surplus value from their labour.
cards.quote: The capitalist class is able to profit from this system by paying the workers less than the value of what they actually produce, and so extracting surplus value from their labour.

source.book: Indian Society
source.section: Understanding Capitalism as a Social System

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: What is commodification?
cards.back: Commodification occurs when things that were earlier not traded in the market become commodities.
cards.quote: Commodification occurs when things that were earlier not traded in the market become commodities.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Which human-organ sale does NCERT cite as a controversy about commodification?
cards.back: For instance, there is a controversy about the sale of kidneys by the poor to cater to rich patients who need kidney transplants. According to many people, human organs should not become commodities.
cards.quote: For instance, there is a controversy about the sale of kidneys by the poor to cater to rich patients who need kidney transplants. According to many people, human organs should not become commodities.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: How do marriage bureaus and websites show commodification in India?
cards.back: For example, traditionally, marriages were arranged by families, but now there are professional marriage bureaus and websites that help people to find brides and grooms for a fee.
cards.quote: For example, traditionally, marriages were arranged by families, but now there are professional marriage bureaus and websites that help people to find brides and grooms for a fee.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: How do ‘personality development’ institutes illustrate commodification?
cards.back: Another example are the many private institutes that offer courses in ‘personality development’, spoken English, and so on, that teach students (mostly middle class youth) the cultural and social skills required to succeed in the contemporary world.
cards.quote: Another example are the many private institutes that offer courses in ‘personality development’, spoken English, and so on, that teach students (mostly middle class youth) the cultural and social skills required to succeed in the contemporary world.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: What is commoditisation/commodification (Activity 4.2)?
cards.back: This is commoditisation/commodification — the process by which something which was not a commodity is made into a commodity and becomes part of the market economy.
cards.quote: This is commoditisation/commodification — the process by which something which was not a commodity is made into a commodity and becomes part of the market economy.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: What is a ‘status symbol’ (Max Weber)?
cards.back: One of sociology’s founders, Max Weber, was among the first to point out that the goods that people buy and use are closely related to their status in society. He coined the term status symbol to describe this relationship.
cards.quote: One of sociology’s founders, Max Weber, was among the first to point out that the goods that people buy and use are closely related to their status in society. He coined the term status symbol to describe this relationship.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Which goods are markers of socio-economic status for India's middle class today?
cards.back: For example, among the middle class in India today, the brand of cell phone or the model of car that one owns are important markers of socio-economic status.
cards.quote: For example, among the middle class in India today, the brand of cell phone or the model of car that one owns are important markers of socio-economic status.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: What kind of significance does exchange have beyond its immediate economic purpose?
cards.back: Exchange has a social and symbolic significance that goes far beyond its immediate economic purpose.
cards.quote: In addition, we have learned that exchange has a social and symbolic significance that goes far beyond its immediate economic purpose.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Name the forms of mass media NCERT lists.
cards.back:
television
newspapers
films
magazines
radio
advertisements
video games
CDs
cards.quote: The mass media include a wide variety of forms, including television, newspapers, films, magazines, radio, advertisements, video games and CDs.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: What are the mass media, and why are they called 'mass' media?
cards.back: The mass media include a wide variety of forms, including television, newspapers, films, magazines, radio, advertisements, video games and CDs. They are referred to as ‘mass’ media because they reach mass audiences – audiences comprise very large numbers of people.
cards.quote: The mass media include a wide variety of forms, including television, newspapers, films, magazines, radio, advertisements, video games and CDs. They are referred to as ‘mass’ media because they reach mass audiences – audiences comprise very large numbers of people.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: What are the mass media also sometimes referred to as?
cards.back: They are also sometimes referred to as mass communications.
cards.quote: They are also sometimes referred to as mass communications.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: How does NCERT describe the relationship between mass media and society?
cards.back: the relationship between mass media and communication with society is dialectical. Both influence each other.
cards.quote: the relationship between mass media and communication with society is dialectical. Both influence each other.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: What shapes the structure and content of mass media, like any other social institution?
cards.back: like any other social institution the structure and content of mass media is shaped by changes in the economic, political and socio-cultural contexts.
cards.quote: like any other social institution the structure and content of mass media is shaped by changes in the economic, political and socio-cultural contexts.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Which actor shaped the media after independence, and which after the post-1990 globalisation?
cards.back: we see how central the state and its vision of development influenced the media in the first decades after independence. And how in the post 1990 period of globalisation, the market has a key role to play.
cards.quote: we see how central the state and its vision of development influenced the media in the first decades after independence. And how in the post 1990 period of globalisation, the market has a key role to play.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Name the three contexts in which the chapter discusses media and society.
cards.back:
(a) the role of media in colonial India
(b) in the first decades after independence
(c) and finally in the context of globalisation
cards.quote: (a) the role of media in colonial India, (b) in the first decades after independence and (c) and finally in the context of globalisation.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: What does mass communication require that other means of communication do not?
cards.back: Third, mass communication is different from other means of communication as it requires a formal structural organisation to meet large-scale capital, production and management demands.
cards.quote: Third, mass communication is different from other means of communication as it requires a formal structural organisation to meet large-scale capital, production and management demands.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: You will find, therefore, that the ____ have a major role in the structure and functioning of mass media.
cards.back: You will find, therefore, that the state and/or the market have a major role in the structure and functioning of mass media.
cards.quote: You will find, therefore, that the state and/or the market have a major role in the structure and functioning of mass media.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Which was the first modern mass media institution?
cards.back: The first modern mass media institution began with the development of the printing press.
cards.quote: The first modern mass media institution began with the development of the printing press.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India
source.section: The Beginnings of Modern Mass Media

cards.subject: sociology
