cards.front: Who first developed the technique of printing books using modern technologies in Europe, and when?
cards.back: the first attempts at printing books using modern technologies began in Europe. This technique was first developed by Johann Gutenberg in 1440.
cards.quote: the first attempts at printing books using modern technologies began in Europe. This technique was first developed by Johann Gutenberg in 1440.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India
source.section: The Beginnings of Modern Mass Media

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: What were the initial attempts at printing restricted to?
cards.back: Initial attempts at printing were restricted to religious books.
cards.quote: Initial attempts at printing were restricted to religious books.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India
source.section: The Beginnings of Modern Mass Media

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: When did newspapers begin to reach out to a mass audience?
cards.back: It was only in the mid 19th century, with further development in technologies, transportation and literacy that newspapers began to reach out to a mass audience.
cards.quote: It was only in the mid 19th century, with further development in technologies, transportation and literacy that newspapers began to reach out to a mass audience.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India
source.section: The Beginnings of Modern Mass Media

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: What is an 'imagined community' (Benedict Anderson)?
cards.back: The well known scholar Benedict Anderson has thus argued that this helped the growth of nationalism, the feeling that people who did not even know of each other's existence feel like members of a family. It gave people who would never meet each other a sense of togetherness. Anderson thus suggested that we could think of the nation as an 'imagined community'.
cards.quote: The well known scholar Benedict Anderson has thus argued that this helped the growth of nationalism, the feeling that people who did not even know of each other's existence feel like members of a family. It gave people who would never meet each other a sense of togetherness. Anderson thus suggested that we could think of the nation as an 'imagined community'.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India
source.section: The Beginnings of Modern Mass Media

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Anderson thus suggested that we could think of the nation as an '____'.
cards.back: Anderson thus suggested that we could think of the nation as an 'imagined community'.
cards.quote: Anderson thus suggested that we could think of the nation as an 'imagined community'.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India
source.section: The Beginnings of Modern Mass Media

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Where did 19th century social reformers often write and debate?
cards.back: You will recall how 19th century social reformers often wrote and debated in newspapers and journals.
cards.quote: You will recall how 19th century social reformers often wrote and debated in newspapers and journals.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India
source.section: The Beginnings of Modern Mass Media

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: What nurtured and channelised anti-colonial public opinion in India?
cards.back: Anti-colonial public opinion was nurtured and channelised by the nationalist press, which was vocal in its opposition to the oppressive measures of the colonial state.
cards.quote: Anti-colonial public opinion was nurtured and channelised by the nationalist press, which was vocal in its opposition to the oppressive measures of the colonial state.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India
source.section: The Beginnings of Modern Mass Media

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: When did the colonial government impose censorship on the nationalist press, as during the Ilbert Bill agitation?
cards.back: This led the colonial government to clamp down on the nationalist press and impose censorship, for instance during the Ilbert Bill agitation in 1883.
cards.quote: This led the colonial government to clamp down on the nationalist press and impose censorship, for instance during the Ilbert Bill agitation in 1883.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India
source.section: The Beginnings of Modern Mass Media

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Which publications of 1821 and 1822 were the first in India with a distinct nationalist and democratic approach?
cards.back: Though a few newspapers had been started by people before Raja Rammohun Roy, his Sambad-Kaumudi in Bengali published in 1821, and Mirat-Ul-Akbar in Persian published in 1822, were the first publications in India with a distinct nationalist and democratic approach.
cards.quote: Though a few newspapers had been started by people before Raja Rammohun Roy, his Sambad-Kaumudi in Bengali published in 1821, and Mirat-Ul-Akbar in Persian published in 1822, were the first publications in India with a distinct nationalist and democratic approach.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Who started the Bombay Samachar as a daily in 1822?
cards.back: Fardoonji Murzban was the pioneer of the Gujarati Press in Bombay. It was as early as 1822 that he started the Bombay Samachar as a daily.
cards.quote: Fardoonji Murzban was the pioneer of the Gujarati Press in Bombay. It was as early as 1822 that he started the Bombay Samachar as a daily.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Which Bengali paper did Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar start in 1858?
cards.back: Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar started the Shome Prakash in Bengali in 1858.
cards.quote: Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar started the Shome Prakash in Bengali in 1858.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: What comprised the range of mass media under British rule?
cards.back: Under British rule newspapers and magazines, films and radio comprised the range of mass media.
cards.quote: Under British rule newspapers and magazines, films and radio comprised the range of mass media.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India
source.section: The Beginnings of Modern Mass Media

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Who wholly owned radio under British rule?
cards.back: Radio was wholly owned by the state. National views could not be, therefore, expressed.
cards.quote: Radio was wholly owned by the state. National views could not be, therefore, expressed.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India
source.section: The Beginnings of Modern Mass Media

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: How were newspapers and films treated under the Raj?
cards.back: Newspapers and films though autonomous from the state were strictly monitored by the Raj.
cards.quote: Newspapers and films though autonomous from the state were strictly monitored by the Raj.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India
source.section: The Beginnings of Modern Mass Media

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: In independent India, Jawaharlal Nehru, the first prime minister, called upon the media to function as the ____.
cards.back: In independent India, Jawaharlal Nehru, the first prime minister, called upon the media to function as the watchdog of democracy.
cards.quote: In independent India, Jawaharlal Nehru, the first prime minister, called upon the media to function as the watchdog of democracy.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: What did the Films Division of the government produce, and where were they shown?
cards.back: The Films Division of the government produced newsreels and documentaries. These were shown before the screening of films in every movie theatre, documenting the development process as directed by the state.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: How did radio broadcasting commence in India, and what did it become in the 1940s?
cards.back: Radio broadcasting which commenced in India through amateur 'ham' broadcasting clubs in Kolkata and Chennai in the 1920s matured into a public broadcasting system in the 1940s during the World War II when it became a major instrument of propaganda for Allied forces in South-east Asia.
cards.quote: Radio broadcasting which commenced in India through amateur 'ham' broadcasting clubs in Kolkata and Chennai in the 1920s matured into a public broadcasting system in the 1940s during the World War II when it became a major instrument of propaganda for Allied forces in South-east Asia.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: How many radio stations were there at the time of independence, and whom did they cater to?
cards.back: At the time of independence there were only six radio stations located in the major cities catering primarily to an urban audience.
cards.quote: At the time of independence there were only six radio stations located in the major cities catering primarily to an urban audience.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Which campaign did All India Radio run for over 10 years from 1967?
cards.back: In the 1960s, when the high yielding varieties of food crops, as a part of the Green Revolution, were introduced for the first time in the country. It was All India Radio which undertook a major countryside campaign on these crops on a sustained day-to-day basis for over 10 years from 1967.
cards.quote: In the 1960s, when the high yielding varieties of food crops, as a part of the Green Revolution, were introduced for the first time in the country. It was All India Radio which undertook a major countryside campaign on these crops on a sustained day-to-day basis for over 10 years from 1967.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Name the three tiers of AIR's service.
cards.back:
national
regional
local
cards.quote: It operates a three-tiered -- national, regional, and local -- service to cater to India's geographic, linguistic and cultural diversity.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: What was the major constraint for the popularisation of radio initially?
cards.back: The major constraint for the popularisation of radio initially was the cost of the radio set.
cards.quote: The major constraint for the popularisation of radio initially was the cost of the radio set.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: The ____ in the 1960s made the radio more accessible by making it mobile as battery operated sets and reducing the unit price substantially.
cards.back: The transistor revolution in the 1960s made the radio more accessible by making it mobile as battery operated sets and reducing the unit price substantially.
cards.quote: The transistor revolution in the 1960s made the radio more accessible by making it mobile as battery operated sets and reducing the unit price substantially.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: How did wars and tragedies spur AIR to expand its activities?
cards.back:
The 1962 war with China prompted the launching of a 'talks' unit to put out a daily programme.
In August 1971, with the Bangladesh crisis looming, the News Service Division introduced news on the hour, from 6 o' clock in the morning to midnight.
It took another crisis, the tragic assassination of Rajeev Gandhi in 1991, for AIR to take one more step of having bulletins round the clock.
cards.quote: The 1962 war with China prompted the launching of a 'talks' unit to put out a daily programme. In August 1971, with the Bangladesh crisis looming, the News Service Division introduced news on the hour, from 6 o' clock in the morning to midnight. It took another crisis, the tragic assassination of Rajeev Gandhi in 1991, for AIR to take one more step of having bulletins round the clock.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: When was television programming introduced experimentally in India, and for what purpose?
cards.back: Television programming was introduced experimentally in India to promote rural development as early as 1959.
cards.quote: Television programming was introduced experimentally in India to promote rural development as early as 1959.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: What was SITE, and when did it broadcast?
cards.back: Later, the Satellite Instructional Television Experiment (SITE) broadcasted directly to community viewers in the rural areas of six states between August 1975 and July 1976. These instructional broadcasts were broadcast to 2,400 TV sets directly for four hours daily.
cards.quote: Later, the Satellite Instructional Television Experiment (SITE) broadcasted directly to community viewers in the rural areas of six states between August 1975 and July 1976. These instructional broadcasts were broadcast to 2,400 TV sets directly for four hours daily.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Name the four cities where Doordarshan television stations were set up by 1975.
cards.back:
Delhi
Mumbai
Srinagar
Amritsar
cards.quote: Meanwhile, television stations were set up under Doordarshan in four cities (Delhi, Mumbai, Srinagar and Amritsar) by 1975.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: What shift in target audience followed the commercialisation of television programmes?
cards.back: As programmes become commercialised and were allowed to carry advertisements of their sponsors, a shift in the target audience was evident. Entertainment programmes grew and were directed to the urban consuming class.
cards.quote: As programmes become commercialised and were allowed to carry advertisements of their sponsors, a shift in the target audience was evident. Entertainment programmes grew and were directed to the urban consuming class.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Which event saw the advent of colour broadcasting in India?
cards.back: The advent of colour broadcasting during the 1982 Asian Games in Delhi
cards.quote: The advent of colour broadcasting during the 1982 Asian Games in Delhi

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Name the soap operas and epics that earned Doordarshan substantial advertising revenue, with years.
cards.back:
Hum Log (1984–85)
Buniyaad (1986–87)
Ramayana (1987–88)
Mahabharata (1988–90)
cards.quote: It was also the time when indigenous soap operas, like Hum Log (1984–85) and Buniyaad (1986–87) were aired. They were hugely popular and attracted substantial advertising revenue for Doordarshan as did the broadcasting of the epics--Ramayana (1987–88) and Mahabharata (1988–90).

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Which was India's first long-running soap opera?
cards.back: Hum Log was India's first long-running soap opera
cards.quote: Hum Log was India's first long-running soap opera

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Which strategy did the soap opera Hum Log use to place educational content in an entertainment message?
cards.back: Hum Log was India’s first long-running soap opera… This pioneering programme utilised the entertainment-education strategy by intentionally placing educational content in this entertainment message.
cards.quote: Hum Log was India’s first long-running soap opera… This pioneering programme utilised the entertainment-education strategy by intentionally placing educational content in this entertainment message.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Name the social themes promoted by Hum Log.
cards.back:
gender equality
small family size
national integration
cards.quote: The television programme promoted social themes, such as gender equality, small family size and national integration.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Who summarised the educational lessons at the end of each Hum Log episode, and how?
cards.back: At the end of each 22-minute episode, a famous Indian actor, Ashok Kumar, summarised the educational lessons from the episode in an epilogue of 30 to 40 seconds.
cards.quote: At the end of each 22-minute episode, a famous Indian actor, Ashok Kumar, summarised the educational lessons from the episode in an epilogue of 30 to 40 seconds.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: A study of Hum Log's audience showed that a high degree of ____ occurred between the audience members and their favourite Hum Log characters.
cards.back: A study of Hum Log's audience showed that a high degree of parasocial interaction occurred between the audience members and their favourite Hum Log characters.
cards.quote: A study of Hum Log's audience showed that a high degree of parasocial interaction occurred between the audience members and their favourite Hum Log characters.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Which new consumer product did the advertising carried by Hum Log promote?
cards.back: The advertising carried by Hum Log promoted a new consumer product in India, Maggi 2-Minute noodles. The public rapidly accepted this new consumer product, suggesting the power of television commercials.
cards.quote: The advertising carried by Hum Log promoted a new consumer product in India, Maggi 2-Minute noodles. The public rapidly accepted this new consumer product, suggesting the power of television commercials.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: What was the gravest challenge the media faced after independence?
cards.back: The gravest challenge that the media faced was with the declaration of Emergency in 1975 and censorship of the media. Fortunately, the period ended and democracy was restored in 1977.
cards.quote: The gravest challenge that the media faced was with the declaration of Emergency in 1975 and censorship of the media. Fortunately, the period ended and democracy was restored in 1977.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: How does the role of the state and the market in the media vary over time?
cards.back: At some points, the state has a greater role to play. At other times the market does. In India this shift is very visible in recent times.
cards.quote: At some points, the state has a greater role to play. At other times the market does. In India this shift is very visible in recent times.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Until which decade did most media companies operate within specific domestic markets under national regulations?
cards.back: However, until the 1970s most media companies operated within specific domestic markets in accordance with regulations from national governments.
cards.quote: However, until the 1970s most media companies operated within specific domestic markets in accordance with regulations from national governments.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: How did the media industry's sectors operate until the 1970s?
cards.back: The media industry was also differentiated into distinct sectors — for the most part, cinema, print media, radio and television broadcasting all operated independently of one another.
cards.quote: The media industry was also differentiated into distinct sectors — for the most part, cinema, print media, radio and television broadcasting all operated independently of one another.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Why does the musical form lend itself to globalisation more efficiently than any other?
cards.back: It has been argued that the musical form is one that lends itself to globalisation more efficiently than any other. This is because music is able to reach people who may not know the written and spoken language.
cards.quote: It has been argued that the musical form is one that lends itself to globalisation more efficiently than any other. This is because music is able to reach people who may not know the written and spoken language.

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Why do some feel the concentrated music industry is under a great threat?
cards.back: Although the music industry is becoming ever more concentrated in the hands of a few international conglomerates, some feel that it is under a great threat. This is because the Internet allows music to be downloaded digitally, rather than purchased in the form of CDs or cassettes from local music stores.

This is because the Internet allows music to be downloaded digitally, rather than purchased in the form of CDs or cassettes from local music stores.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Did newspaper circulation in India fall as television and the Internet grew?
cards.back: It is often believed that with the growth of the television and the Internet, the print media would be sidelined. However, in India, we have seen the circulation of newspapers grow.
cards.quote: It is often believed that with the growth of the television and the Internet, the print media would be sidelined. However, in India, we have seen the circulation of newspapers grow.

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: What is the first reason for the amazing growth of Indian language newspapers?
cards.back: First, there is a rise in the number of literate people who are migrating to cities.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: What is the second reason for the growth of Indian language newspapers?
cards.back: Second, the needs of the readers in the small towns and villages are different from that of the cities and the Indian language newspapers cater to those needs.
cards.quote: Second, the needs of the readers in the small towns and villages are different from that of the cities and the Indian language newspapers cater to those needs.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Which newspapers launched the concept of local news with district and block editions?

cards.quote: Dominant Indian language newspapers such as Malayala Manorama and the Eenadu launched the concept of local news in a significant manner by introducing district and whenever necessary, block editions.

cards.back: Dina Thanthi, another leading Tamil newspaper, has always used simplified and colloquial language.

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Which languages recorded the highest growth in the Indian language newspaper revolution?

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: How do English 'national dailies' differ from vernacular newspapers in circulation?

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: How did newspapers compete with the electronic media?
cards.back: In order to compete with the electronic media, newspapers, especially English language newspapers have on the one hand reduced prices and on the other hand brought out editions from multiple centres.

use of newsmaking softwares like Newsmaker and other customised softwares

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Name the three key principles that help explain social stratification.
cards.back:
Social stratification is a characteristic of society, not simply a function of individual differences.
Social stratification persists over generations.
Social stratification is supported by patterns of belief, or ideology.
cards.quote: Three key principles help explain social stratification: 1. Social stratification is a characteristic of society, not simply a function of individual differences. Social stratification is a society-wide system that unequally distributes social resources among categories of people. In the most technologically primitive societies – hunting and gathering societies, for instance – little was produced so only rudimentary social stratification could exist. In more technologically advanced societies where people produce a surplus over and above their basic needs, however, social resources are unequally distributed to various social categories regardless of people’s innate individual abilities. 2. Social stratification persists over generations. It is closely linked to the family and to the inheritance of social resources from one generation to the next. A person’s social position is ascribed. That is, children assume the social positions of their parents. Within the caste system, birth dictates occupational opportunities. The ascribed aspect of social inequality is reinforced by the practice of endogamy. That is, marriage is usually restricted to members of the same caste, ruling out the potential for blurring caste lines through inter-caste marriage. 3. Social stratification is supported by patterns of belief, or ideology.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Social stratification persists over generations. What is it closely linked to?
cards.back: Social stratification persists over generations. It is closely linked to the family and to the inheritance of social resources from one generation to the next.
cards.quote: Social stratification persists over generations. It is closely linked to the family and to the inheritance of social resources from one generation to the next.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Within the caste system, ____ dictates occupational opportunities.
cards.back: Within the caste system, birth dictates occupational opportunities.
cards.quote: Within the caste system, birth dictates occupational opportunities.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: The ascribed aspect of social inequality is reinforced by the practice of ____.
cards.back: The ascribed aspect of social inequality is reinforced by the practice of endogamy.
cards.quote: The ascribed aspect of social inequality is reinforced by the practice of endogamy.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: No system of social stratification is likely to persist over generations unless it is widely viewed as being either fair or ____.
cards.back: No system of social stratification is likely to persist over generations unless it is widely viewed as being either fair or inevitable.
cards.quote: No system of social stratification is likely to persist over generations unless it is widely viewed as being either fair or inevitable.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: The caste system, for example, is justified in terms of the opposition of ____ and pollution
cards.back: The caste system, for example, is justified in terms of the opposition of purity and pollution
cards.quote: The caste system, for example, is justified in terms of the opposition of purity and pollution

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Who express the strongest support for systems of stratification such as caste and race?
cards.back: Typically, people with the greatest social privileges express the strongest support for systems of stratification such as caste and race.
cards.quote: Typically, people with the greatest social privileges express the strongest support for systems of stratification such as caste and race.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Name the grounds on which people often face discrimination and exclusion.
cards.back:
gender
religion
ethnicity
language
caste
disability
cards.quote: People often face discrimination and exclusion because of their gender, religion, ethnicity, language, caste and disability.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: What are prejudices?
cards.back: Prejudices refer to pre-conceived opinions or attitudes held by members of one group towards another.
cards.quote: Prejudices refer to pre-conceived opinions or attitudes held by members of one group towards another.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: What does the word ‘prejudice’ literally mean?
cards.back: The word literally means ‘pre-judgement’, that is, an opinion formed in advance of any familiarity with the subject, before considering any available evidence.
cards.quote: The word literally means ‘pre-judgement’, that is, an opinion formed in advance of any familiarity with the subject, before considering any available evidence.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Is prejudice always negative, according to NCERT?
cards.back: Prejudice may be either positive or negative.
cards.quote: Prejudice may be either positive or negative.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: What are stereotypes?
cards.back: Prejudices are often grounded in stereotypes, fixed and inflexible characterisations of a group of people.
cards.quote: Prejudices are often grounded in stereotypes, fixed and inflexible characterisations of a group of people.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: In a country such as India, which was colonised for a long time, many of these stereotypes are partly ____ creations.
cards.back: In a country such as India, which was colonised for a long time, many of these stereotypes are partly colonial creations.
cards.quote: In a country such as India, which was colonised for a long time, many of these stereotypes are partly colonial creations.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Some communities were characterised as ‘____ races’, some others as effeminate or cowardly, yet others as untrustworthy.
cards.back: Some communities were characterised as ‘martial races’, some others as effeminate or cowardly, yet others as untrustworthy.
cards.quote: Some communities were characterised as ‘martial races’, some others as effeminate or cowardly, yet others as untrustworthy.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: What is discrimination (as against prejudice)?
cards.back: If prejudice describes attitudes and opinions, discrimination refers to actual behaviour towards another group or individual.
cards.quote: If prejudice describes attitudes and opinions, discrimination refers to actual behaviour towards another group or individual.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: A person is refused a job because of their gender or religion. Which concept does this illustrate?
cards.back:
Discrimination
Discrimination can be seen in practices that disqualify members of one group from opportunities open to others, as when a person is refused a job because of their gender or religion.
cards.quote: Discrimination can be seen in practices that disqualify members of one group from opportunities open to others, as when a person is refused a job because of their gender or religion.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Discrimination can be very hard to ____ because it may not be open or explicitly stated.
cards.back: Discrimination can be very hard to prove because it may not be open or explicitly stated.
cards.quote: Discrimination can be very hard to prove because it may not be open or explicitly stated.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: What is social exclusion?
cards.back: Social exclusion refers to ways in which individuals may become cut off from full involvement in the wider society.
cards.quote: Social exclusion refers to ways in which individuals may become cut off from full involvement in the wider society.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: What does the concept of social exclusion focus attention on?
cards.back: Social exclusion refers to ways in which individuals may become cut off from full involvement in the wider society. It focuses attention on a broad range of factors that prevent individuals or groups from having opportunities open to the majority of the population.
cards.quote: Social exclusion refers to ways in which individuals may become cut off from full involvement in the wider society. It focuses attention on a broad range of factors that prevent individuals or groups from having opportunities open to the majority of the population.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Name the essential goods and services to which individuals need access for a full and active life.
cards.back:
education
health
transportation
insurance
social security
banking
access to the police or judiciary
cards.quote: In order to live a full and active life, individuals must not only be able to feed, clothe and house themselves, but should also have access to essential goods and services such as education, health, transportation, insurance, social security, banking and even access to the police or judiciary.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Social exclusion is not accidental but ____ – it is the result of structural features of society.
cards.back: Social exclusion is not accidental but systematic – it is the result of structural features of society.
cards.quote: Social exclusion is not accidental but systematic – it is the result of structural features of society.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Prejudices remain and new ones emerge. What alone is unable to transform society or produce lasting social change?
cards.back: Yet prejudices remain and often, new ones emerge. Thus, legislation alone is unable to transform society or produce lasting social change.
cards.quote: Yet prejudices remain and often, new ones emerge. Thus, legislation alone is unable to transform society or produce lasting social change.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Name the four groups on which the chapter focuses as having suffered serious social inequality and exclusion.
cards.back:
Dalits or the ex-untouchable castes
adivasis or communities refered to as ‘tribal’
women
the differently abled
cards.quote: In this chapter we focus on four such groups who have suffered from serious social inequality and exclusion, namely Dalits or the ex-untouchable castes; adivasis or communities refered to as ‘tribal’; women, and the differently abled.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: How does NCERT describe the caste system as a discriminatory system?
cards.back: The caste system is a distinct Indian social institution that legitimises and enforces practices of discrimination against people born into particular castes.
cards.quote: The caste system is a distinct Indian social institution that legitimises and enforces practices of discrimination against people born into particular castes.

source.book: Indian Society
source.section: The Caste System as a Discriminatory System

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Name the three characteristics of the practices of discrimination in the caste system.
cards.back:
humiliating
exclusionary
exploitative
cards.quote: These practices of discrimination are humiliating, exclusionary and exploitative.

source.book: Indian Society
source.section: The Caste System as a Discriminatory System

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Historically, the caste system classified people by their ____ and status.
cards.back: Historically, the caste system classified people by their occupation and status.
cards.quote: Historically, the caste system classified people by their occupation and status.

source.book: Indian Society
source.section: The Caste System as a Discriminatory System

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: In the caste system, persons born into a caste were also ‘born into’ what?
cards.back: Every caste was associated with an occupation, which meant that persons born into a particular caste were also ‘born into’ the occupation associated with their caste – they had no choice.
cards.quote: Every caste was associated with an occupation, which meant that persons born into a particular caste were also ‘born into’ the occupation associated with their caste – they had no choice.

source.book: Indian Society
source.section: The Caste System as a Discriminatory System

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: In strict scriptural terms, which caste was ritually highest but not supposed to amass wealth?
cards.back: For example, the ritually highest caste – the Brahmins – were not supposed to amass wealth, and were subordinated to the secular power of kings and rulers belonging to the Kshatriya castes.
cards.quote: For example, the ritually highest caste – the Brahmins – were not supposed to amass wealth, and were subordinated to the secular power of kings and rulers belonging to the Kshatriya castes.

source.book: Indian Society
source.section: The Caste System as a Discriminatory System

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Despite the highest secular status and power, whom was the king subordinated to in the ritual-religious sphere?
cards.back: On the other hand, despite having the highest secular status and power, the king was subordinated to the Brahmin in the ritual-religious sphere.
cards.quote: On the other hand, despite having the highest secular status and power, the king was subordinated to the Brahmin in the ritual-religious sphere.

source.book: Indian Society
source.section: The Caste System as a Discriminatory System

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: In actual historical practice, what was the correlation between caste status and economic status?
cards.back: There was thus a fairly close correlation between social (i.e. caste) status and economic status – the ‘high’ castes were almost invariably of high economic status, while the ‘low’ castes were almost always of low economic status.
cards.quote: There was thus a fairly close correlation between social (i.e. caste) status and economic status – the ‘high’ castes were almost invariably of high economic status, while the ‘low’ castes were almost always of low economic status.

source.book: Indian Society
source.section: The Caste System as a Discriminatory System

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: In modern times, and particularly since the ____ century, the link between caste and occupation has become much less rigid.
cards.back: In modern times, and particularly since the nineteenth century, the link between caste and occupation has become much less rigid.
cards.quote: In modern times, and particularly since the nineteenth century, the link between caste and occupation has become much less rigid.

source.book: Indian Society
source.section: The Caste System as a Discriminatory System

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: But – and this is the key point – the caste-class correlation is still remarkably stable at the ____ level.
cards.back: But – and this is the key point – the caste-class correlation is still remarkably stable at the macro level.
cards.quote: But – and this is the key point – the caste-class correlation is still remarkably stable at the macro level.

source.book: Indian Society
source.section: The Caste System as a Discriminatory System

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: What is ‘untouchability’?
cards.back: ‘Untouchability’ is an extreme and particularly vicious aspect of the caste system that prescribes stringent social sanctions against members of castes located at the bottom of the purity-pollution scale.
cards.quote: ‘Untouchability’ is an extreme and particularly vicious aspect of the caste system that prescribes stringent social sanctions against members of castes located at the bottom of the purity-pollution scale.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: In fact, notions of ‘____’ existed in many regions of India (particularly in the south)
cards.back: In fact, notions of ‘distance pollution’ existed in many regions of India (particularly in the south)
cards.quote: In fact, notions of ‘distance pollution’ existed in many regions of India (particularly in the south)

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Under notions of ‘distance pollution’, what besides the mere presence of an ‘untouchable’ person was considered polluting?
cards.back: In fact, notions of ‘distance pollution’ existed in many regions of India (particularly in the south) such that even the mere presence or the shadow of an ‘untouchable’ person is considered polluting.
cards.quote: In fact, notions of ‘distance pollution’ existed in many regions of India (particularly in the south) such that even the mere presence or the shadow of an ‘untouchable’ person is considered polluting.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Beyond avoidance of physical contact, what does the institution of ‘untouchability’ refer to?
cards.back: Despite the limited literal meaning of the word, the institution of ‘untouchability’ refers not just to the avoidance or prohibition of physical contact but to a much broader set of social sanctions.
cards.quote: Despite the limited literal meaning of the word, the institution of ‘untouchability’ refers not just to the avoidance or prohibition of physical contact but to a much broader set of social sanctions.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Name the three main dimensions of untouchability.
cards.back:
exclusion
humiliation-subordination
exploitation
cards.quote: It is important to emphasise that the three main dimensions of untouchability – namely, exclusion, humiliation-subordination and exploitation – are all equally important in defining the phenomenon.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Name the forms of exclusion unique to Dalits mentioned by NCERT.
cards.back:
being prohibited from sharing drinking water sources
participating in collective religious worship, social ceremonies and festivals
cards.quote: Dalits experience forms of exclusion that are unique and not practised against other groups – for instance, being prohibited from sharing drinking water sources or participating in collective religious worship, social ceremonies and festivals.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Which term did Mahatma Gandhi popularise in the 1930s for the ‘untouchables’, and what does it mean?
cards.back: Mahatma Gandhi had popularised the term ‘Harijan’ (literally, children of God) in the 1930s to counter the pejorative charge carried by caste names.
cards.quote: Mahatma Gandhi had popularised the term ‘Harijan’ (literally, children of God) in the 1930s to counter the pejorative charge carried by caste names.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Which term, coined by the ex-untouchable communities and their leaders, is now the generally accepted term for these groups?
cards.back: However, the ex-untouchable communities and their leaders have coined another term, ‘Dalit’, which is now the generally accepted term for referring to these groups.
cards.quote: However, the ex-untouchable communities and their leaders have coined another term, ‘Dalit’, which is now the generally accepted term for referring to these groups.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: What does the term Dalit literally mean?
cards.back: In Indian languages, the term Dalit literally means ‘downtrodden’ and conveys the sense of an oppressed people.
cards.quote: In Indian languages, the term Dalit literally means ‘downtrodden’ and conveys the sense of an oppressed people.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: When did the term Dalit receive wide currency?
cards.back: It received wide currency during the caste riots in Mumbai in the early 1970s.
cards.quote: It received wide currency during the caste riots in Mumbai in the early 1970s.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Which radical group that emerged in western India used the term Dalit to assert identity?
cards.back: The Dalit Panthers, a radical group that emerged in western India during that time, used the term to assert their identity as part of their struggle for rights and dignity.
cards.quote: The Dalit Panthers, a radical group that emerged in western India during that time, used the term to assert their identity as part of their struggle for rights and dignity.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: When and by whom were the ‘Schedules’ listing castes and tribes deserving special treatment drawn up?
cards.back: The ‘Schedules’ listing the castes and tribes recognised as deserving of special treatment because of the massive discrimination practiced against them were drawn up in 1935, by the British Indian government.
cards.quote: The ‘Schedules’ listing the castes and tribes recognised as deserving of special treatment because of the massive discrimination practiced against them were drawn up in 1935, by the British Indian government.

source.book: Indian Society
source.section: State and Non-State Initiatives Addressing Caste and Tribe Discrimination

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Since when have special programmes been extended to the Other Backward Classes (OBCs)?
cards.back: Among the most significant additions is the extension of special programmes to the Other Backward Classes (OBCs) since the early 1990s.
cards.quote: Among the most significant additions is the extension of special programmes to the Other Backward Classes (OBCs) since the early 1990s.

source.book: Indian Society
source.section: State and Non-State Initiatives Addressing Caste and Tribe Discrimination

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: What is the most important state initiative to compensate for past and present caste discrimination?
cards.back: The most important state initiative attempting to compensate for past and present caste discrimination is the one popularly known as ‘reservations’.
cards.quote: The most important state initiative attempting to compensate for past and present caste discrimination is the one popularly known as ‘reservations’.

source.book: Indian Society
source.section: State and Non-State Initiatives Addressing Caste and Tribe Discrimination

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: What does the policy of ‘reservations’ involve?
cards.back: This involves the setting aside of some places or ‘seats’ for members of the Scheduled Castes and Tribes in different spheres of public life.
cards.quote: This involves the setting aside of some places or ‘seats’ for members of the Scheduled Castes and Tribes in different spheres of public life.

source.book: Indian Society
source.section: State and Non-State Initiatives Addressing Caste and Tribe Discrimination

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Name the three spheres of public life in which seats are reserved for Scheduled Castes and Tribes.
cards.back:
reservation of seats in the State and Central legislatures (i.e., state assemblies, Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha)
reservation of jobs in government service across all departments and public sector companies
reservation of seats in educational institutions
cards.quote: These include reservation of seats in the State and Central legislatures (i.e., state assemblies, Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha); reservation of jobs in government service across all departments and public sector companies; and reservation of seats in educational institutions.

source.book: Indian Society
source.section: State and Non-State Initiatives Addressing Caste and Tribe Discrimination

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: The proportion of reserved seats is equal to the ____ share of the Scheduled Castes and Tribes in the total population.
cards.back: The proportion of reserved seats is equal to the percentage share of the Scheduled Castes and Tribes in the total population.
cards.quote: The proportion of reserved seats is equal to the percentage share of the Scheduled Castes and Tribes in the total population.

source.book: Indian Society
source.section: State and Non-State Initiatives Addressing Caste and Tribe Discrimination

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Which early law disallowed the curtailment of rights of citizens due solely to change of religion or caste?
cards.back: One of the earliest such laws was the Caste Disabilities Removal Act of 1850, which disallowed the curtailment of rights of citizens due solely to change of religion or caste.
cards.quote: One of the earliest such laws was the Caste Disabilities Removal Act of 1850, which disallowed the curtailment of rights of citizens due solely to change of religion or caste.

source.book: Indian Society
source.section: State and Non-State Initiatives Addressing Caste and Tribe Discrimination

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Which is the most recent law NCERT names for addressing caste inequality, and when did it become law?
cards.back: The most recent such law was the Constitution Amendment (Ninety Third Amendment) Act of 2005, which became law on 23rd January 2006.
cards.quote: The most recent such law was the Constitution Amendment (Ninety Third Amendment) Act of 2005, which became law on 23rd January 2006.

source.book: Indian Society
source.section: State and Non-State Initiatives Addressing Caste and Tribe Discrimination

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: What is the 93rd Amendment for, and what was the 1850 Act used for?
cards.back: The 93rd Amendment is for introducing reservation for the Other Backward Classes in institutions of higher education, while the 1850 Act was used to allow entry of Dalits to government schools.
cards.quote: The 93rd Amendment is for introducing reservation for the Other Backward Classes in institutions of higher education, while the 1850 Act was used to allow entry of Dalits to government schools.

source.book: Indian Society
source.section: State and Non-State Initiatives Addressing Caste and Tribe Discrimination

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: National development, particularly in the ____ era, involved the building of large dams, factories and mines.
cards.back: National development, particularly in the Nehruvian era, involved the building of large dams, factories and mines.
cards.quote: National development, particularly in the Nehruvian era, involved the building of large dams, factories and mines.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Why have tribals paid a disproportionate price for national development?
cards.back: Because the tribal areas were located in mineral rich and forest covered parts of the country, tribals have paid a disproportionate price for the development of the rest of Indian society.
cards.quote: Because the tribal areas were located in mineral rich and forest covered parts of the country, tribals have paid a disproportionate price for the development of the rest of Indian society.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Which Article of the Constitution abolished untouchability?
cards.back: The Constitution abolished untouchability (Article 17) and introduced the reservation provisions mentioned above.
cards.quote: The Constitution abolished untouchability (Article 17) and introduced the reservation provisions mentioned above.

source.book: Indian Society
source.section: State and Non-State Initiatives Addressing Caste and Tribe Discrimination

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: How has the coming of private property in land affected tribals?
cards.back: The coming of private property in land has also adversely affected tribals, whose community-based forms of collective ownership were placed at a disadvantage.
cards.quote: The coming of private property in land has also adversely affected tribals, whose community-based forms of collective ownership were placed at a disadvantage.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: What did the 1989 Prevention of Atrocities Act do?
cards.back: The 1989 Prevention of Atrocities Act revised and strengthened the legal provisions punishing acts of violence or humiliation against Dalits and adivasis.
cards.quote: The 1989 Prevention of Atrocities Act revised and strengthened the legal provisions punishing acts of violence or humiliation against Dalits and adivasis.

source.book: Indian Society
source.section: State and Non-State Initiatives Addressing Caste and Tribe Discrimination

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Which state had the tribal share of its population halved within a single decade?
cards.back: A state like Tripura had the tribal share of its population halved within a single decade, reducing them to a minority.
cards.quote: A state like Tripura had the tribal share of its population halved within a single decade, reducing them to a minority.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: The fact that legislation was passed repeatedly on this subject is proof of the fact that the law ____ cannot end a social practice.
cards.back: The fact that legislation was passed repeatedly on this subject is proof of the fact that the law alone cannot end a social practice.
cards.quote: The fact that legislation was passed repeatedly on this subject is proof of the fact that the law alone cannot end a social practice.

source.book: Indian Society
source.section: State and Non-State Initiatives Addressing Caste and Tribe Discrimination

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Which contemporary political organisations does NCERT name as examples of Dalit political assertion?
cards.back: From the pre-Independence struggles and movements launched by people like Jyotiba Phule, Iyotheedas, Periyar, Ambedkar and others (See Chapter 3) to contemporary political organisations like the Bahujan Samaj Party in Uttar Pradesh or the Dalit Sangharsh Samiti of Karnataka, Dalit political assertion has come a long way.
cards.quote: From the pre-Independence struggles and movements launched by people like Jyotiba Phule, Iyotheedas, Periyar, Ambedkar and others (See Chapter 3) to contemporary political organisations like the Bahujan Samaj Party in Uttar Pradesh or the Dalit Sangharsh Samiti of Karnataka, Dalit political assertion has come a long way.

source.book: Indian Society
source.section: State and Non-State Initiatives Addressing Caste and Tribe Discrimination

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: What is the constitutional basis of the term ‘Other Backward Classes’ (OBCs)?
cards.back: These groups – which need not be based on caste alone, but generally are identified by caste – were described as the ‘socially and educationally backward classes’. This is the constitutional basis of the popular term ‘Other Backward Classes’ (OBCs), which is in common use today.
cards.quote: These groups – which need not be based on caste alone, but generally are identified by caste – were described as the ‘socially and educationally backward classes’. This is the constitutional basis of the popular term ‘Other Backward Classes’ (OBCs), which is in common use today.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Like the category of the ‘tribe’ (see Chapter 3), the OBCs are defined ____, by what they are not.
cards.back: Like the category of the ‘tribe’ (see Chapter 3), the OBCs are defined negatively, by what they are not.
cards.quote: Like the category of the ‘tribe’ (see Chapter 3), the OBCs are defined negatively, by what they are not.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Caste has entered all the major Indian religions. It is not confined to which religion alone?
cards.back: But since caste has entered all the major Indian religions and is not confined to Hinduism alone, there are also members of other religions who belong to the backward castes and share the same traditional occupational identification and similar or worse socio-economic status.
cards.quote: But since caste has entered all the major Indian religions and is not confined to Hinduism alone, there are also members of other religions who belong to the backward castes and share the same traditional occupational identification and similar or worse socio-economic status.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: For these reasons, the OBCs are a much more ____ group than the Dalits or adivasis.
cards.back: For these reasons, the OBCs are a much more diverse group than the Dalits or adivasis.
cards.quote: For these reasons, the OBCs are a much more diverse group than the Dalits or adivasis.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Which commission, headed by whom, submitted its report on the OBCs in 1953?
cards.back: The First Backward Classes Commission headed by Kaka Kalelkar submitted its report in 1953.
cards.quote: The First Backward Classes Commission headed by Kaka Kalelkar submitted its report in 1953.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: From the mid-fifties, the OBC issue became a ____ affair pursued at the state rather than the central level.
cards.back: From the mid-fifties, the OBC issue became a regional affair pursued at the state rather than the central level.
cards.quote: From the mid-fifties, the OBC issue became a regional affair pursued at the state rather than the central level.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: The ____ states had a long history of backward caste political agitation that had started in the early twentieth century.
cards.back: The southern states had a long history of backward caste political agitation that had started in the early twentieth century.
cards.quote: The southern states had a long history of backward caste political agitation that had started in the early twentieth century.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: When did the OBC issue return to the central level?
cards.back: The OBC issue returned to the central level in the late 1970s after the Emergency when the Janata Party came to power.
cards.quote: The OBC issue returned to the central level in the late 1970s after the Emergency when the Janata Party came to power.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: When did the OBC issue become a major one in national politics?
cards.back: However, it was only in 1990, when the central government decided to implement the ten-year old Mandal Commission report, that the OBC issue became a major one in national politics.
cards.quote: However, it was only in 1990, when the central government decided to implement the ten-year old Mandal Commission report, that the OBC issue became a major one in national politics.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Since the 1990s we have seen the ____ of lower caste movements in north India, among both the OBCs and Dalits.
cards.back: Since the 1990s we have seen the resurgence of lower caste movements in north India, among both the OBCs and Dalits.
cards.quote: Since the 1990s we have seen the resurgence of lower caste movements in north India, among both the OBCs and Dalits.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: What share of the national population are the OBCs, according to recent surveys cited by NCERT?
cards.back: The politicisation of the OBCs allows them to convert their large numbers – recent surveys show that they are about 41% of the national population – into political influence.
cards.quote: The politicisation of the OBCs allows them to convert their large numbers – recent surveys show that they are about 41% of the national population – into political influence.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: What disparity within the OBCs makes them a difficult political category to work with?
cards.back: The large disparities between the upper OBCs (who are largely landed castes and enjoy dominance in rural society in many regions of India) and the lower OBCs (who are very poor and disadvantaged, and are often not very different from Dalits in socio-economic terms) make this a difficult political category to work with.
cards.quote: The large disparities between the upper OBCs (who are largely landed castes and enjoy dominance in rural society in many regions of India) and the lower OBCs (who are very poor and disadvantaged, and are often not very different from Dalits in socio-economic terms) make this a difficult political category to work with.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: In which spheres are the OBCs not under-represented?
cards.back: However, the OBCs are severely under-represented in all spheres except landholding and political representation (they have a large number of MLAs and MPs).
cards.quote: However, the OBCs are severely under-represented in all spheres except landholding and political representation (they have a large number of MLAs and MPs).

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Like the Scheduled Castes, the Scheduled Tribes are also social groups that are duly recognised by the ____ of India.
cards.back: Like the Scheduled Castes, the Scheduled Tribes are also social groups that are duly recognised by the Constitution of India.
cards.quote: Like the Scheduled Castes, the Scheduled Tribes are also social groups that are duly recognised by the Constitution of India.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: How were the jana or tribes believed to be?
cards.back: The jana or tribes were believed to be ‘people of the forest’ whose distinctive habitat in the hill and forest areas shaped their economic, social and political attributes.
cards.quote: The jana or tribes were believed to be ‘people of the forest’ whose distinctive habitat in the hill and forest areas shaped their economic, social and political attributes.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Tribal groups have had long and close association with Hindu society and culture, making the boundaries between ‘tribe’ and ‘caste’ quite ____.
cards.back: Tribal groups have had long and close association with Hindu society and culture, making the boundaries between ‘tribe’ and ‘caste’ quite porous.
cards.quote: Tribal groups have had long and close association with Hindu society and culture, making the boundaries between ‘tribe’ and ‘caste’ quite porous.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: What did the colonial government do to adivasis’ forest rights from the late nineteenth century?
cards.back: From the late nineteenth century onwards, the colonial government reserved most forest tracts for its own use, severing the rights that adivasis had long exercised to use the forest for gathering produce and for shifting cultivation.
cards.quote: From the late nineteenth century onwards, the colonial government reserved most forest tracts for its own use, severing the rights that adivasis had long exercised to use the forest for gathering produce and for shifting cultivation.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Why did capital-intensive industrialisation affect adivasi areas?
cards.back: The policy of capital-intensive industrialisation adopted by the Indian government required mineral resources and power-generation capacities which were concentrated in Adivasi areas.
cards.quote: The policy of capital-intensive industrialisation adopted by the Indian government required mineral resources and power-generation capacities which were concentrated in Adivasi areas.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: What did NCERT call the policies that displaced adivasis in the name of ‘national development’ and ‘economic growth’?
cards.back: were also a form of internal colonialism, subjugating adivasis and alienating the resources upon which they depended.
cards.quote: were also a form of internal colonialism, subjugating adivasis and alienating the resources upon which they depended.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Which dams on the Narmada and the Godavari displaced hundreds of thousands of adivasis?
cards.back: Projects such as the Sardar Sarovar dam on the river Narmada in Western India and the Polavaram dam on the river Godavari in Andhra Pradesh displaced hundreds of thousands of adivasis from their original habitats.
cards.quote: Projects such as the Sardar Sarovar dam on the river Narmada in Western India and the Polavaram dam on the river Godavari in Andhra Pradesh displaced hundreds of thousands of adivasis from their original habitats.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Dam projects like Sardar Sarovar displaced adivasis. Which 1990s policies made these processes even more powerful?
cards.back: Projects such as the Sardar Sarovar dam on the river Narmada in Western India and the Polavaram dam on the river Godavari in Andhra Pradesh displaced hundreds of thousands of adivasis from their original habitats. These processes continue to prevail and have become even more powerful since the 1990s when economic liberalisation policies were officially adopted by the Indian government.
cards.quote: Projects such as the Sardar Sarovar dam on the river Narmada in Western India and the Polavaram dam on the river Godavari in Andhra Pradesh displaced hundreds of thousands of adivasis from their original habitats. These processes continue to prevail and have become even more powerful since the 1990s when economic liberalisation policies were officially adopted by the Indian government.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Like the term Dalit, the term ____ connotes political awareness and the assertion of rights.
cards.back: Like the term Dalit, the term Adivasi connotes political awareness and the assertion of rights.
cards.quote: Like the term Dalit, the term Adivasi connotes political awareness and the assertion of rights.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: What does ‘Adivasi’ literally mean, and when was the term coined?
cards.back: Literally meaning ‘original inhabitants’, the term was coined in the 1930s as part of the struggle against the intrusion by the colonial government and outside settlers and moneylenders.
cards.quote: Literally meaning ‘original inhabitants’, the term was coined in the 1930s as part of the struggle against the intrusion by the colonial government and outside settlers and moneylenders.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Name the shared experiences that being Adivasi is about.
cards.back:
the loss of forests
the alienation of land
repeated displacements since Independence in the name of ‘development projects’
cards.quote: Being Adivasi is about shared experiences of the loss of forests, the alienation of land, repeated displacements since Independence in the name of ‘development projects’ and much more.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: What are outsiders called in the tribal groups’ struggles?
cards.back: many tribal groups have been waging struggles against outsiders (called ‘dikus’) and the state.
cards.quote: many tribal groups have been waging struggles against outsiders (called ‘dikus’) and the state.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Which statehood achievements are the most significant of post-Independence Adivasi movements?
cards.back: In post-Independence India, the most significant achievements of Adivasi movements include the attainment of statehood for Jharkhand and Chattisgarh, which were originally part of Bihar and Madhya Pradesh respectively.
cards.quote: In post-Independence India, the most significant achievements of Adivasi movements include the attainment of statehood for Jharkhand and Chattisgarh, which were originally part of Bihar and Madhya Pradesh respectively.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Adivasi struggle vs Dalit struggle: the difference on territory.
cards.back: In this respect adivasis and their struggles are different from the Dalit struggle because, unlike Dalits, adivasis were concentrated in contiguous areas and could demand states of their own.
cards.quote: In this respect adivasis and their struggles are different from the Dalit struggle because, unlike Dalits, adivasis were concentrated in contiguous areas and could demand states of their own.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Though gender inequality is often treated as natural, what have scholars shown the inequalities between men and women to be?
cards.back: Because of the obvious biological and physical differences between men and women, gender inequality is often treated as natural. However, despite appearances, scholars have shown that the inequalities between men and women are social rather than natural.
cards.quote: Because of the obvious biological and physical differences between men and women, gender inequality is often treated as natural. However, despite appearances, scholars have shown that the inequalities between men and women are social rather than natural.

source.book: Indian Society
source.section: Struggle for women’s equality and rights

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: ____ is thus also a form of social inequality and exclusion like caste and class, but with its own specific features.
cards.back: Gender is thus also a form of social inequality and exclusion like caste and class, but with its own specific features.
cards.quote: Gender is thus also a form of social inequality and exclusion like caste and class, but with its own specific features.

source.book: Indian Society
source.section: Struggle for women’s equality and rights

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: The women’s question arose in modern India as part of the ____ century middle class social reform movements.
cards.back: The women’s question arose in modern India as part of the nineteenth century middle class social reform movements.
cards.quote: The women’s question arose in modern India as part of the nineteenth century middle class social reform movements.

source.book: Indian Society
source.section: Struggle for women’s equality and rights

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Why are the nineteenth century social reform movements on the women’s question often termed middle class reform movements?
cards.back: The women’s question arose in modern India as part of the nineteenth century middle class social reform movements. The nature of these movements varied from region to region. They are often termed as middle class reform movements because many of these reformers were from the newly emerging western educated Indian middle class.
cards.quote: The women’s question arose in modern India as part of the nineteenth century middle class social reform movements. The nature of these movements varied from region to region. They are often termed as middle class reform movements because many of these reformers were from the newly emerging western educated Indian middle class.

source.book: Indian Society
source.section: Struggle for women’s equality and rights

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Name the reform movements and leaders NCERT draws from for women’s rights.
cards.back:
the anti-sati campaign led by Raja Rammohun Roy in Bengal
the widow remarriage movement in the Bombay Presidency where Ranade was one of the leading reformers
Jyotiba Phule’s simultaneous attack on caste and gender oppression
the social reform movement in Islam led by Sir Syed Ahmed Khan
cards.quote: We draw from the anti-sati campaign led by Raja Rammohun Roy in Bengal, the widow remarriage movement in the Bombay Presidency where Ranade was one of the leading reformers, from Jyotiba Phule’s simultaneous attack on caste and gender oppression, and from the social reform movement in Islam led by Sir Syed Ahmed Khan.

source.book: Indian Society
source.section: Struggle for women’s equality and rights

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Which campaign did Raja Rammohun Roy undertake a decade before establishing the Brahmo Samaj in 1828?
cards.back: A decade before establishing the Brahmo Samaj in 1828, Roy undertook the campaign against ‘sati’ which was the first women’s issue to receive public attention.
cards.quote: A decade before establishing the Brahmo Samaj in 1828, Roy undertook the campaign against ‘sati’ which was the first women’s issue to receive public attention.

source.book: Indian Society
source.section: Struggle for women’s equality and rights

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Rammohun Roy’s ideas represented a curious mixture of Western ____ and an assertion of Indian traditionality.
cards.back: Rammohun Roy’s ideas represented a curious mixture of Western rationality and an assertion of Indian traditionality.
cards.quote: Rammohun Roy’s ideas represented a curious mixture of Western rationality and an assertion of Indian traditionality.

source.book: Indian Society
source.section: Struggle for women’s equality and rights

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: On what basis did Rammohun Roy attack the practice of sati?
cards.back: Rammohun thus attacked the practice of sati on the basis of both appeals to humanitarian and natural rights doctrines as well as Hindu shastras.
cards.quote: Rammohun thus attacked the practice of sati on the basis of both appeals to humanitarian and natural rights doctrines as well as Hindu shastras.

source.book: Indian Society
source.section: Struggle for women’s equality and rights

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: The deplorable and unjust treatment of the Hindu upper caste ____ was a major issue taken up by the social reformers.
cards.back: The deplorable and unjust treatment of the Hindu upper caste widows was a major issue taken up by the social reformers.
cards.quote: The deplorable and unjust treatment of the Hindu upper caste widows was a major issue taken up by the social reformers.

source.book: Indian Society
source.section: Struggle for women’s equality and rights

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Jotiba Phule came from a socially excluded caste and his attack was directed against both caste and ____ discrimination.
cards.back: Jotiba Phule came from a socially excluded caste and his attack was directed against both caste and gender discrimination.
cards.quote: Jotiba Phule came from a socially excluded caste and his attack was directed against both caste and gender discrimination.

source.book: Indian Society
source.section: Struggle for women’s equality and rights

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Which samaj did Jotiba Phule found, with its primary emphasis on ‘truth seeking’?
cards.back: He founded the Satyashodak Samaj with its primary emphasis on ‘truth seeking’.
cards.quote: He founded the Satyashodak Samaj with its primary emphasis on ‘truth seeking’.

source.book: Indian Society
source.section: Struggle for women’s equality and rights

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Which two groups did Phule’s first practical social reform efforts aim to aid?
cards.back: Phule’s first practical social reform efforts were to aid the two groups considered lowest in traditional Brahmin culture: women and untouchables.
cards.quote: Phule’s first practical social reform efforts were to aid the two groups considered lowest in traditional Brahmin culture: women and untouchables.

source.book: Indian Society
source.section: Struggle for women’s equality and rights

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: What kind of education for girls did Sir Syed Ahmed Khan want?
cards.back: He wanted girls to be educated, but within the precincts of their homes.
cards.quote: He wanted girls to be educated, but within the precincts of their homes.

source.book: Indian Society
source.section: Struggle for women’s equality and rights

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: What curriculum did Sir Syed Ahmed Khan and Dayanand Saraswati seek for women’s education?
cards.back: Like Dayanand Saraswati of the Arya Samaj, he stood for women’s education but sought for a curriculum that included instruction in religious principles, training in the arts of housekeeping and handicrafts and rearing of children.
cards.quote: Like Dayanand Saraswati of the Arya Samaj, he stood for women’s education but sought for a curriculum that included instruction in religious principles, training in the arts of housekeeping and handicrafts and rearing of children.

source.book: Indian Society
source.section: Struggle for women’s equality and rights

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Which two books written by women does NCERT cite, and in which years were they written?
cards.back: To learn how wrong both these assumptions are, read the following extracts from two books written by women, Stree Purush Tulana written in 1882 and Sultana’s Dream written in 1905.
cards.quote: To learn how wrong both these assumptions are, read the following extracts from two books written by women, Stree Purush Tulana written in 1882 and Sultana’s Dream written in 1905.

source.book: Indian Society
source.section: Struggle for women’s equality and rights

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Who wrote Stree Purush Tulana (or Comparison of Men and Women), and as a protest against what?
cards.back: Stree Purush Tulana (or Comparison of Men and Women) was written by a Maharashtrian housewife, Tarabai Shinde, as a protest against the double standards of a male dominated society.
cards.quote: Stree Purush Tulana (or Comparison of Men and Women) was written by a Maharashtrian housewife, Tarabai Shinde, as a protest against the double standards of a male dominated society.

source.book: Indian Society
source.section: Struggle for women’s equality and rights

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Sultana’s Dream (1905) is described as probably the earliest example of what in India?
cards.back: This remarkable short story is probably the earliest example of science fiction writing in India, and among the first by a woman author anywhere in the world.
cards.quote: This remarkable short story is probably the earliest example of science fiction writing in India, and among the first by a woman author anywhere in the world.

source.book: Indian Society
source.section: Struggle for women’s equality and rights

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: What did the Karachi Session of the Indian National Congress issue in 1931?
cards.back: In 1931, the Karachi Session of the Indian National Congress issued a declaration on the Fundamental Rights of Citizenship in India whereby it committed itself to women’s equality.
cards.quote: In 1931, the Karachi Session of the Indian National Congress issued a declaration on the Fundamental Rights of Citizenship in India whereby it committed itself to women’s equality.

source.book: Indian Society
source.section: Struggle for women’s equality and rights

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: The franchise shall be on the basis of universal adult ____.
cards.back: The franchise shall be on the basis of universal adult suffrage.
cards.quote: The franchise shall be on the basis of universal adult suffrage.

source.book: Indian Society
