source.section: Struggle for women’s equality and rights

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Two decades after Independence, women’s issues re-emerged in the ____.
cards.back: Two decades after Independence, women’s issues re-emerged in the 1970s.
cards.quote: Two decades after Independence, women’s issues re-emerged in the 1970s.

source.book: Indian Society
source.section: Struggle for women’s equality and rights

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Women’s issues: 19th-century reform vs the 1970s: the difference on emphasis.
cards.back: In the nineteenth century reform movements, the emphasis had been on the backward aspects of tradition like sati, child marriage, or the ill treatment of widows. In the 1970s, the emphasis was on ‘modern’ issues – the representation of women in popular media, and the gendered consequences of unequal development.
cards.quote: In the nineteenth century reform movements, the emphasis had been on the backward aspects of tradition like sati, child marriage, or the ill treatment of widows. In the 1970s, the emphasis was on ‘modern’ issues – the representation of women in popular media, and the gendered consequences of unequal development.

source.book: Indian Society
source.section: Struggle for women’s equality and rights

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Why was the law a major site for reform in the 1980s and after?
cards.back: The law was a major site for reform in the 1980s and after, specially when it was discovered that many laws of concern to women had not been changed since the 19th century.
cards.quote: The law was a major site for reform in the 1980s and after, specially when it was discovered that many laws of concern to women had not been changed since the 19th century.

source.book: Indian Society
source.section: Struggle for women’s equality and rights

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: What does NCERT name as one of the new challenges of gender inequality?
cards.back: The sharp fall in the child sex ratio and the implicit social bias against the girl child represents one of the new challenges of gender inequality.
cards.quote: The sharp fall in the child sex ratio and the implicit social bias against the girl child represents one of the new challenges of gender inequality.

source.book: Indian Society
source.section: Struggle for women’s equality and rights

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Besides being physically or mentally ‘impaired’, why are the differently abled ‘disabled’?
cards.back: The differently abled are not ‘disabled’ only because they are physically or mentally ‘impaired’ but also because society is built in a manner that does not cater to their needs.
cards.quote: The differently abled are not ‘disabled’ only because they are physically or mentally ‘impaired’ but also because society is built in a manner that does not cater to their needs.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: In contrast to the struggles over Dalit, adivasi or women’s rights, the rights of the disabled have been recognised only very ____.
cards.back: In contrast to the struggles over Dalit, adivasi or women’s rights, the rights of the disabled have been recognised only very recently.
cards.quote: In contrast to the struggles over Dalit, adivasi or women’s rights, the rights of the disabled have been recognised only very recently.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Which scholar compares the invisibility of the disabled to Ralph Ellison’s Invisible Man?
cards.back: One of the leading activists and scholars of disability in the Indian context, Anita Ghai, argues that this invisibility of the disabled can be compared to the Invisible Man of Ralph Ellison.
cards.quote: One of the leading activists and scholars of disability in the Indian context, Anita Ghai, argues that this invisibility of the disabled can be compared to the Invisible Man of Ralph Ellison.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Name the common features of the public perception of ‘disability’ all over the world.
cards.back:
Disability is understood as a biological given.
Whenever a disabled person is confronted with problems, it is taken for granted that the problems originate from her/his impairment.
The disabled person is seen as a victim.
Disability is supposed to be linked with the disabled individual’s self perception.
The very idea of disability suggests that they are in need of help.
cards.quote: Here are some common features central to the public perception of ‘diability’ all over the world — Disability is understood as a biological given. Whenever a disabled person is confronted with problems, it is taken for granted that the problems originate from her/his impairment. The disabled person is seen as a victim. Disability is supposed to be linked with the disabled individual’s self perception. The very idea of disability suggests that they are in need of help.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: In a culture that looks up to bodily ‘perfection’, all deviations from the ‘perfect body’ signify ____, defect and distortion.
cards.back: In a culture that looks up to bodily ‘perfection’, all deviations from the ‘perfect body’ signify abnormality, defect and distortion.
cards.quote: In a culture that looks up to bodily ‘perfection’, all deviations from the ‘perfect body’ signify abnormality, defect and distortion.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Labels such as ____ (poor thing) accentuate the victim status for the disabled person.
cards.back: Labels such as bechara (poor thing) accentuate the victim status for the disabled person.
cards.quote: Labels such as bechara (poor thing) accentuate the victim status for the disabled person.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: The common perception views disability as retribution for past ____ (actions) from which there can be no reprieve.
cards.back: The common perception views disability as retribution for past karma (actions) from which there can be no reprieve.
cards.quote: The common perception views disability as retribution for past karma (actions) from which there can be no reprieve.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: The dominant cultural construction in India therefore looks at disability as essentially a characteristic of the ____.
cards.back: The dominant cultural construction in India therefore looks at disability as essentially a characteristic of the individual.
cards.quote: The dominant cultural construction in India therefore looks at disability as essentially a characteristic of the individual.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Which terms came to replace ‘retarded’, ‘crippled’ and ‘lame’?
cards.back: Terms such as ‘mentally challenged’, ‘visually impaired’ and ‘physically impaired’ came to replace the more trite negative terms such as ‘retarded’, ‘crippled’ or ‘lame’.
cards.quote: Terms such as ‘mentally challenged’, ‘visually impaired’ and ‘physically impaired’ came to replace the more trite negative terms such as ‘retarded’, ‘crippled’ or ‘lame’.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: The disabled are rendered disabled not because they are biologically disabled but because ____ renders them so.
cards.back: The disabled are rendered disabled not because they are biologically disabled but because society renders them so.
cards.quote: The disabled are rendered disabled not because they are biologically disabled but because society renders them so.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: There is a close relationship between disability and ____.
cards.back: There is a close relationship between disability and poverty.
cards.quote: There is a close relationship between disability and poverty.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Name the factors that contribute to a higher incidence of disability among poor people.
cards.back:
Malnutrition
mothers weakened by frequent childbirth
inadequate immunisation programmes
accidents in overcrowded homes
cards.quote: Malnutrition, mothers weakened by frequent childbirth, inadequate immunisation programmes, accidents in overcrowded homes, all contribute to an incidence of disability among poor people

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: How does disability create and exacerbate poverty?
cards.back: Furthermore, disability creates and exacerbates poverty by increasing isolation and economic strain, not just for the individual but for the family; there is little doubt that disabled people are among the poorest in poor countries.
cards.quote: Furthermore, disability creates and exacerbates poverty by increasing isolation and economic strain, not just for the individual but for the family; there is little doubt that disabled people are among the poorest in poor countries.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: How many types of disabilities did Census 2011 try to collect information on, against how many in Census 2001?
cards.back: Attempt was made to collect information on eight types of disabilities as against five in Census 2001.
cards.quote: Attempt was made to collect information on eight types of disabilities as against five in Census 2001.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Significantly, efforts to redress the situation have come from the disabled ____.
cards.back: Significantly, efforts to redress the situation have come from the disabled themselves.
cards.quote: Significantly, efforts to redress the situation have come from the disabled themselves.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: How do educational practices continue to marginalise the issue of disability?
cards.back: This is evident from the historical practices within the educational system that continue to marginalise the issue of disability by maintaining two separate streams – one for disabled students and one for everyone else.
cards.quote: This is evident from the historical practices within the educational system that continue to marginalise the issue of disability by maintaining two separate streams – one for disabled students and one for everyone else.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Which four categories does NCERT examine as generating and perpetuating inequalities and exclusion?
cards.back:
caste
tribe
gender
disability
cards.quote: In this chapter we have looked at caste, tribe, gender and disability as institutions that generate and perpetuate inequalities and exclusion.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Which categories does NCERT say still need attention?
cards.back: But there remain categories that are still in need of attention, such as those who are marginalised by religion or by a combination of categories.
cards.quote: But there remain categories that are still in need of attention, such as those who are marginalised by religion or by a combination of categories.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Which report on the Muslim community does NCERT cite for groups defined by religion and caste, gender and religion, or caste and region?
cards.back: More complex formations like groups defined by religion and caste, gender and religion, or caste and region are likely to claim our attention in the near future, as shown, for example, by the Sachar Committee Report on the Muslim community.
cards.quote: More complex formations like groups defined by religion and caste, gender and religion, or caste and region are likely to claim our attention in the near future, as shown, for example, by the Sachar Committee Report on the Muslim community.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: With which region is caste uniquely associated, per NCERT?
cards.back: Caste is an institution uniquely associated with the Indian sub-continent.
cards.quote: Caste is an institution uniquely associated with the Indian sub-continent.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.note: Similar arrangements exist elsewhere, but the exact form of caste is found only in the Indian sub-continent.

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Caste is characteristic of Hindu society; to which non-Hindu communities has it spread?
cards.back: Although it is an institution characteristic of Hindu society, caste has spread to the major non-Hindu communities of the Indian sub-continent. This is specially true of Muslims, Christians and Sikhs.
cards.quote: Although it is an institution characteristic of Hindu society, caste has spread to the major non-Hindu communities of the Indian sub-continent. This is specially true of Muslims, Christians and Sikhs.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: By which two terms is caste referred to in Indian languages, beginning with Sanskrit?
cards.back: The word refers to a broad institutional arrangement that in Indian languages (beginning with the ancient Sanskrit) is referred to by two distinct terms, varna and jati.
cards.quote: The word refers to a broad institutional arrangement that in Indian languages (beginning with the ancient Sanskrit) is referred to by two distinct terms, varna and jati.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: What is varna?
cards.back: Varna, literally ‘colour’, is the name given to a four-fold division of society into brahmana, kshatriya, vaishya and shudra, though this excludes a significant section of the population composed of the ‘outcastes’, foreigners, slaves, conquered peoples and others, sometimes refered to as the panchamas or fifth category.
cards.quote: Varna, literally ‘colour’, is the name given to a four-fold division of society into brahmana, kshatriya, vaishya and shudra, though this excludes a significant section of the population composed of the ‘outcastes’, foreigners, slaves, conquered peoples and others, sometimes refered to as the panchamas or fifth category.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.note: Varna means colour: the four-fold division into brahmana, kshatriya, vaishya and shudra; outcastes were left out.

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: What is jati?
cards.back: Jati is a generic term referring to species or kinds of anything, ranging from inanimate objects to plants, animals and human beings.
cards.quote: Jati is a generic term referring to species or kinds of anything, ranging from inanimate objects to plants, animals and human beings.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Varna vs jati: the most common interpretation of their relationship.
cards.back: The most common interpretation is to treat varna as a broad all-India aggregative classification, while jati is taken to be a regional or local sub-classification involving a much more complex system consisting of hundreds or even thousands of castes and sub-castes.
cards.quote: The most common interpretation is to treat varna as a broad all-India aggregative classification, while jati is taken to be a regional or local sub-classification involving a much more complex system consisting of hundreds or even thousands of castes and sub-castes.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: How old is the four varna classification, roughly, per NCERT?
cards.back: It is generally agreed though, that the four varna classification is roughly three thousand years old.
cards.quote: It is generally agreed though, that the four varna classification is roughly three thousand years old.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: What was the caste system in its earliest phase, the late Vedic period (roughly 900 — 500 BC)?
cards.back: In its earliest phase, in the late Vedic period roughly between 900 — 500 BC, the caste system was really a varna system and consisted of only four major divisions.
cards.quote: In its earliest phase, in the late Vedic period roughly between 900 — 500 BC, the caste system was really a varna system and consisted of only four major divisions.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: How rigid were the early divisions of the varna system, and could people move between them?
cards.back: These divisions were not very elaborate or very rigid, and they were not determined by birth. Movement across the categories seems to have been not only possible but quite common.
cards.quote: These divisions were not very elaborate or very rigid, and they were not determined by birth. Movement across the categories seems to have been not only possible but quite common.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: In which period did caste become the rigid institution that is familiar to us from well known definitions?
cards.back: It is only in the post-Vedic period that caste became the rigid institution that is familiar to us from well known definitions.
cards.quote: It is only in the post-Vedic period that caste became the rigid institution that is familiar to us from well known definitions.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Name the six most commonly cited defining features of caste.
cards.back:
Caste is determined by birth
Membership in a caste involves strict rules about marriage.
Caste membership also involves rules about food and food-sharing.
Caste involves a system consisting of many castes arranged in a hierarchy of rank and status.
Castes also involve sub-divisions within themselves
Castes were traditionally linked to occupations.
cards.quote: The most commonly cited defining features of caste are the following: 1. Caste is determined by birth – a child is “born into” the caste of its parents. Caste is never a matter of choice. One can never change one’s caste, leave it, or choose not to join it, although there are instances where a person may be expelled from their caste. 2. Membership in a caste involves strict rules about marriage. Caste groups are “endogamous”, i.e. marriage is restricted to members of the group. 3. Caste membership also involves rules about food and food-sharing. What kinds of food may or may not be eaten is prescribed and who one may share food with is also specified. 4. Caste involves a system consisting of many castes arranged in a hierarchy of rank and status. In theory, every person has a caste, and every caste has a specified place in the hierarchy of all castes. While the hierarchical position of many castes, particularly in the middle ranks, may vary from region to region, there is always a hierarchy. 5. Castes also involve sub-divisions within themselves, i.e., castes almost always have sub-castes and sometimes sub-castes may also have sub-castes. This is referred to as a segmental organisation. 6. Castes were traditionally linked to occupations. A person born into a caste could only practice the occupation associated with that caste, so that occupations were hereditary, i.e. passed on from generation to generation.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Caste is determined by ____ – a child is “born into” the caste of its parents.
cards.back: Caste is determined by birth – a child is “born into” the caste of its parents.
cards.quote: Caste is determined by birth – a child is “born into” the caste of its parents.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Caste groups are “____”, i.e. marriage is restricted to members of the group.
cards.back: Caste groups are “endogamous”, i.e. marriage is restricted to members of the group.
cards.quote: Caste groups are “endogamous”, i.e. marriage is restricted to members of the group.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Caste membership also involves rules about food and ____.
cards.back: Caste membership also involves rules about food and food-sharing.
cards.quote: Caste membership also involves rules about food and food-sharing.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: What is a segmental organisation of castes?
cards.back: Castes also involve sub-divisions within themselves, i.e., castes almost always have sub-castes and sometimes sub-castes may also have sub-castes. This is referred to as a segmental organisation.
cards.quote: Castes also involve sub-divisions within themselves, i.e., castes almost always have sub-castes and sometimes sub-castes may also have sub-castes. This is referred to as a segmental organisation.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: What did the traditional link between caste and occupation mean for a person born into a caste?
cards.back: A person born into a caste could only practice the occupation associated with that caste, so that occupations were hereditary, i.e. passed on from generation to generation.
cards.quote: A person born into a caste could only practice the occupation associated with that caste, so that occupations were hereditary, i.e. passed on from generation to generation.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: The caste system combines which two sets of principles?
cards.back:
difference and separation
wholism and hierarchy
cards.quote: the combination of two sets of principles, one based on difference and separation and the other on wholism and hierarchy.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: The hierarchical ordering of castes is based on the distinction between ‘____’ and ‘____’.
cards.back: The hierarchical ordering of castes is based on the distinction between ‘purity’ and ‘pollution’.
cards.quote: The hierarchical ordering of castes is based on the distinction between ‘purity’ and ‘pollution’.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: What do historians believe happened to those who were defeated in wars, in caste terms?
cards.back: Historians believe that those who were defeated in wars were often assigned low caste status.
cards.quote: Historians believe that those who were defeated in wars were often assigned low caste status.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Besides being unequal in ritual terms, how are castes supposed to relate to each other?
cards.back: Finally, castes are not only unequal to each other in ritual terms, they are also supposed to be complementary and non-competing groups.
cards.quote: Finally, castes are not only unequal to each other in ritual terms, they are also supposed to be complementary and non-competing groups.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Since caste is also linked with occupation, the system functions as the ____, except that, in principle, it allows no mobility.
cards.back: Since caste is also linked with occupation, the system functions as the social division of labour, except that, in principle, it allows no mobility.
cards.quote: Since caste is also linked with occupation, the system functions as the social division of labour, except that, in principle, it allows no mobility.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: In fact, some scholars argue that what we know today as caste is more a product of ____ than of ancient Indian tradition.
cards.back: In fact, some scholars argue that what we know today as caste is more a product of colonialism than of ancient Indian tradition.
cards.quote: In fact, some scholars argue that what we know today as caste is more a product of colonialism than of ancient Indian tradition.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Which official effort was most important in collecting information on caste, and from when was it regular?
cards.back: But by far the most important official effort to collect information on caste was through the census. First begun in the 1860s, the census became a regular ten-yearly exercise conducted by the British Indian government from 1881 onwards.
cards.quote: But by far the most important official effort to collect information on caste was through the census. First begun in the 1860s, the census became a regular ten-yearly exercise conducted by the British Indian government from 1881 onwards.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Why was the 1901 Census under Herbert Risley particularly important for caste?
cards.back: The 1901 Census under the direction of Herbert Risley was particularly important as it sought to collect information on the social hierarchy of caste – i.e., the social order of precedence in particular regions, as to the position of each caste in the rank order.
cards.quote: The 1901 Census under the direction of Herbert Risley was particularly important as it sought to collect information on the social hierarchy of caste – i.e., the social order of precedence in particular regions, as to the position of each caste in the rank order.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: What did the counting and recording of caste do to caste identities, per NCERT?
cards.back: Before this kind of intervention, caste identities had been much more fluid and less rigid; once they began to be counted and recorded, caste began to take on a new life.
cards.quote: Before this kind of intervention, caste identities had been much more fluid and less rigid; once they began to be counted and recorded, caste began to take on a new life.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Which Act gave legal recognition to the ‘schedules’ of castes and tribes, and what terms came from it?
cards.back: It was as part of these efforts that the Government of India Act of 1935 was passed which gave legal recognition to the lists or ‘schedules’ of castes and tribes marked out for special treatment by the state. This is how the terms ‘Scheduled Tribes’ and the ‘Scheduled Castes’ came into being.
cards.quote: It was as part of these efforts that the Government of India Act of 1935 was passed which gave legal recognition to the lists or ‘schedules’ of castes and tribes marked out for special treatment by the state. This is how the terms ‘Scheduled Tribes’ and the ‘Scheduled Castes’ came into being.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Both Mahatma Gandhi and Babasaheb Ambedkar began organising protests against untouchability from the ____ onwards.
cards.back: Both Mahatma Gandhi and Babasaheb Ambedkar began organising protests against untouchability from the 1920s onwards.
cards.quote: Both Mahatma Gandhi and Babasaheb Ambedkar began organising protests against untouchability from the 1920s onwards.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: The dominant view in the nationalist movement was to treat caste as a ____ and as a ____ to divide Indians.
cards.back: The dominant view in the nationalist movement was to treat caste as a social evil and as a colonial ploy to divide Indians.
cards.quote: The dominant view in the nationalist movement was to treat caste as a social evil and as a colonial ploy to divide Indians.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Who took the initiative to organise the ‘depressed classes’, and which reformers does NCERT name?
cards.back: This was an initiative taken from both ends of the caste spectrum – by upper caste progressive reformers as well as by members of the lower castes such as Mahatma Jotiba Phule and Babasaheb Ambedkar in western India, Ayyankali, Sri Narayana Guru, Iyotheedass and Periyar (E.V. Ramaswamy Naickar) in the South.
cards.quote: This was an initiative taken from both ends of the caste spectrum – by upper caste progressive reformers as well as by members of the lower castes such as Mahatma Jotiba Phule and Babasaheb Ambedkar in western India, Ayyankali, Sri Narayana Guru, Iyotheedass and Periyar (E.V. Ramaswamy Naickar) in the South.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: What did the state assume would happen if it operated in a caste-blind manner?
cards.back: At yet another level, the state assumed that if it operated in a caste-blind manner, this would automatically lead to the undermining of caste based privileges and the eventual abolition of the institution.
cards.quote: At yet another level, the state assumed that if it operated in a caste-blind manner, this would automatically lead to the undermining of caste based privileges and the eventual abolition of the institution.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: ____ and the conditions of collective living in the cities made it difficult for the caste-segregated patterns of social interaction to survive.
cards.back: Urbanisation and the conditions of collective living in the cities made it difficult for the caste-segregated patterns of social interaction to survive.
cards.quote: Urbanisation and the conditions of collective living in the cities made it difficult for the caste-segregated patterns of social interaction to survive.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: ____, or the practice of marrying within the caste, remained largely unaffected by modernisation and change.
cards.back: Endogamy, or the practice of marrying within the caste, remained largely unaffected by modernisation and change.
cards.quote: Endogamy, or the practice of marrying within the caste, remained largely unaffected by modernisation and change.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Perhaps, the most eventful and important sphere of change has been that of ____.
cards.back: Perhaps, the most eventful and important sphere of change has been that of politics.
cards.quote: Perhaps, the most eventful and important sphere of change has been that of politics.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Since the ____ we have also seen the emergence of explicitly caste-based political parties.
cards.back: Since the 1980s we have also seen the emergence of explicitly caste-based political parties.
cards.quote: Since the 1980s we have also seen the emergence of explicitly caste-based political parties.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Which two common concepts were contributed by M.N. Srinivas?
cards.back: Perhaps the most common of these are ‘sanskritisation’ and ‘dominant caste’, both contributed by M.N. Srinivas, but discussed extensively and criticised by other scholars.
cards.quote: Perhaps the most common of these are ‘sanskritisation’ and ‘dominant caste’, both contributed by M.N. Srinivas, but discussed extensively and criticised by other scholars.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: What is a ‘dominant caste’?
cards.back: ‘Dominant caste’ is a term used to refer to those castes which had a large population and were granted land rights by the partial land reforms effected after Independence.
cards.quote: ‘Dominant caste’ is a term used to refer to those castes which had a large population and were granted land rights by the partial land reforms effected after Independence.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Name the examples of dominant castes that NCERT gives.
cards.back:
the Yadavs of Bihar and Uttar Pradesh
the Vokkaligas of Karnataka
the Reddys and Khammas of Andhra Pradesh
the Marathas of Maharashtra
the Jats of Punjab, Haryana and Western Uttar Pradesh
the Patidars of Gujarat
cards.quote: Examples of such dominant castes include the Yadavs of Bihar and Uttar Pradesh, the Vokkaligas of Karnataka, the Reddys and Khammas of Andhra Pradesh, the Marathas of Maharashtra, the Jats of Punjab, Haryana and Western Uttar Pradesh and the Patidars of Gujarat.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: What paradoxical change has come to caste for the upper caste, urban middle and upper classes?
cards.back: One of the most significant yet paradoxical changes in the caste system in the contemporary period is that it has tended to become ‘invisible’ for the upper caste, urban middle and upper classes.
cards.quote: One of the most significant yet paradoxical changes in the caste system in the contemporary period is that it has tended to become ‘invisible’ for the upper caste, urban middle and upper classes.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: For the scheduled castes and tribes and the backward castes, what has happened to the visibility of caste?
cards.back: For the scheduled castes and tribes and the backward castes – the opposite has happened. For them, caste has become all too visible, indeed their caste has tended to eclipse the other dimensions of their identities.
cards.quote: For the scheduled castes and tribes and the backward castes – the opposite has happened. For them, caste has become all too visible, indeed their caste has tended to eclipse the other dimensions of their identities.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: For the scheduled castes and tribes and the backward castes, which policies serve as their lifelines?
cards.back: The policies of reservation and other forms of protective discrimination instituted by the state in response to political pressure serve as their lifelines.
cards.quote: The policies of reservation and other forms of protective discrimination instituted by the state in response to political pressure serve as their lifelines.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: What did the efforts of Ayyankali, a Kerala leader of the lower castes and Dalits, achieve?
cards.back: Ayyankali, born in Kerala, was a leader of the lower castes and Dalits. With his efforts, Dalits got the freedom to walk on public roads, and Dalit children were allowed to join schools.
cards.quote: Ayyankali, born in Kerala, was a leader of the lower castes and Dalits. With his efforts, Dalits got the freedom to walk on public roads, and Dalit children were allowed to join schools.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: In 1873, which society did Jotirao Govindrao Phule found, and for what?
cards.back: In 1873 he founded the Satyashodhak Samaj (Truth Seekers Society), which was devoted to securing human rights and social justice for low-caste people.
cards.quote: In 1873 he founded the Satyashodhak Samaj (Truth Seekers Society), which was devoted to securing human rights and social justice for low-caste people.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Who was the first headmistress of the country’s first school for girls, in Pune?
cards.back: Savitri Bai Phule was the first headmistress of the country’s first school for girls in Pune. She devoted her life to educating Shudras and Ati-Shudras.
cards.quote: Savitri Bai Phule was the first headmistress of the country’s first school for girls in Pune. She devoted her life to educating Shudras and Ati-Shudras.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Which watchwords did Sri Narayana Guru give?
cards.back: Sri Narayana Guru, born in Kerala, preached brotherhood for all and fought against the ill effects of the caste system. He led a quiet but significant social revolution and gave the watchwords ‘One Caste, One Religion, One God for all men’.
cards.quote: Sri Narayana Guru, born in Kerala, preached brotherhood for all and fought against the ill effects of the caste system. He led a quiet but significant social revolution and gave the watchwords ‘One Caste, One Religion, One God for all men’.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Which book by M. N. Srinivas is one of the best known village studies in Social Anthropology?
cards.back: Mysore Narasimhachar Srinivas was one of India’s foremost sociologists and social anthropologists. He was known for his works on the caste system and terms such as ‘sanskritisation’ and ‘dominant caste’. His book The Remembered Village is one of the best known village studies in Social Anthropology.
cards.quote: Mysore Narasimhachar Srinivas was one of India’s foremost sociologists and social anthropologists. He was known for his works on the caste system and terms such as ‘sanskritisation’ and ‘dominant caste’. His book The Remembered Village is one of the best known village studies in Social Anthropology.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: What is a ‘tribe’, according to NCERT?
cards.back: ‘Tribe’ is a modern term for communities that are very old, being among the oldest inhabitants of the sub-continent.
cards.quote: ‘Tribe’ is a modern term for communities that are very old, being among the oldest inhabitants of the sub-continent.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Tribes in India were generally defined by what they were not. Name the three things.
cards.back:
did not practice a religion with a written text
did not have a state or political form of the normal kind
did not have sharp class divisions
cards.quote: Tribes were communities that did not practice a religion with a written text; did not have a state or political form of the normal kind and did not have sharp class divisions.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: In terms of positive characteristics, tribes have been classified according to their ‘____’ and ‘____’ traits.
cards.back: In terms of positive characteristics, tribes have been classified according to their ‘permanent’ and ‘acquired’ traits.
cards.quote: In terms of positive characteristics, tribes have been classified according to their ‘permanent’ and ‘acquired’ traits.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: What share of the tribal population lives in ‘middle India’?
cards.back: About 85% of the tribal population lives in ‘middle India’, a wide band stretching from Gujarat and Rajasthan in the west to West Bengal and Odisha in the east, with Madhya Pradesh, Jharkhand, Chattisgarh and parts of Maharashtra and Andhra Pradesh forming the heart of this region.
cards.quote: About 85% of the tribal population lives in ‘middle India’, a wide band stretching from Gujarat and Rajasthan in the west to West Bengal and Odisha in the east, with Madhya Pradesh, Jharkhand, Chattisgarh and parts of Maharashtra and Andhra Pradesh forming the heart of this region.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Which states have the highest concentrations of tribals in the state population?
cards.back: If we look at the share of tribals in the state population, then the North Eastern states have the highest concentrations, with all states, except Assam, having concentrations of more than 30%, and some, like Arunachal Pradesh, Meghalaya, Mizoram and Nagaland with more than 60% and upto 95% of tribal population.
cards.quote: If we look at the share of tribals in the state population, then the North Eastern states have the highest concentrations, with all states, except Assam, having concentrations of more than 30%, and some, like Arunachal Pradesh, Meghalaya, Mizoram and Nagaland with more than 60% and upto 95% of tribal population.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Into which four language categories are tribes categorised?
cards.back:
Indo-Aryan
Dravidian
Austric
Tibeto-Burman
cards.quote: In terms of language, tribes are categorised into four categories. Two of them, Indo-Aryan and Dravidian, are shared by the rest of the Indian population as well, and tribes account for only about 1% of the former and about 3% of the latter. The other two language groups, the Austric and Tibeto-Burman, are primarily spoken by tribals, who account for all of the first and over 80% of the second group.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Under which categories are tribes classified in physical-racial terms?
cards.back:
Negrito
Australoid
Mongoloid
Dravidian
Aryan
cards.quote: In physical-racial terms, tribes are classified under the Negrito, Australoid, Mongoloid, Dravidian and Aryan categories.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Which two main criteria do classifications based on acquired traits use?
cards.back:
mode of livelihood
extent of incorporation into Hindu society
cards.quote: Classifications based on acquired traits use two main criteria – mode of livelihood, and extent of incorporation into Hindu society – or a combination of the two.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: In classifying tribes by acquired traits, what is the dominant classification in sociology and public affairs?
cards.back: However, the dominant classification both in academic sociology as well as in politics and public affairs is the degree of assimilation into Hindu society.
cards.quote: However, the dominant classification both in academic sociology as well as in politics and public affairs is the degree of assimilation into Hindu society.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: What did those who saw tribes as one end of a continuum with caste-based peasant society argue?
cards.back: Those who argued for the continuum saw tribes as not being fundamentally different from caste-peasant society, but merely less stratified (fewer levels of hierarchy) and with a more community-based rather than individual notion of resource ownership.
cards.quote: Those who argued for the continuum saw tribes as not being fundamentally different from caste-peasant society, but merely less stratified (fewer levels of hierarchy) and with a more community-based rather than individual notion of resource ownership.

source.book: Indian Society
source.section: Tribe – The Career of a Concept

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Tribe vs caste: the cultural difference behind the argument for a tribe-caste distinction.
cards.back: In short, the argument for a tribe-caste distinction was founded on an assumed cultural difference between Hindu castes, with their beliefs in purity and pollution and hierarchical integration, and ‘animist’ tribals with their more egalitarian and kinship based modes of social organisation.
cards.quote: In short, the argument for a tribe-caste distinction was founded on an assumed cultural difference between Hindu castes, with their beliefs in purity and pollution and hierarchical integration, and ‘animist’ tribals with their more egalitarian and kinship based modes of social organisation.

source.book: Indian Society
source.section: Tribe – The Career of a Concept

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: The tribe-peasantry distinction did not hold in terms of which commonly advanced criteria?
cards.back:
size
isolation
religion
means of livelihood
cards.quote: It was pointed out that the tribe-peasantry distinction did not hold in terms of any of the commonly advanced criteria: size, isolation, religion, and means of livelihood.

source.book: Indian Society
source.section: Tribe – The Career of a Concept

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: How do some scholars say tribes should really be seen, instead of as “pristine” societies?
cards.back: They propose instead that tribes should really be seen as “secondary” phenomena arising out of the exploitative and colonialist contact between pre-existing states and non-state groups like the tribals.
cards.quote: Some scholars have also argued that there is no coherent basis for treating tribes as “pristine” – i.e., original or pure – societies uncontaminated by civilisation. They propose instead that tribes should really be seen as “secondary” phenomena arising out of the exploitative and colonialist contact between pre-existing states and non-state groups like the tribals.

source.book: Indian Society
source.section: Tribe – The Career of a Concept

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: How are tribal identities formed today, according to NCERT?
cards.back: Tribal identities today are formed by this interactional process rather than any primordial (orginal, ancient) characteristics peculiar to tribes.
cards.quote: Tribal identities today are formed by this interactional process rather than any primordial (orginal, ancient) characteristics peculiar to tribes.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Why are many tribal identities today centred on resistance and opposition?
cards.back: Because the interaction with the mainstream has generally been on terms unfavourable to the tribal communities, many tribal identities today are centred on ideas of resistance and opposition to the overwhelming force of the non-tribal world.
cards.quote: Because the interaction with the mainstream has generally been on terms unfavourable to the tribal communities, many tribal identities today are centred on ideas of resistance and opposition to the overwhelming force of the non-tribal world.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Another significant development is the gradual emergence of an ____ among tribal communities.
cards.back: Another significant development is the gradual emergence of an educated middle class among tribal communities.
cards.quote: Another significant development is the gradual emergence of an educated middle class among tribal communities.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Which two broad sets of issues have been most important in giving rise to tribal movements?
cards.back:
issues relating to control over vital economic resources like land and specially forests
issues relating to matters of ethnic-cultural identity
cards.quote: Two broad sets of issues have been most important in giving rise to tribal movements. These are issues relating to control over vital economic resources like land and specially forests, and issues relating to matters of ethnic-cultural identity.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: In itself, how can a family be defined? (NCERT's three pairs)
cards.back:
nuclear or extended
male-headed or female-headed
matrilineal or patrilineal
cards.quote: In itself a family can be defined as nuclear or extended. It can be male-headed or female-headed. The line of descent can be matrilineal or patrilineal.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: The family (the ____ sphere) is linked to the economic, political, cultural, and educational (the ____) spheres.
cards.back: The family (the private sphere) is linked to the economic, political, cultural, and educational (the public) spheres.
cards.quote: The family (the private sphere) is linked to the economic, political, cultural, and educational (the public) spheres.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: How can the migration of men from Himalayan villages change family structure?
cards.back: Thus the migration of men from the villages of the Himalayan region can lead to an unusual proportion of women-headed families in the village.
cards.quote: Thus the migration of men from the villages of the Himalayan region can lead to an unusual proportion of women-headed families in the village.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: In what two ways do changes in family structures occur?
cards.back:
accidentally, as when a war takes place or people migrate in search of work
purposely brought about, as when young people decide to choose their spouses instead of letting elders decide
cards.quote: Sometimes these changes occur accidentally, as when a war takes place or people migrate in search of work. Sometimes these changes are purposely brought about, as when young people decide to choose their spouses instead of letting elders decide.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: What is a nuclear family?
cards.back: A nuclear family consists of only one set of parents and their children.
cards.quote: A nuclear family consists of only one set of parents and their children.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: What is an extended family (commonly known as the ‘joint family’)?
cards.back: An extended family (commonly known as the ‘joint family’) can take different forms, but has more than one couple, and often more than two generations, living together.
cards.quote: An extended family (commonly known as the ‘joint family’) can take different forms, but has more than one couple, and often more than two generations, living together.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Is the extended family the dominant form in India, now or earlier?
cards.back: Yet this is by no means the dominant form now or earlier. It was confined to certain sections and certain regions of the community.
cards.quote: Yet this is by no means the dominant form now or earlier. It was confined to certain sections and certain regions of the community.

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Whose observation is this: ‘joint family’ is not the translation of any Indian word?
cards.back: As I.P. Desai observes, “The expression ‘joint family’ is not the translation of any Indian word like that. It is interesting to note that the words used for joint family in most of the Indian languages are the equivalents of translations of the English word ‘joint family’.”
cards.quote: As I.P. Desai observes, “The expression ‘joint family’ is not the translation of any Indian word like that. It is interesting to note that the words used for joint family in most of the Indian languages are the equivalents of translations of the English word ‘joint family’.”

source.book: Indian Society

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Matrilocal vs patrilocal: the difference on rule of residence.
cards.back: With regard to the rule of residence, some societies are matrilocal in their marriage and family customs while others are patrilocal. In the first case, the newly married couple stays with the woman’s parents, whereas in the second case the couple lives with the man’s parents.
cards.quote: With regard to the rule of residence, some societies are matrilocal in their marriage and family customs while others are patrilocal. In the first case, the newly married couple stays with the woman’s parents, whereas in the second case the couple lives with the man’s parents.

source.book: Indian Society
source.section: The Diverse Forms of the Family

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Matrilineal vs patrilineal societies: the difference on rules of inheritance.
cards.back: With regard to the rules of inheritance, matrilineal societies pass on property from mother to daughter while patrilineal societies do so from father to son.
cards.quote: With regard to the rules of inheritance, matrilineal societies pass on property from mother to daughter while patrilineal societies do so from father to son.

source.book: Indian Society
source.section: The Diverse Forms of the Family

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Patriarchal family structure vs matriarchy: who holds authority?
cards.back: A patriarchal family structure exists where the men exercise authority and dominance, and matriarchy where the women play a similarly dominant role.
cards.quote: A patriarchal family structure exists where the men exercise authority and dominance, and matriarchy where the women play a similarly dominant role.

source.book: Indian Society
source.section: The Diverse Forms of the Family

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Matriliny vs matriarchy: the difference (NCERT).
cards.back: There is no historical or anthropological evidence of matriarchy – i.e., societies where women exercise dominance. However, there do exist matrilineal societies, i.e., societies where women inherit property from their mothers but do not exercise control over it, nor are they the decision makers in public affairs.
cards.quote: There is no historical or anthropological evidence of matriarchy – i.e., societies where women exercise dominance. However, there do exist matrilineal societies, i.e., societies where women inherit property from their mothers but do not exercise control over it, nor are they the decision makers in public affairs.

source.book: Indian Society
source.section: The Diverse Forms of the Family

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: What does a social movement require, and against whom is its action often directed?
cards.back: A social movement requires sustained collective action over time. Such action is often directed against the state and takes the form of demanding changes in state policy or practice.
cards.quote: A social movement requires sustained collective action over time. Such action is often directed against the state and takes the form of demanding changes in state policy or practice.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Name the defining features of a social movement.
cards.back:
sustained collective action over time
often directed against the state and takes the form of demanding changes in state policy or practice
some degree of organisation
shared objectives and ideologies
a general orientation or way of approaching to bring about (or to prevent) change
cards.quote: A social movement requires sustained collective action over time. Such action is often directed against the state and takes the form of demanding changes in state policy or practice. Spontaneous, disorganised protest cannot be called a social movement either. Collective action must be marked by some degree of organisation. This organisation may include a leadership and a structure that defines how members relate to each other, make decisions and carry them out. Those participating in a social movement also have shared objectives and ideologies. A social movement has a general orientation or way of approaching to bring about (or to prevent) change.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: What may the organisation that marks a social movement's collective action include?
cards.back: Collective action must be marked by some degree of organisation. This organisation may include a leadership and a structure that defines how members relate to each other, make decisions and carry them out.
cards.quote: Collective action must be marked by some degree of organisation. This organisation may include a leadership and a structure that defines how members relate to each other, make decisions and carry them out.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: While social movements seek to bring in social change, ____ sometimes arise in defence of ____.
cards.back: While social movements seek to bring in social change, counter movements sometimes arise in defence of status quo.
cards.quote: While social movements seek to bring in social change, counter movements sometimes arise in defence of status quo.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Which body did defenders of sati form against Raja Rammohun Roy's campaign (a counter movement)?
cards.back: When Raja Rammohun Roy campaigned against sati and formed the Brahmo Samaj, defenders of sati formed Dharma Sabha and petitioned the British not to legislate against sati.
cards.quote: When Raja Rammohun Roy campaigned against sati and formed the Brahmo Samaj, defenders of sati formed Dharma Sabha and petitioned the British not to legislate against sati.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Social movements cannot change society easily. Since it goes against both ____ and values, there is bound to be opposition and resistance.
cards.back: Social movements cannot change society easily. Since it goes against both entrenched interests and values, there is bound to be opposition and resistance.
cards.quote: Social movements cannot change society easily. Since it goes against both entrenched interests and values, there is bound to be opposition and resistance.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: While ____ is the most visible form of collective action, a social movement also acts in other, equally important ways.
cards.back: While protest is the most visible form of collective action, a social movement also acts in other, equally important ways.
cards.quote: While protest is the most visible form of collective action, a social movement also acts in other, equally important ways.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Gandhi adopted novel ways such as ahimsa, satyagraha and his use of the ____ in the freedom movement.
cards.back: Gandhi adopted novel ways such as ahimsa, satyagraha and his use of the charkha in the freedom movement.
cards.quote: Gandhi adopted novel ways such as ahimsa, satyagraha and his use of the charkha in the freedom movement.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Which legendary march to make salt protested British taxation policies on basic commodities?
cards.back: The legendary Dandi March to make salt was a protest against British taxation policies that placed a huge burden on the consumers of basic commodities in order to benefit the empire.
cards.quote: The legendary Dandi March to make salt was a protest against British taxation policies that placed a huge burden on the consumers of basic commodities in order to benefit the empire.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Gandhi took items of everyday mass consumption like ____, and transformed them into symbols of resistance.
cards.back: Gandhi took items of everyday mass consumption like cloth and salt, and transformed them into symbols of resistance.
cards.quote: Gandhi took items of everyday mass consumption like cloth and salt, and transformed them into symbols of resistance.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Sanskritisation and westernisation are social changes; what does NCERT call the 19th century reformers' efforts?
cards.back: To draw from our discussion in Chapter 2, we can view sanskritisation and westernisation as social changes and see the 19th century social reformers' efforts to change the society as social movements.
cards.quote: To draw from our discussion in Chapter 2, we can view sanskritisation and westernisation as social changes and see the 19th century social reformers' efforts to change the society as social movements.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India
source.section: Distinguishing Social Change and Social Movements

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Types of social movements.
cards.back:
redemptive or transformatory
reformist
revolutionary
cards.quote: There are different kinds of social movements. They can be classified as: (i) redemptive or transformatory; (ii) reformist; and (iii) revolutionary.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: What is a redemptive (transformatory) social movement?
cards.back: A redemptive social movement aims to bring about a change in the personal consciousness and actions of its individual members.
cards.quote: A redemptive social movement aims to bring about a change in the personal consciousness and actions of its individual members.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: What are reformist social movements?
cards.back: Reformist social movements strive to change the existing social and political arrangements through gradual, incremental steps.
cards.quote: Reformist social movements strive to change the existing social and political arrangements through gradual, incremental steps.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: What are revolutionary social movements?
cards.back: Revolutionary social movements attempt to radically transform social relations, often by capturing state power.
cards.quote: Revolutionary social movements attempt to radically transform social relations, often by capturing state power.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: The Ezhava community of Kerala led by Narayana Guru: which type of social movement is this?
cards.back: A redemptive social movement aims to bring about a change in the personal consciousness and actions of its individual members. For instance, people in the Ezhava community in Kerala were led by Narayana Guru to change their social practices.
cards.quote: A redemptive social movement aims to bring about a change in the personal consciousness and actions of its individual members. For instance, people in the Ezhava community in Kerala were led by Narayana Guru to change their social practices.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Name NCERT's two examples of reformist movements.
cards.back: The 1960s movement for the reorganisation of Indian states on the basis of language and the recent Right to Information campaign are examples of reformist movements.
cards.quote: The 1960s movement for the reorganisation of Indian states on the basis of language and the recent Right to Information campaign are examples of reformist movements.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Name NCERT's two examples of revolutionary movements.
cards.back: The Bolshevik revolution in Russia that deposed the Tsar to create a communist state and the Naxalite movement in India that seeks to remove oppressive landlords and state officials can be described as revolutionary movements.
cards.quote: The Bolshevik revolution in Russia that deposed the Tsar to create a communist state and the Naxalite movement in India that seeks to remove oppressive landlords and state officials can be described as revolutionary movements.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: What do social scientists call the move of a movement from mass mobilisation towards becoming more institutionalised?
cards.back: A movement may start from a phase of mass mobilisation and collective protest to become more institutionalised. Social scientists who study the life cycles of social movements call this a move towards ‘social movement organisations’.
cards.quote: A movement may start from a phase of mass mobilisation and collective protest to become more institutionalised. Social scientists who study the life cycles of social movements call this a move towards ‘social movement organisations’.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: For instance, what was a 'mutiny' or 'rebellion' for British colonial rulers in 1857 was 'the ____' for Indian nationalists.
cards.back: For instance, what was a 'mutiny' or 'rebellion' for British colonial rulers in 1857 was 'the first war of Independence' for Indian nationalists.
cards.quote: For instance, what was a 'mutiny' or 'rebellion' for British colonial rulers in 1857 was 'the first war of Independence' for Indian nationalists.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: The old social movements clearly saw ____ as a central goal.
cards.back: The old social movements clearly saw reorganisation of power relations as a central goal.
cards.quote: The old social movements clearly saw reorganisation of power relations as a central goal.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: The old social movements functioned within the frame of ____.
cards.back: The old social movements functioned within the frame of political parties.
cards.quote: The old social movements functioned within the frame of political parties.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: What were the 'new' social movements about, rather than changing the distribution of power in society?
cards.back: So the ‘new’ social movements were not about changing the distribution of power in society but about quality-of-life issues such as having a clean environment.
cards.quote: So the ‘new’ social movements were not about changing the distribution of power in society but about quality-of-life issues such as having a clean environment.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: To what does Rajni Kothari attribute the surge of social movements in India in the 1970s?
cards.back: Political scientist Rajni Kothari attributes the surge of social movements in India in the 1970s to people's growing dissatisfaction with parliamentary democracy.
cards.quote: Political scientist Rajni Kothari attributes the surge of social movements in India in the 1970s to people's growing dissatisfaction with parliamentary democracy.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Kothari argues that the institutions of the state have been captured by ____.
cards.back: Kothari argues that the institutions of the state have been captured by elites.
cards.quote: Kothari argues that the institutions of the state have been captured by elites.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: People left out by the formal political system join social movements or ____ in order to put pressure on the state from outside.
cards.back: People left out by the formal political system join social movements or non-party political formations in order to put pressure on the state from outside.
cards.quote: People left out by the formal political system join social movements or non-party political formations in order to put pressure on the state from outside.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: What does NCERT say the term civil society refers to today?
cards.back: Today, the broader term of civil society is used to refer to both old social movements represented by political parties and trade unions and to new non-governmental organisations, women's groups, environmental groups and tribal activists.
cards.quote: Today, the broader term of civil society is used to refer to both old social movements represented by political parties and trade unions and to new non-governmental organisations, women's groups, environmental groups and tribal activists.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Which alliance, in which old and new movements work together, has raised awareness about the hazards of globalisation?
cards.back: What is significant, however, is that the old and new movements are working together in new alliances such as the World Social Forum that have been raising awareness about the hazards of globalisation.
cards.quote: What is significant, however, is that the old and new movements are working together in new alliances such as the World Social Forum that have been raising awareness about the hazards of globalisation.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Which elements are essential in creating social movements and difficult to trace to class-based inequality?
cards.back: Identity politics, cultural anxieties and aspirations are essential elements in creating social movements and occur in ways that are difficult to trace to class-based inequality.
cards.quote: Identity politics, cultural anxieties and aspirations are essential elements in creating social movements and occur in ways that are difficult to trace to class-based inequality.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Which movement does NCERT cite as uniting urban middle-class feminists and poor peasant women?
cards.back: Often, these social movements unite participants across class boundaries. For instance, the women's movement includes urban, middle-class feminists as well as poor peasant women.
cards.quote: Often, these social movements unite participants across class boundaries. For instance, the women's movement includes urban, middle-class feminists as well as poor peasant women.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: What has the model of development, demanding greater exploitation of resources, been critiqued for assuming?
cards.back: This model of development has also been critiqued for assuming that all sections of people will be beneficiaries of development.
cards.quote: This model of development has also been critiqued for assuming that all sections of people will be beneficiaries of development.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Which book of Ramachandra Guha does NCERT cite for the Chipko Movement, and what did villagers rally to save?
cards.back: According to Ramachandra Guha in his book, Unquiet Woods, villagers rallied together to save the oak and rhododendron forests near their villages.
cards.quote: According to Ramachandra Guha in his book, Unquiet Woods, villagers rallied together to save the oak and rhododendron forests near their villages.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: What did villagers, including many women, do in the Chipko Movement to prevent trees from being felled?
cards.back: When government forest contractors came to cut down the trees, villagers, including large number of women, stepped forward to hug the trees to prevent their being felled.
cards.quote: When government forest contractors came to cut down the trees, villagers, including large number of women, stepped forward to hug the trees to prevent their being felled.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: The economy of ____ was pitted against the economy of ____.
cards.back: The economy of subsistence was pitted against the economy of profit.
cards.quote: The economy of subsistence was pitted against the economy of profit.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Cutting down natural forests was a form of environmental destruction that had resulted in devastating ____ in the region.
cards.back: Cutting down natural forests was a form of environmental destruction that had resulted in devastating floods and landslides in the region.
cards.quote: Cutting down natural forests was a form of environmental destruction that had resulted in devastating floods and landslides in the region.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: What concerns underlay the Chipko Movement?
cards.back: So, concerns about economy, ecology and political representation underlay the Chipko Movement.
cards.quote: So, concerns about economy, ecology and political representation underlay the Chipko Movement.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Which cooperative organisation took up the villagers' cause in the Chipko Movement?
cards.back: The villagers' cause was taken up by the Dashauli Gram Swaraja Sangh (DGSS), a cooperative organisation based in Chamoli district.
cards.quote: The villagers' cause was taken up by the Dashauli Gram Swaraja Sangh (DGSS), a cooperative organisation based in Chamoli district.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Who was the head of the village Mahila Mandal (Women's Club) at Reni in the Chipko Movement?
cards.back: A small girl who spied the workers with their implements rushed to Gaura Devi, the head of the village Mahila Mandal (Women's Club).
cards.quote: A small girl who spied the workers with their implements rushed to Gaura Devi, the head of the village Mahila Mandal (Women's Club).

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: What were the Bardoli Satyagraha (1928) and the Champaran Satyagraha (1917–18)?
cards.back: For instance, the Bardoli Satyagraha (1928, Surat District) a 'non-tax' campaign as part of the nationwide non-cooperation movement, a campaign of refusal to pay land revenue and the Champaran Satyagraha (1917–18) directed against indigo plantations.
cards.quote: For instance, the Bardoli Satyagraha (1928, Surat District) a 'non-tax' campaign as part of the nationwide non-cooperation movement, a campaign of refusal to pay land revenue and the Champaran Satyagraha (1917–18) directed against indigo plantations.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Which was the first peasant organisation founded between 1920 and 1940, and what came in 1936?
cards.back: Between 1920 and 1940 peasant organisations arose. The first organisation to be founded was the Bihar Provincial Kisan Sabha (1929), and in 1936 the All India Kisan Sabha.
cards.quote: Between 1920 and 1940 peasant organisations arose. The first organisation to be founded was the Bihar Provincial Kisan Sabha (1929), and in 1936 the All India Kisan Sabha.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Which two classical peasant movements does NCERT name at the time of Independence, with dates?
cards.back: At the time of Independence, we had the two most classical cases of peasant movements, namely the Tebhaga movement (1946–47) and the Telangana movement (1946–51).
cards.quote: At the time of Independence, we had the two most classical cases of peasant movements, namely the Tebhaga movement (1946–47) and the Telangana movement (1946–51).

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: What did the Tebhaga movement's sharecroppers struggle for?
cards.back: The first was a struggle of sharecroppers in Bengal in North Bihar for two thirds share of their produce instead of the customary half.
cards.quote: The first was a struggle of sharecroppers in Bengal in North Bihar for two thirds share of their produce instead of the customary half.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Against what was the Telangana movement directed, and who led it?
cards.back: The second was directed against the feudal conditions in the princely state of Hyderabad and was led by the CPI.
cards.quote: The second was directed against the feudal conditions in the princely state of Hyderabad and was led by the CPI.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Where and when did the new farmers' movements begin?
cards.back: New farmer's movements began in the 1970s in Punjab and Tamil Nadu.
cards.quote: New farmer's movements began in the 1970s in Punjab and Tamil Nadu.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: New farmers' movements vs peasant movements: who do the new movements involve, and what are farmers said to be?
cards.back: These movements were regionally oganised, were non-party, and involved farmers rather than peasants (farmers are said to be market-involved as both commodity producers and purchasers).
cards.quote: These movements were regionally oganised, were non-party, and involved farmers rather than peasants (farmers are said to be market-involved as both commodity producers and purchasers).

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Name NCERT's examples of the 'price and related issues' demanded by new farmers' movements.
cards.back:
price procurement
remunerative prices
prices for agricultural inputs
taxation
non-repayment of loans
cards.quote: The focus of demand were 'price and related issues' (for example, price procurement, remunerative prices, prices for agricultural inputs, taxation, non-repayment of loans).

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Why can the farmers' movements be seen as part of the worldwide 'new social movements'?
cards.back: It has been argued that the farmers’ movements have broadened their agenda and ideology and include environment and women’s issues. Therefore, they can be seen as a part of the worldwide ‘new social movements’.
cards.quote: It has been argued that the farmers’ movements have broadened their agenda and ideology and include environment and women’s issues. Therefore, they can be seen as a part of the worldwide ‘new social movements’.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Factory production began in India in the early part of the ____.
cards.back: Factory production began in India in the early part of the 1860s.
cards.quote: Factory production began in India in the early part of the 1860s.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: In which port towns were India's early factories established?
cards.back: These factories were, thus established in the port towns of Calcutta (Kolkata) and Bombay (Mumbai).
cards.quote: These factories were, thus established in the port towns of Calcutta (Kolkata) and Bombay (Mumbai).

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: In the early stages of colonialism, ____ as the colonial government did not regulate either wages or working conditions.
cards.back: In the early stages of colonialism, labour was very cheap as the colonial government did not regulate either wages or working conditions.
cards.quote: In the early stages of colonialism, labour was very cheap as the colonial government did not regulate either wages or working conditions.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Who established the first trade union in India, where and when?
cards.back: The first trade union was established in April 1918 in Madras by B.P. Wadia, a social worker and member of the Theosophical Society.
cards.quote: The first trade union was established in April 1918 in Madras by B.P. Wadia, a social worker and member of the Theosophical Society.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Which union did Mahatma Gandhi found in 1918?
cards.back: During the same year, Mahatma Gandhi founded the Textile Labour Association (TLA).
cards.quote: During the same year, Mahatma Gandhi founded the Textile Labour Association (TLA).

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: When and where was the All India Trade Union Congress (AITUC) formed?
cards.back: In 1920, the All India Trade Union Congress (AITUC) was formed in Bombay.
cards.quote: In 1920, the All India Trade Union Congress (AITUC) was formed in Bombay.

source.book: Social Change and Development in India

cards.subject: sociology
cards.front: Name the main ideological groups in the AITUC and their leaders.
cards.back:
the communists led by S.A. Dange and M.N. Roy
the moderates led by M. Joshi and V.V. Giri
the nationalist movements which involved people like Lala Lajpat Rai and Jawaharlal Nehru
